case_source: From the judgment and order dated March 24, 1977 passed by the High Court Division In Civil Revision No. 928 of 1973
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—This appeal by special leave is from a judgment and order of the High Court Division dated March 24, 1977 allowing pre-emption under section 96 of East Bengal State Acquisition and Tenancy Act on setting aside order of Subordinate Judge and revering that of the Munsif in Miscellaneous case No. 214 of 1970.

2. Respondent No.1 filed the Misc. case for pre-emption of a land sold under a Kabala dated 18-6-70 alleging that he was a co-sharer of the land but was not given any notice of the transfer to a stranger. The transferee; who is the appellant here, contested the application contending, among, other things, that the application suffered from defect of parties in that a number of co-sharers by inheritance were not impleaded in the application for pre-emotion. The learned Munsif infected this contention holding that the omission of certain persons as referred to in section 96(2) was not fatal to the proceeding and allowed the pre-emption. On appeal the learned Subordinate lodge found that a number of co-sharers by inheritance were notes pleaded even after objection was taken by the pre-emptee at the earliest opportunity and held that this nova joinder of parts was fatal to the proceeding and on such findings reversed the Munsif's order. In revision under section 115, Civil Procedure Code the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division relying upon the decision of this Division in Motilal Sikdar Vs. Binodini Dasi 28 DLR (AD) 5 held that the cleft out co-sharers were not necessary parties as they got no subsisting interests in the land transferred end as such the defect of parties was not fatal to the proceeding.

3. In this appeal the question raised is whether in the light of the decision in Motilal Sikdar's case as clarified by a subsequent decision in the case of Abdus Samad vs. Sohrab A. (1981) 33 DLR (AD) 113 the High Court Division was well founded in law to hold that the left out co-sharers of the pre-emptor had no subsisting right of pre-emption and as such the non-joinder of parties was not fatal to tire proceeding.

4. Determination of the question involved in this case depends upon the  correct interpretation of section 96 (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, This section provides that in application for pre-emption made by a co-sharers  all other co-shares shall be made parties. This provision of law came up for consideration of this Division in the two cases referred to above. In both these cases there were defects of parties by omission of certain co-sharers or contiguous land holders, but in the former case the defect of parties was held to be not fatal to the proceeding, whereas in the latter case, the defect of party’s watt held to be fatal to the proceeding for pre-emption. Section 96(2) reads thus:

"In an application made under sub-section (1) by a co-sharer tenant or co-sharer tenants, all other co-sharer tenants of the holding and the transferee shall be mace parties and in such an appellation made by a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred, all the co sharer tenants of the holding and all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land referred and the transferee shall be made parties."

5. On Interpreting section 96(2) in the background of facts of the former case namely, Motilal Sikdar vs. Benodini Dasi this Division held:

"It does not appear from a perusal of the provision of section 96 that it was the intent of the legislature that the penalty for non-impleading a person as contemplated in subsection (2) is the invalidity of the order which may ultimately be made in the said proceeding. The question whether a person it a necessary party under sub-section (2) is a question of fact and the object of this provision seems to provide the co-sharer tenants and the holders of the contiguous lands with the opportunity of availing of the provision of the said subsection. Since the benefit conferred under the said provisions is meant for certain individuals; they can very well be waived. In that view of the matter the positive injunction contained in the said sub-section as to the making of parties in spite of its being couched in mandatory language should be read as directory”.

6. And in the other ease newly Samad vs. Sohrab Ali, this Division on consideration of the facts of that case held:

"The right of pre-emption as provided under sub-section (1) of section 96 is a statutory right To give full effect to the statutory provision, all the necessary parties must be impleaded, because, relief cannot be give in the absence of such party Object of sub-section (2) is to have all the co-sharer tenants or all the tenants holding lands contiguous to the land transferred before the Court for proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. A co-sharer tenant or a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred may waive his right to purchase the land, but on this consideration there is hardly any scope for taking the view that requirement of sub-section (2) is not mandatory but is merely directory." '

7. These two decisions may appear to be rather inconsistent, but a close examination will show that there is no inconsistency if these decisions are considered against the facts of the respective cases. That is why in the later case of Abdus Samad vs. Sohrab Ali it was observed that the opinion expressed in the judgment of Motilal Sikder's case that the positive injunction contained in sub-section (2) of section 96 as to making parties is to be read as directory and not mandatory as its language indicates, is limited to the particular facts of that case. The distinction between the two decisions may be better appreciated if the facts of these cases are examined.

8. In the case of Motilal Sikder pre-emption was sought by the holder of a land contiguous to the land transferred but it was resisted on the ground that other contiguous land holders were not impleaded, and when those persons were impleaded later on by the pre-emptor with a view to meet this objection the petition for pre-emption was allowed on merits. The order for pre-emption was however challenged by an appeal on grounds other that any ground of defect of parties. The appeal was dismissed whereupon a revision, under section 115, Civil Procedure Code was filed in which an application was made for taking an additional ground as to defeat of parties in respect of a different person for the first time. It was alleged that one Mozaffar AIi Khan was a contiguous land holder but was not impleaded in the pre-emption proceeding. It was found by the High Court Division that Mozaffar Ali Khan, along with his brother Ledu Khan, who was already impleaded, had purchased a contiguous land by a kabala, Exhibit 1(b). The High Court Division held that Muzaffar Ali Khan was a necessary party but as he was not impleaded the High Court Division set aside the order of pre-emption and dismissed the application for pre-emption altogether. In appeal before this Division it was found that Muzaffar Ali Khan, though he was a co-purchaser with Ledu Khan under the Kabala Exhibit 1(b), by amicable partition with his brother possessed only that part of the land which was not contiguous to the land transferred but the part which fell to the share of Ledu Khan was contiguous to the land transferred and consequently only Ledu Khan was held to be the contiguous land holder within the meaning of section 96(2). In view of the fact this Division held that Muzaffar Ali Khan, though apparently a contiguous land holder by kabala Exhibit 1(b), got no subsisting right to claim pre-emption and as such he was not a necessary party. Furthermore this Division observed that the ground as to defect of parties in respect of Muzaffar Ali Khan having been taken for the first time in revision under section 115 Civil Procedure Code should have been rejected outright under Order 1, rule 13 C. P, Code which its applicable to a pre-emption proceeding by virtue of section 141 C. P. Code.,

9. Facts in the ease of Abdus Samad Vs. Sohrabali are that the petition for pre-emption was filed by a non-notified co-sharer but It was opposed on the ground that many other co-sharers by inheritance were not impleaded and that though this objection was raised at the earliest possible opportunity the defect was not rectified. The trial court allowed the pre-emption disregarding the objection, but the lower appellate court set aside the pre-emption and dismissed the application for pre-emption holding that the defect of patties was fatal to the proceeding. The High Court Division, however, relying upon the decision in Motilal Sikder's case allowed the pre-emption holding that the requirement for impleading the co-sharer or contiguous land-holders as referred to In section 96 (2) is not mandatory but is merely directory. This Division, on appeal, held that the defect of parties was fatal to the proceeding of Pre-emption and that the ratio decidendi of Motilal Sikder's case was not properly appreciated and correctly applied by the High Court Division.

10. In the instant case the land transferred originally belonged to one Barku who died leaving five sons, three daughters and two widows. Aushi Bali is one of the daughters on whore death her son Jainuddin and daughter Jarunnessa inherited her share and at the time of the transfer to question they were alive but were not impleaded in the pre-emption cage Afzau Bibi was another daughter of Barku. She died leaving four sons including Momtaj on whos death his two sons Karamat Ali and Giasuddin inherited his share but they were not impleaded in the proceeding. Again, one Sahera, grand-daughter of Elahi who was the 4th son of Barku, though admittedly a co-sharer was not impleaded. The explanation for non-joinder of parties on such a large scale was that the pre-emptee objector did not furnish the names and particulars of the left-out co-sharers under an affidavit though he was directed to do so by the trial court. It appears that when obj clan was raised as to defect of parties at the earliest possible opportunity the pre-emptor submitted to the pre-emptee an interrogatory asking him to furnish the names and particulars of the left-out co-sharers. Those particulars were in fact furnished accordingly but without an affidavit. The trial court at the instance of the pre-emptor rejected the objection as to defect of parties holding the pre-emptor objector was responsible for the omission and allowed the pre-emption. The order for pre-emption was set aside in appeal by the learned Subordinate Judge who held that the objector pre-emptee was under no legal obligation to furnish by affidavit the names and particulars of the let out co-sharers and that the non-joinder of parties was fatal to the pre-emption proceeding As against this order, the High Court was moved by an application under section 115 Civil Procedure Code in which a ground was taken that the left out to sharers had no subsisting right of pre-emption and as such their omission was not fats to the proceeding. The High Court Division accepted this contention observing that "it does not appear that there is anything on record to indicate that the alleged left-out heirs of Barka bad a subsisting right of pre-emption."

11. Mr Anil Chandra Sarker, learned Advocate for the appellant has contended that it was for the pre-emptor to lead evidence showing that the left-out co-sharers had lost their interest in the laud in question by transfer or otherwise and that the High Court Division shitted the burden of proof upon the pre-emptee in this respect. It is not disputed that the left-out persons are co-sharers by inheritance. But there is no evidence whatever to show that they got no subsisting interest in the land under pre-emption. Mr. Yeasin, the learned Advocate for the respondent, has failed to show us how it could be held that the left-out co-sharers lost or transferred their interest in the land under pre-emption. The onus of proof in this respect is upon the pre-emptor but this onus has not been discharged. The observation of the High Court Division as quoted above shows that it was for the pre-emptee to lead evidence to the effect that the left out co-sharers still get interest in the land sought to be  pre-emptee The High Court Division in this connection relied upon the decision in Motilal Sikder's case in which it was observed that the positive injunction as to parties under section 96 (2) is directory. The facts of this case as set out above are not attracted by the decision in Motilal's case ; on the contrary, these facts are attracted by the decision in the case of Abdus Scoriae vs. Sohrab Ali an which it has been held that non-joinder of parties who got right of preemption is fatal to the proceeding".

<u>12. In Motilal Sikdar's case it was observed that the question as to joinder of parties Is essentially a matter of procedure and that this procedure has been laid down in Order 1, Civil Procedure Code. It was further observed that by virtue of section 141 of this Code the provisions of Order 1 are applicable to a pre-emption proceeding which is of original nature Rule 9 of Order 1, C.P. Code provides that "no suit shall be defeated by reason of the mis-joinder or non-joinder of parties and the court may in every suit deal with the matter in controversy so far as regards the rights and interests of the parties actually before it". In the said case, the left out contiguous land owner lost the contiguity between his land and the land transferred after the partition with his brother. In that back ground it was observed by this Division that the provision as to Parties under section 90 (2) is merely directory. It may be "stated here for clarification that though the provisions of Order 1, Civil Procedure Code are applicable to a pre-emption proceeding, this provision is subject to the special provision of section 96 (2) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.</u>

<u>13. Mr. Anil Chandra Sarker, the learned Advocate has in this. connection referred to an observation of the then High Court of East Pakistan in the case of "Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendra Chondra Dhupi, 14 DLR, 847 Which is to the effect that the provision as to joinder of parties in a suit for partition is the same as that in a suit for pre-emption" since in both the cases the presence of the necessary parties is Indispensably required not only as a matter or convenience but also to enable the court to adjudicate more effectively and completely. The decision in that case Syed Abdul Karim vs. Harendra Chandra Dhupi, was referred to in the judgment of Motilal Sikder's case. We however see. no necessity to draw any such analogy between a partition suit and a pre-emption case as to the making of parties in that the provision as to parties in a partition suit is governed by Order 1, rule 10, C. P. Code whereas the provision as to parties in a pre-emption proceeding is governed by section 96 (2), State. Acquisition and Tenancy Act. This section specifically provides that all co-sharer tenants, if preemption is sought by a co sharer, and all co-sharer tenants and all contiguous land holders, if pre-emption is sought by a contiguous land holder "shall be made parties". Impleading of such persons will not however be necessary if they have lost their interests in the land to be pre-empted or if they have waived their right to the pre-emption. Neither of these two ingredients is present in instant case where a number of co-sharers were omitted and the omission was not supplied even when opportunity was given. The High Court Division is found to bays erroneously held that the “left-out co-sharers" got no subsisting right of pre-emption, they are necessary parties and the non-joinder of these parties is fatal to the application for pre-emption.</u>

<u>In the result, the appeal is allowed with costs. The judgment and order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the lower appellate court is restored.</u>

End.

full_judgment:
Md. Gholam Rabbani J: This Rule questions the extent of the discretion of the Courts to add third party as defendant in a suit. This judicial discretion given in sub-rule 2, rule10, Order 1, CPC is required to be set at right as we are experiencing now-a-days trial Court's lack of judicial consideration while allowing or disallowing an application of a third party for adding him as defendant in a suit.

2. Said sub-rule 2 runs as follows:

"The Court may at any stage of the proceedings, either upon or without the application of either party, and on such terms as may appear to the Court to be just, order that the name of any party improperly joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, be struck out, and that the name of any person who ought to have been joined, whether as plaintiff or defendant, or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added."

3. For better understanding we now re-quote sub-rule 2 omitting the portion unnecessary for the question involved in this Rule as hereunder:

"The Court may at any stage of the proceeding upon the application of party, on such term as may appear to be just, order that the name of any person who ought to have been joined as defendant or whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit, be added."

4. Now we further omit the part not required comment and split up the rest into paragraphs to make the intention clear as hereunder:-

"The Court  may order that the name of any person (a) who ought to have been joined as defendant or (b) whose presence before the Court may be necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely to adjudicate upon and settle all the questions in the suit, be added."

5. It is to be kept in mind that addition of a party must be subject to the provisions of section 22 of the Limitation Act (see sub-rule 4).

6. The very basic principle of judgments inter partis is that the judgments are not judgments in rem, but declaratory and operative only as between the parties in the suit. This principle is even stronger in the case of a plaintiff as against whom another defendant is sought to be added. The plaintiff being dominus litus, he cannot be compelled to fight against some other litigant not of his own choice unless required by the positive rule of law.

7. Now we consider the persons falling in category (a) i.e. the persons who ought to have been joined as defendants. For the answer we are to read Order 1, rule 3 keeping in mind firstly, whether a certain person is a necessary defendant or not the allegations in the plaint alone should be looked into and then secondly, (i) whether the right to relief against all the defendants will arise out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transaction and (ii) whether any common question of law or fact will arise if separate suits are brought against the different defendants.

8. Order 1, rule 3 reads as follows: "All persons may be joined as defendants against whom any right to relief in respect of or arising out of the same act or transaction or series of acts or transactions is alleged to exist, whether jointly, severally or in the alternative, where, if separate suits were brought against such persons, any common question of law or fact would arise."

9. Now we come to consider the persons falling in category (b). This is the difficult part. Who are the persons whose presence are necessary in order to enable the Court effectually and completely adjudicate upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit?

10. For its answer there is no absolute standard, but guideline can be given by illustrations upon which judicial discretion given under the Rule should be exercised. However, this much can be stated that the intervener third party must be legally interested in the answers to the questions involved in the suit and its true test is not that he has a proprietary right in the subject matter of an action, but the result on the subject matter will affect him legally.

11. Take a suit for partition of the joint family properties. A third party wants to be added as a defendant claiming an item of the suit properties as his own. He is a necessary party. Insofar as the decision whether this item of property will or will not be available for partition is concerned the question involved is no longer between the parties to the suit alone, but between also this third party. So also a third party is a necessary party in a partition suit disputing altogether the title of the plaintiff, but admitting the defendants as his co-owners. A court can pass a decree for partition among the defendants even dismissing the plaintiff's claim. A third party will be a necessary party in a partition suit when he denies the title of both the plaintiffs and defendants to the suit property.

12. Why the aforesaid three interveners are necessary parties? Because each of them has proprietary right in the subject matter in action No decree can be passed without affecting their rights. But where in a suit for declaration of title to a house and for cancellation of a sale deed executed by his co-sharer-defendant in favour of another defendant the plaintiff claims the suit property exclusively by way of family settlement, his other co-sharers in case the allegation of family settlement fails or not are not necessary parties because it is not necessary for adjudication of the said controversy to implead all the co-sharers.

13. So also in a suit for possession against a trespasser in respect of entire property by a co-owner, other co-owners are not necessary parties. But in a suit for declaration by a co-owner that sale by another co-owner is valid to a certain extent against the vendee, the vendor-co-owner is a necessary party while in a suit for possession by a third party against A who has purchased the suit property from B,B is not a necessary party. In a suit for specific performance of contract by A against B, a third party claiming title adverse to B is not a necessary party, but C, a co-owner of B, challenging the extent of share of B is a necessary party.

14. Thus sub-rule 2 cannot be read as requiring the persons who have or likely to have any sort of right, title or interest in respect of any portion of the subject-matter of a suit should all be made parties. The expression "all the questions involved in the suit" can only be the questions as between the parties to the litigation. Therefore, in a suit against the Government for declaration that the suit property is not an enemy property, lessee thereof whose lease was liable to be renewed or terminated at the end of every year is not a necessary party. Similarly, in a suit for possession by a dispossessed tenant against his landlord a third party—who was inducted as tenant after plaintiff's dispossession is not a necessary party. But in a suit for declaration that an order cancelling the order of lease of the government land to plaintiff and granting lease thereof to a third party as illegal, that third party will be a necessary party.

<u>15. In view of the discussion as above the question of addition of an intervener in a suit as necessary party under Order 1, rule 10, sub-rule 2, we find, is not one of initial jurisdiction of the court, but of a judicial discretion which has to be exercised in terms of this sub-rule. In order to be impleaded in a suit the third party must have a legal interest as distinguished from a commercial interest, that is, assertion of the third party that his addition will avoid multiplicity of suits or will be convenient for the purpose of trial or will not cause prejudice to any party will not be of any avail. He must be legally interested in the answers to the issues in the suit, that is, it will affect or curtail his legal right. And what are issues to be answered in a suit (p) To find out them the averments in the plaint alone should be looked into.</u>

16. Now we consider the instant civil revision. Plaint case briefly, is this. Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate was the owner of the suit property at the time of C S operation. Anand Lal Dhupi took pattan thereof on 24-5-32. By an unregistered deed of sale dated 1-1-43 Ananda sold the property to Nazrul Islam who accordingly possessed the same and got his name recorded in RS Khatian. Plaintiff purchased the suit property from Nazrul Islam by a registered sale deed on 5-7-93. Thus the plaintiff is now the owner of the suit property, but the defendants are trying to lease out the same. Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate, Dhaka Division Commissioner and Chairman of Land Reform Board are the defendants in the suit.

17. It appears from the application dated 25-10-94 of the opposite party Nos.1 to 7 under Order 1, rule 10, sub-rule 2, CPC that there are at least seven shop rooms in the suit property, that the applicants took sub-lease of the shop rooms each separately from the plaintiff on the understanding that the plaintiff had taken lease of the property from the Court of Wards Estate, that the said lease of the plaintiff was cancelled on 17-2-94 by the Land Reforms Board and that two years before the applicants applied for granting them lease of their respective shop rooms.

18. By the order dated 12-1-95 impugned in this Rule opposite party Nos.1 to 7 were added as defendants in this suit.

19. Heard Mr. AKM Asaduzzaman for the plaintiff-petitioner and Mr. Md. Khorshed Alam Khan for the added defendants-opposite parties.

<u>20. In view of the legal position as discussed above, the allegation made in the plaint and the allegations made in the application for addition of parties we do not find that the said opposite parties arc necessary parties in this suit. The issue involved in the suit is whether the plaintiff has title to the suit property or whether the suit property is the Khas property of Bhawal Raj Court of Wards Estate and to adjudicate the issue presence of the opposite parties in not necessary. A court has jurisdiction to add as defendant a person even when a plaintiff does not wish to sue him only in a case where the plaintiff is seeking a relief which may directly affect the intervener by curtailing the enjoyment of his legal rights and consequently his presence is "necessary to enable the court to adjudicate completely and effectually upon and settle all the questions involved in the suit."</u>

21. This Rule is, therefore, made absolute without costs. Impugned order dated 12-1-95 is set aside and the names of the added defendants are struck out from the plaint.

End.

full_judgment:
Mahmud Husain CJ. - I have had the advantage of reading in advance the separate judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers D.C. Bhattacharya and Fazle Munim, JJ. I concur with the reasonings of my learned brother Fazle Munim, J.

Ahsanuddin Chowdhury J. - I read in advance the separate judgments proposed to be delivered by my learned brothers D.C. Bhattacharya and F. Munim, JJ. I agree with my learned brother F. Munim, J.

Fazle Munim J. - This appeal is against the Judgment and order of a Bench of the High Court Division in Petition No.134 of 1976.

Facts of the case may shortly be stated thus:

The respondent No.1 to 3 who are partners of the registered firm named and styled as M/s. Masood Reza and Co. (hereinafter referred to as "the firm") filed an application under Article 102 of the Constitution for directing the appellant and respondents No.4 to 8 to restore to them the possession, control and management of this firm in pursuance of an order of release of the same by the Government (as contained in <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> No. SRO. 31-L/76 No. Industries/13-3M/104/75/11 dated 17-1-76 together with all papers, documents and properties both moveable and immovable. The said firm used to carry on export, import, indenting and commission agency business.

2. By <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on March 20, 1972 of the <u>Ministry of Industries</u>, the Management of M/s. E. Pak Traders, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca and M/s. Masood Reza & Company, Reza Chamber, 75, Motijheel Commercial Area, under M/s. Masood Reza Group of Industries including all the properties and assets wherever located in Bangladesh was taken over under the Acting President's Order No. Sec. XI/IM-35/71/17 dated 30-12-71. The <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> is as follows:

"The Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary published by Authority Monday March 20, 1972, No.1A (80) 72-297-7th March, 1972 in partial modification of the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> No.IA (80) 72-282 dated 18th February, 1972 of this Ministry and in exercise of the authority given by the Acting President's Order No. Sec. XI/IM-35/71/17 dated 30th December, 1971 the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders the, management of M/s. E. Pak Traders, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca and M/s. Masood Reza & Co. Reza Chamber, 75, Motijheel Commercial, Area, Dacca under M/s. Masood Reza Group of Industries including all the properties and assets wherever located in Bangladesh and to appoint Mr. A.K.M. Shamsul Huq, M.A. C/o. Reza Chamber, 75, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dacca as Administrator for the units. He shall operate the Mill and generally conduct all their affairs including operation of bank accounts, subject to the general supervision, of the Management Board under Group ‘F’ (11) Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca and the Chief Administrator of the Masood Reza Group of Industries.

K. A. Zaman

<u>Secretary</u>

<u>Ministry of Industries</u>".

This <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>, it may be noted, mentions the earlier <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 18-2-72, which, along with an earlier <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> issued on December 31, 1971 does not mention the respondent firm.

3. However, by the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 27-1-75 of Nationalised Industries Division of the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> which was published in the Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary on 30-1-75, the aforesaid firm was placed under the appellant in exercise of the powers conferred by Clause 1 of Article 10 of the Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order No.72, (hereinafter referred to as "the Nationalisation Order" P.O. No.27 of 1972. The <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> is as follows:

"The Bangladesh Gazette Extraordinary published by Authority Thursday January 30. 1975. Ministry of Cabinet Affairs, Establishment Division Section Ed/IV.

<u>Ministry of Industries</u> Nationalised Industries Division Dacca, the 27th January, 1975. No. S.R.O. 60-L/75/F/ST-E. 8/72. In exercise of the powers conferred by clause (1) of Article 10 of the Bangladesh Industrial Enterprises (Nationalisation) Order, 1972 (President's Order No.27 of 1972) the Government is pleased to place M/s. Mohammad Masood Reza & Co. Dacca under the Bangladesh Steel Mills Corporation.

BY order of the President

Sd/- S. K. Safiuddin

Deputy <u>Secretary</u>."

4. On representations by the respondents No.1 to 3 the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> released the firm to them under Article 15(3) of the Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972. 6. As the latter refused to deliver possession, the respondents No.1 to 3 moved the High Court Division of the Supreme Court, as it then was, under Article 102 of the Constitution. A rule nisi was issued upon the appellant who is the Chairman of Bangladesh Steel Mills Corporation, a Statutory Corporation, and the Respondents No.4 to 8 to show cause why they should not be directed to restore possession of the firm to the respondents No.1 to 3.

The separate affidavits-in-oppositions were filed by the appellant and the respondent No.4.

7. On behalf of the respondent No.4, it was stated that after the order of release they received a representation from the appellant that if the firm of the respondents No.1 to 3 is released they would face difficulties in running the industrial unit of M/s. Md. Masood Reza Group of Industries. Further, the entire master was being examined by the Government and they have no mala fide intention to frustrate or defeat the legitimate claim of the respondents No.1 to 3.

8. The appellant’s contention was that since they took over possession of the affairs of the aforesaid firm on 5th February, 1975 they have incurred considerable expenses in running the said firm and paid the liabilities of the film which amounted to several lacs of takas.

In reply the respondents No.1 to 3 mentioned that they did not actually knew what were the difficulties of the appellant in releasing the firm as there is no express mention about them in the affidavit filed by the appellant.

9. The rule nisi came up for hearing before a Bench of the High Court Division which by an order dated 6th May, 1977 made the Rule absolute and directed the delivery of physical possession of the firm to the respondents No.1 to 3 and also made absolute the interim order of injunction restraining the appellant and the respondents No.4 to 8 from dealing with the firm. It was found by the High Court that the appellant which was a statutory corporation was bound, by the order of release made by the Government arid that the difficulties which were alleged by the appellant could be resolved by mutual discussions. It was observed that "as no case has been made out that there is any lien of anybody in the firm the financial involvement can be sorted out either mutually or by way of civil proceeding but that would not stand in the way of issuing the writ as has been prayed for".

10. Leave to appeal against the aforesaid decision was granted by this court on 2nd September, 1976 to consider the following:

1. Whether the order of release dated 17-1-76 purported to be made under article 15(3) of 1972 (P.O.16/72) was lawful;

2. Whether the order dated 11-2-76 purporting to cancel an earlier order dated 27-1-75 made under article 10(1) of the President's Order No.27 of 1972 was with lawful authority and

3. Whether the appellant has any locus standi to dispute the validity of the orders made or the directions given by the Government of Bangladesh.

11. Mr. S.R. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, submitted that once the property in question vested in the Government according to the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, it had no jurisdiction to release the same, there being no provisions enabling the Government to do so. For the release of this firm, the respondents No.1 to 3 could only avail of the remedy as provided in the aforesaid Order. The learned Counsel next contended that apart from the absence of any provisions enabling the release of property, there was further difficulty in the way of the Government releasing such property once it has been placed with any corporation under article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972. Thus, according to him, there are two bars in the way of the Government to release any property placed under the control of any Statutory Corporation under the provisions of the Nationalisation Order, whether abandoned or not.

12. The learned Counsel also contended that, the Government had no power either under the Nationalisation Order or section 21 of the General Clauses Act to cancel the order of placement of any property under the provisions of article 10(1) (d) and (1A) of the Nationalisation Order; nor, having regard to the provisions of (1A) of article 10 of the Nationalisation Order, can the respondents No.1 to 3 challenge the vesting of the property in the Government.

13. Mr. S.R. Pal, finally contended that the appellant which is not department of Government but a statutory corporation is not bound by any order of the Government which is in excess of the powers given under the Nationalisation Order or any other statute. Its entity being separate and distinct from that of the Government, it can raise the question of the validity of the order of release as well as of cancellation of placement dated 11-2-76. Since the order of release and cancellation directly affect the appellant, it has the locus standi to challenge the same. As the appellant invested its own fund in the affairs of the firm in question it had direct interest in the matter. It was further pointed out by the Counsel that since the appellant was made a party to the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the appellant had locus standi to question the validity of the impugned orders.

14. In support of his contentions mentioned above, the learned counsel referred to the relevant <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s issued by the Government since the respondent’s firm was taken over by it on 7th March, 1972. These <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s have already been mentioned and quoted above. The two main <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s with which Mr. Pal were concerned are the, <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s dated 17th January, 1976 which released the film in favour of the respondents No.1 to 3 and the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 11th February, 1976 which cancelled the earlier <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 27th January, 1975 by which the firm was placed under the Steel Mills Corporation. As regards the contention that the Government has no power to release any property vested in the Government as abandoned property, the learned Counsel referred to the decision reported in 27 DLR 468. He went so far as to suggest that even if any property which could not be taken over by the Government as an abandoned property as defined it the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, but has been treated as such, it cannot be released by the Government of its own motion. It is true that having regard to the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, which provided or vesting of the abandoned property in the Government and also set the machinery for releasing the same, no proper which falls within the definition of abandoned property as given in article 2(1) of the said Order can be released by the Government excepting in accordance with the procedure laid down in the said Order or under any other statute which may enable the Government to do so. Simple as this proposition is which is not also disputed by any one, the real question is whether this can lead to the inference that the Government must be denied the power of release any property forthwith, if it appears that any property taken over as an abandoned property was not in fact an abandoned property at the time it was taken over as such. Or, in other words, whether there is any difference between a property which is an abandoned property within the meaning of the same expression used in article 2(1) of the Abandoned Property Order and any property which is merely treated as abandoned property. Mr. Pal submitted that once any property is taken over as abandoned property it becomes an abandoned property and vests absolutely in the Government, as provided in Article 4 of the Abandoned Property Order which says "on the commencement of this Order all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provision of this Order." The question is whether the expressions "all abandoned properties used in this article mean such properties as come within the definition of abandoned properties in article 2(1) of the same Order or any property which though not covered by this definition, is treated as abandoned property. Article 2(1) provides as follows:

"2. In this order, unless there is anything repugnant in the subject or context:

(1) "abandoned property" means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, (i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's <u>REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH</u>; (ii) any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972), but does not include—

(a) any property the owner of which is residing outside Bangladesh for any purpose which, in the opinion of the Government, is not prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh;

(b) any property which is in the possession or under the control of the Government under any law for the time being in force. Explanation: "Person who is not present in Bangladesh" includes anybody of persons or Company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's <u>REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH</u>."

<u>15. On a proper consideration of these provisions, it would appear that unless any property answers the description of abandoned property, the merely taking of such property on the assumption or mistaken belief that it falls within that description will not vest it in the Government, the obvious reason being that, in the case of such property no occasion arises for the application of the Abandoned Property Order. As was pointed out by the learned Counsel for the respondents No.1 to 3 that if on a wrong assumption or by mistake any property has been taken over as abandoned property, it is not required to take recourse to the remedy provided in the Order itself. A mere representation by the owner of such property should suffice to get the property released.</u>

<u>16. Mr. Pal submitted that in view of the provisions of Article 15(1) of the Abandoned Property Order the owner of any property which is treated by the Government as abandoned property must apply to the Government for its release as provided in that article. Article 15(1) provides as follows:</u>

<u>"15. (1) Any person claiming any right or interest in any property treated by Government as abandonee property may make an application to the prescribed authority on the ground that-</u>

<u>(a) the property is not abandoned property; or</u>

<u>(b) his interest in the property has not been affected by the provisions of this Order."</u>

<u>(2) An application under clause (1) shall be made within three months of the date of the commencement of this Order.</u>

<u>(3) On receiving an application under clause (2), the authority to which the application is made shall hold a summary inquiry in the prescribed manner and, after taking such evidence as may be produced, shall pass an order, stating the reasons therefore, rejecting the application or allowing it, wholly or in part, on such terms and conditions as it thinks fit to impose.</u>

<u>If, any person is aggrieved by an order refusing to release the property he can take recourse to the procedure for appeal or revision as provided in article 16(1) of the said Order which is as follows:</u>

<u>"16. (1) Any person aggrieved by an order under article 7 or article 15 of this Order may, within one month of such order, file an appeal before such authority as may be prescribed."</u>

<u>17. If these provisions are duly considered, it would appear that they do not take away the power of the Government to release any property suo motu if it appears that any property which it had taken over was not in fact an abandoned cannot be intended to have enabled the Government to retain any property which does not fall within the definition of abandoned property in the Abandoned Property Order merely because the Government had somehow or other taken it over as such and the aggrieved owner had somehow failed to follow the aforesaid procedure. It is not, however, true that the respondents No.1 to 3 did not make any representation to the Government for release of their firm after it had been taken over by the Government. A number of letters which have been annexed to the petition, under Article 102, Annexure 1 to IX, show that the respondents No.1 to 3 were moving the Government for release of their firm. An enquiry by the Government was also held in the middle of May, 1973.</u>

<u>18. As regards the contention that the property in question was validly taken over by the Government as abandoned property it is necessary to mention the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated, 7th March, 1972 quoted earlier, which mentions that "in partial modification of the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> No.1A (80)72-282 dated 18th February, 1972 of this Ministry and in exercise of the authority given by the Acting President's Order No. Sec.-XI/IM-35/71/17 dated 30th December, 1971 the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders the management of M/s. E. Pak Traders, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca M/s. Masood Reza & Co. Reza Chamber, 75, Motijheel Commercial Area, Dacca."</u>

<u>19. Mr. T.H. Naturally, the conclusion which arises from the omission of Masood Reza & Co. in these two <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s is that it was not taken over under the Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971.

20. By the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7th March, 1972 the concerns mentioned in the aforesaid <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s along with the respondent's firm, Masood Reza & Co. were purported to be taken over under the Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971.

21. Mr. T. H. Khan, Counsel for the respondent's No.1 to 3 submitted that by the Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971 some minor amendment was effected to the Acting President's Order dated 26th December, 1971. The amendment merely substituted the words "the Ministry of Commerce" by the words "the Ministry of Commerce arid the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> and Natural Resources". He further submitted that the President's Order dated 26th December, 1971 was repealed by the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. Section 6 of the latter Order which effected the repeal provided that "Notwithstanding the repeal all <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s issued under the said Order (Abandoned Property) Order dated 26th December, 1971) shall be deemed to have been issued under the relevant provisions of the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. This Order was promulgated on 3rd January, 1972. The taking over of the respondent's firm on 7th March, 1972 under the Abandoned Property Order dated 30th December, 1971 must have, therefore, been illegal. Even assuming that by mistake Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971 was mentioned in place of Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972, two questions would seem relevant. First, whether the taking of any property mentioning a law under which is no longer in force is permissible. Secondly, even if it be assumed that the law under which any property was supposed to have been taken was not mentioned by some clerical mistake and some other law has wrongly been mentioned, can it be held that the taking of property has been legal? As regards the first question, it should be quite obvious that property of citizen cannot be seized or taken over under repealed statute. If any <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> issued after the repeal of a statute has been saved by the repealing statute, only then the taking over could have been justified. In the present case no <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> issued after the repeal of Acting President's Order dated 30th December, 1971 was saved by the repealing statute, i.e. Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. So far as the second question is concerned even the analogy of quoting a wrong section of an Act in a application before a Court of law which is often condoned will not be of much help to the appellant. First, even assuming that there has been a mistake, though it has not been established to be so it shows the lack of proper application of mind on the part of the authority concerned. Next, there is considerable scope for doubt whether, after the promulgation of the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, any property could be taken over as abandoned property under Acting President’s Order No.1 of 1972. Mr. T. H. Khan, Counsel for the respondent Nos.1 to 3, submitted that after the promulgation of the former Order, the latter Order should be deemed to have been impliedly repealed by the former.

<u>22. Mr. Pal, Counsel for the appellant intervened to say that had the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 become ineffective it would not have been protected by the Constitution. In the First Schedule to the Constitution that Order (Abandoned Property Order No.1 of 1972) along with several other Presidential Orders have been preserved and protected against any challenge on the ground of any conflict with the provisions of the Constitution, particularly the fundamental rights of the citizens.</u>

<u>Since it is not necessary to hold whether, the Acting President Order No.1 was impliedly repealed by the Abandoned Property Order 1972, it would be sufficient to say that the preservation and protection of the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 by the Constitution were considered necessary to protect any action taken under that order and not for continuing its operation after the Abandoned Property Order 1972, came into force. Moreover, the Abandoned Property Order provided all necessary legislative authorisation for taking over all properties which were abandoned or had already been taken over under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1973. It, therefore, follows that on March 7, 1972, the date of taking over of the respondent’s firm Government would not take it over as abandoned property purporting to exercise its powers under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. It appears that the respondent's firm which was not taken over under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 before the commencement of the Abandoned Property Order, could no longer be looked upon as abandoned property.</u>

<u>23. From the expressions "any property taken over under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972)" used in Article 2(1)(ii) of the Abandoned Property Order, it would seem that they refer to past action and not any action in the future. It would, therefore, appear that they mean any property which had already been taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and would not mean any property which shall be taken over under that Order in future after the Abandoned Property Order came into force. On and from 26th February, 1972 when the Abandoned Property Order of 1972 (P.O. 16/72) was promulgated, any property which was owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property will be abandoned property. Such property will also include (i) any property owned by any person who is a citizen of a state which was at war with Bangladesh and (ii) any property taken-over under the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. Any property which answered the above mentioned definition of abandoned property in the Abandoned Property Order was to vest in the Government on the commencement of this Order. In these circumstances, the order of release by the Government of the respondent's firm cannot be held to be void and illegal.</u>

24. The next contention of Mr. Pal. Counsel for the appellant, was that once the Government has placed any property, taken over as abandoned property under the appellant, which is one of the Corporations set up under Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, the Government has no power to cancel the order of placement as by such placement the property becomes vested in the Government. Article 10(a) (d) of the Nationalisation Order is as follows:

10. (1) On the commencement of this Order, there shall be established the following corporations:

(4) Bangladesh Steel Mills Corporations; which shall respectively have and exercise the powers of a Corporation in respect of such industrial enterprises, including industrial enterprises owned wholly or partly by the Government or vested in Government under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 or owned and managed by a statutory corporation, which the Government may place under it by an order notified in the official Gazette."

The aforesaid clause shows that in respect of industrial enterprises such as:

(i) are owned wholly or partly by the Government, or

(ii) vested in the Government under the Abandoned Property Order, 1972, or

(iii) are owned and managed by a statutory corporation, the statutory corporation mentioned in the article shall exercise powers.

26. Mr. Pal, submitted that among the three categories of industrial enterprises which can be placed by the Government under the appellant corporation, the respondents firm falls under the second category. It has already been seen that the respondent's firm did not lawfully vest in the Government under the Abandoned Property Order 1972. It was neither wholly nor partly owned by Government, nor was it owned and managed by a statutory corporation before it was placed under the appellant. Having been outside any of these categories as the above, how the respondent's firm, it has been rightly asked, could at all be placed by the Government under the aforesaid article. Being confronted with this difficulty Mr. Pal next submitted that as soon as any industrial enterprises is placed under a corporation by an order under clause 1 of Article 10 of the Nationalisation Order, it vests in the Government which then, has no power to divest it irrespective of whether it had lawfully vested in the Government as an abandoned property under the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, 1972. He first referred to the unamended provisions of Article 4 of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, which runs as follows:

"On the commencement of this order, all the shares in each of the scheduled industrial enterprises or, as the case may be, the industrial enterprises placed under a corporation by an Order under clause (1) of Article 10, which have not already vested in the Government by or under any other law for the time being, in force, shall, by virtue of this Article and without further assurance, stand vested in and allotted to the Government free of any trust, mortgage, charge, lien, interest to other encumbrance whatsoever and the government free from such commencement, be the sole shareholder of such industrial enterprises."

27. The learned Counsel then referred to the provisions of article 4 as amended on 17th April, 1976 by Ordinance No. XXV of 1976:

"4. (1) All such share and other proprietary interests in each of the scheduled industrial enterprise, and all such industrial enterprises paced under a Corporation by or by an order under clause (1) of article 10, and all shares and proprietary and other interests, as have not already vested in the Government by or under any law for the time being in force, shall by virtue of this Article and without any further proceeding or formality, stand vested in, and allotted to, the Government free of any trust, mortgage, charge, lien, interest or other encumbrance whatsoever,—

a) in the case of a scheduled industrial enterprise, on the commencement of this Order; and

b) in the case of an industrial enterprise placed under a Corporation by order under clause (1) of Article 10, on the date on which it is so placed; and subject to the provisions of clause (2), the Government shall, as from such commencement or date, be the sole shareholder in or owner of, such industrial enterprises.

(2) The Government may, if in the national interest it deems it expedient, so to do, sell or otherwise transfer to any person, on such terms and conditions as may be settled with him. any industrial enterprise or any share or proprietary or other interest in such an enterprise, vested in the Government under clause (1):

Provided that the power of sale or transfer under this clause shall not be exercisable in respect of the scheduled industrial enterprises other than industrial enterprises relating to specialised textiles:

Provided further that no such sale or transfer of industrial enterprises, share or interest shall be made except after making an offer on like terms and conditions to the person entitled to receive payment of compensation under Article 9 in respect of such enterprise, share or interest and such person has declined to accept the offer within a reasonable time.

(3) Where the Government sells or otherwise transfers under clause (2) wholly or partly, any industrial enterprises, or any share or proprietor or other interest in an industrial enterprise, it may by <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> in the official Gazette, omit from the schedule, or, as the case may be, withdraw from the Corporation under which it was placed by an order under clause (1) of Article 10, that industrial enterprise.

(4) Where a <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> under clause (3) is issued in respect of any industrial enterprise, the Government may;—

(a) by the same <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> or by a separate <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> direct that the provisions of articles 5, 6, 7 and 8 shall cease to apply or shall apply with such <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> or qualification as may be specified in the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>, to such industrial enterprise and (b) take such measures, including consequential changes in the relevant memorandum or articles of association, as may be necessary to restore, as far as the changed circumstances may permit, to the legal position of the industrial enterprise under the Companies Act, 1913 (VII of 1913) as obtained before it vested in the Government under clause(1)".

28. From clause 1 of the aforesaid provisions, the learned Counsel wanted to show that even if the respondents firm had not already vested in the Government by or under any law for the time being in force, i.e. Abandoned Property Order, 1972, it stood vested in the Government as soon as it was placed under the appellant corporation. Secondly, clause 2 of the aforesaid provisions only permitted the Government to sell or otherwise transfer each industrial enterprise as is placed under a corporation under article 10(1) of the Nationalisation Order in the manner laid down there-in. Since the Government did not take recourse to this clause in the present case, its clients not in accordance with law and as such invalid.

29. Since in our opinion the very basis for treating the respondent’s firm as abandoned property was lacking and since also there was no basis for placing it under a corporation, the aforesaid provisions can have no manner of application in relation to impugned actions of the Government. This observation applies with equal force to the proviso which was added to clause (1A) of article 10 by Ordinance No.1 of 1976, which is quoted further below in this judgment.

It may however, be mentioned that this proviso was subsequently omitted by the amendment of Article 10 by Ordinance No. XXV of 1976.

<u>30. It is difficult to understand how if any industrial enterprise does not fall within any of the three categories mentioned in Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1973 as mentioned above, such industrial enterprise would vest in the Government simple because it has been placed under any statutory corporation set up under the provisions of Article 10 of that Order. Unless the conditions laid down therein or elsewhere in the Order are fulfilled, the mere placing of an industrial enterprise under a corporation set up by the Government for managing nationalised industrial enterprises cannot be said to have vested it in the Government. The provisions, of the Nationalisation Order No.1972 can have no manner of application to an enterprise which is not an industrial enterprise falling in one or the other category.</u>

<u>31. Referring to the preamble of the Nationalisation Order, 1972. Mr. Pal submitted that Government has power to place any new industrial enterprise under any of the Corporations set up under Article 10(1) (d) of the same Order. The preamble to the Nationalisation Order No.1972 provides:</u>

<u>"WHEREAS it is expedient to provide for the nationalisation of certain industrial enterprises in Bangladesh and for the establishment of corporations for the purposes of control, supervision and coordination of the nationalised and some other enterprises and for the establishment and development of new industrial enterprises and for matters connected therewith or incidental thereto.,"</u>

<u>32. Since the entire contention so long has been based on the denial of the Government's power to cancel the order of placement because the firm of the respondent No.1 to 3 vested in the Government as an abandoned property, it is too late in the day to say that the 'Government has also the power to place any new industrial enterprise under the statutory corporation established under the Nationalisation Order. The respondent’s firm does neither come under the expressions "some other enterprises" nor under the expressions "New industrial enterprises" used in the preamble to the Nationalisation Order. Moreover, the preamble cannot control the operative provisions of Article 10(1) (d) which have clearly enumerated three categories of enterprises which can be placed by the Government under any of the corporations set up under that article.</u>

<u>33. Mr. Pal also referred to the provisions of clause (1A) of Article 10 of the Nationalisation Order and submitted that once any industrial enterprise has been placed under any corporation under article 10(1)(d) it shall be deemed to have vested in the Government and the Order of placement cannot be challenged in any court of law. The provisions of clause (1A) areas follow:</u>

<u>"(A) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other law, an industrial enterprise, placed under any corporation by an order notified in the official Gazette under sub-clause (d) of clause (1) of Article 10, and all charges or other proprietary interest in such industrial enterprise shall be deemed to have always vested in the Government and such order shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial enterprise or the shares or interest therein had not vested in the Government, or that the industrial enterprise, or any share or interest therein was not liable to be vested in the Government:</u>

<u>Provided that the Government may, at anytime transfer an industrial enterprise mentioned in this clause and all shares or other proprietory interest therein, in such manner and on such condition as it may deem fit, to the person who owned such industrial enterprise and shares or interest before they were vested in the Government, if such persons are Bangalees and the industrial enterprise and the shares or interest therein were vested in the Government under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal Order), 1972 (P.O.No. 16 of 1972) prior to the placement of the industrial enterprise under any Corporation, and on such transfer the industrial enterprise shall cane to be under the control of any Corporation."</u>

<u>34. From the expressions "shall be deemed to have always vested In the Government" Mr. Pal wanted to assert that event if the respondents firm be found not to have vested in the Government under provisions of the Abandoned Property Order, once the firm has been placed under Article 10(1)(d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, it shall be deemed to have vested in the Government and such vesting cannot be challenged on the ground that it did not vest nor was it liable to be vested in the Government. Had the appellant's claim that the respondent's firm had vested in the Government as an abandoned property been found in fact, there might have been some substance in the contention of the learned Counsel. Since the appellant's claim has been found to be untenable, the mere placement of the respondents firm under the Corporation under Article 10(1) (d) does not invest it with the qualities or status of any of the categories mentioned therein and, therefore, consequently does not empower the Government to retain it. Such claim to retain, if conceded, would amount to putting premium on the illegal seizure of the citizen's property. It requires to be known to all concerned that the property of a citizen can neither be acquired nor be retained by the Government unless it is done under proper legislative authorisation. The seizure of property without legislative sanction whether by a private citizen or the Government amounts to illegal grabbing. A citizen's property cannot be seized also under the colourable exercise of power conferred by the legislature.</u>

35. Apart from the absence of any legal basis for placing the respondent’s firm under Article 10(1) (d) as, in fact it is not an abandoned property, it appears that so far as placement of such property is concerned, it is illegal also on the ground that in so far as the respondents, firm is not an industrial enterprise the Government lacks the necessary power to place it under Article 10(1)(d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972, for, this Article empowers the Government to place only such industrial enterprise as are mentioned therein. Under this article Government has no power to place any enterprise under a statutory corporation which is a commercial firm. In their petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the respondents have all through claimed that their firm is a commercial concern. Moreover, Mr. T.K. Khan, Counsel for the respondents, referred to the following <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> wherein it has been admitted by the Government that on scrutiny the respondent’s firm was found to be a commercial unit which should, therefore, be handed over to the Ministry of Commerce.
