<u>38. Incidentally Mr. Pal. mentioned that since the appellant incurred considerable expenses after the respondent's firm was placed under their management and supervision and the character of the property so placed has been altered due to such expenses, the appellant cannot be asked to release the same unless they have been repaid these expenses in full. Since whether the respondents firm should be released or not is a question which does not depend on the amount of expenses spent by the appellant over it after the same was placed under their control, the learned Counsel's contention cannot, we are afraid, be conceded to.</u>

<u>39. As regards the power of the Government to cancel the order of placement under Artie e 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, Mr. Pal, submitted that since such placement created rights in favour of the appellant, the Government cannot withdraw or rescind it without the appellant's consent. In support, he cited the case of Pakistan Vs. Md. Niayamat-ullah Faruki, (1969) 21 DLR, SC 238. This decision, relied upon in a recent case reported in (1975) 28 DLR 350 by the High Court, concerns the vesting of rights in a Government servant. Such rights which vested in him under order of the appropriate Ministry of the Government was sought to be nullified by an order the Ministry of Finance on the ground that they were not consulted before conferring such rights. On the latter's objection the order originally passed by the appropriate Ministry fixing the initial pay of the Government servant concerned was withdrawn. This decision is not, therefore, applicable to the facts of the present case.</u>

<u>40. Here, no right is created in favour of the appellant corporation to retain the respondent’s firm. The Government can place a property of any of the descriptions mentioned in Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order, 1972 under a corporation and it can as well withdraw the same from it. Such withdrawal does not require the consent of corporation, whether prior or subsequent. Such property after placement, vests in the Government, not in any corporation and also, after withdrawal it remains vested in the Government, excepting, of course, in any case like the present. Since we already exhaustively dealt with the extent of the Government's power to release the same we need not further consider that question.</u>

<u>41. As regards the third contention as to the locus standi of the appellant to dispute the validity of the orders of cancellation and release, Mr. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, vehemently argued that since the appellant is a statutory corporation, it is a separate and distinct entity and can, therefore, challenge the Government's power and competence to pass the impugned orders. In order to substantiate the appellants claim that being a statutory corporation it is not bound to obey any order passed by the Government, particularly of the nature of orders passed by it, Mr. Pal, referred to almost all the provisions of Nationalisation Order, 1972, beginning from its preamble. He particularly mentioned articles 7, 10, 11, 12, 17, 20, 11, 22 and 25 of the same Order.</u>

<u>In this connection he also referred to English decisions, namely Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions, (1948) 2 All. E. R. 76M (1949) 1KB 227 and Howell Vs. Falmouth Boat Construction Ltd. (1951) 2 All E.R. 278 and submitted that the former decision which laid down the principle that one department of the Government was bound by the order parsed by another department of the Government, both being agents of the Crown was overruled by the later decision from which he quoted the following passage from Lord Simon's Judgment:</u>

<u>"The illegality of an act is the same whether or not the sector has been misled by an assumption of authority on the part of a Government Officer however high or low in the hierarchy. 1 do not doubt that in criminal proceedings it would be a material factor that the actor had been thus misled if knowledge was a necessary element of the offence and in any case it would have a bearing the sentence to be imposed, but that is not the question. The question is whether the character of an act done in face of a statutory prohibition is affected by the fact that it has been induced by a misleading assumption of authority. In my opinion, the answer is clearly: No. Such an answer may make more difficult the task of the citizen who is anxious to walk in the narrow way, but that does not justify a different answer being given. I am, therefore, of opinion that the order of the Court of Appeal cannot be sustained for the reasons given by Denning, LJ.</u>

<u>42. Lord Simond, however, mentioned that the appeal should be dismissed for the reasons to be given by Lord Normand. The reasons as given by Lord Normand were "that neither a Minister nor any subordinate Officer of the Crown can by any conduct or representation bar the Crown from enforcing a Statutory prohibition or from 'prosecuting for its breach".</u>

<u>43. Mr. T.H. Khan, Counsel for respondent, referred to the cases of, Wells and others Vs. Minister of Housing etc. (1967) 2 All England Reports and the case of Leaver Finance Ltd. Vs. Westminster (City) London, Borough Council (1970) 3 WLR 732 to show that Robert-son Vs. Minister of Pension cannot be said to have been over-ruled as Mr. Pal had submitted but the principle stated therein was applied and followed in the aforesaid decisions.</u>

<u>44. Without entering into any dispute as to whether the case of Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions was overruled by House of Lords in the Howell's case, it seems to us that the principle stated therein has not been assailed before us. In the present case the problem is not Whether one department of the Government should be estopped from challenging any order passed by another department of the Government on me ground that me former passed an illegal order, rather the issue is whether a statutory corporation which is subject to the superintendence and control by the Government can dispute the validity of an order passed by the Government. Or, in other words, what is the nature of relationship between the Government and the Statutory Corporation with regard to a matter about which the Corporation has no concern. As already seen the power to place any industrial enterprise under any of the Corporation set up under article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation order or withdraw it belonged exclusively to the Government. Such power was not shared by the Corporation which has, therefore, no option or choice in respect of such placement. Its duty as laid down by the several provisions of the Nationalisation Order is merely to administer an industrial enterprise placed under it by the Government. If the Government withdraws any industrial enterprise from any corporation it is none of the concern of the corporation to challenge it nor to claim that as soon as it was placed under it such enterprise vested in it. From the provisions quoted above, it is clear that as soon as an industrial enterprise is placed under any corporation it either vests or shall be deemed to have vested in the Government. If, therefore, the Government has cancelled the order of placement, of the respondents firm under the appellant, if has no cause for grievance nor should it be grieved, if after such cancellation the Government deals with the enterprise so withdrawn in any way it likes.</u>

<u>45. Though the appellant was in the position of respondent in the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution and as such has claimed, the power to resist the impugned Orders, its stand is not justified for the simple reason that it could not be said to be an "aggrieved party" within the meaning of the expressions used in Article 102 of the constitution. If instead of the respondent’s challenge finder Article 102 the appellant chose to challenge the impugned orders by filing a Writ petition, it could not be held to aggrieved by the Government action. And for the same reason the appellant though was made a respondent in the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution, cannot be allowed to challenge the legality or validity of the impugned orders particularly when such petition was filed against its refusal to comply with the aforesaid orders. A statutory corporation enjoys such autonomy as has been granted by the statute and can exercise authority within the ambit of the power given to it by the statute. The matter of placing an industrial enterprise and subsequent withdrawal of such an enterprise from is not within the jurisdiction of the statutory corporation set up under Articles 10(1) (d). It can exercise so much authority in relation to such an enterprise as has been conferred on it and that also as long as it has not been withdrawn from it after its placement. The principle of autonomy which a corporation enjoys under the statute creating it cannot be claimed to militate against the exercise of power by the Government in respect of matters covered by the principle.</u>

<u>46. Mr. Pal, Counsel for the appellant, referred to 'text book on’ ''Administrative Law" by H. W.R. Wade, 3rd Edition, PP. 43-44 (1971) wherein legal independence of statutory corporations has been considered. As no question involving the exercise of the power of internal management of the appellant corporation is involved in the present case, it is not necessary for us to find its degree of independence vis-a-vis the Government. How wide or precarious is the legal independence of statutory corporation like the appellants need not be defined in view of a matter which is external to the corporation's jurisdiction.</u>

<u>47. A Statutory Corporation cannot claim any power to call in question the Government's power to place an industrial enterprise under the control and supervision or its withdrawal after such placement.</u>

Mr. K. A. Bakr, the learned Attorney-General, appeared on behalf of the Government but instead of supporting the impugned orders passed by the Government, advanced reasons in support of the appellant. He did this under Government instructions. Mention may be made that the appeal by the Government was filed after the Attorney-General was served with a notice to appear when the leave petition by the Chairman of the Steel Mills Corporation was being heard. In order to explain why the Government did not make any submissions before the learned Judges of the High Court excepting filing an affidavit in opposition the learned Attorney General submitted that as the prayer for adjournment of delivery of the judgment of the High Court was not conceded to by the learned Judges, the Deputy Attorney-General who appeared for the Government, could not place the relevant files of the Government to explain the necessity for holding up the delivery of the possession of the respondent’s firm. He further submitted that as the firm was placed by the Government under the corporation according to the provisions of the Nationalisation Order, 1972 all interest of the respondents 1 to 3 in the firm vested in the Government under Article 10(1) (d) read with Article 4 of the aforesaid order. The impugned order of release under Article 15(2) of the Abandoned Property Order was, therefore, wrongly made. His submission is that the Government admitted that it gave the order of release not according to law and that the objections raised by the Corporation were correct. He referred to a statement made in the notice demanding justice served by the respondents on the Government as well as the other appellant which says that the respondent’s firm vested in the Government after it was placed under the corporation under Article 10(1) (d) of the Nationalisation Order. His submission which proceeded on the same line as Mr. Pal's were however, brief and related to the legality of the impugned orders of release and cancellation of the placement of the respondent’s firm under the corporation. Since we have already dealt with these questions, there is no further necessity to consider them over again. Before parting with the case it may, however, be mentioned that the present case offered a hard choice to the Court inasmuch as the Government's order was at the first instance not implemented by a statutory corporation which was bound to implement it and secondly, that the Government itself did not come forward in support of the order made by itself. Between the date on which the order was made and the date of filing the Writ petition there was a sufficient gap. Nothing was done by the Government in rescinding the same during this period. Even the Government did not file an appeal in time which was only filed after notice was served by the Court upon the Attorney General during the hearing of the leave petition. There is no precedence, as was admitted by the learned Attorney-General, of opposition by a Statutory Corporation to a Government order particularly when it is passed by the <u>Secretary</u> to the Ministry.

<u>For the reasons stated above, the appeal is dismissed with costs. This judgment will govern the connected appeal being C.A. No. 37 of 1976 which is dismissed, but without any order as to costs.</u>

<u>Debesh Chandra Bhattacharya J.—I have perused the judgment prepared by my learned brother Mr. Justice Munim and concur with him in the final order prepared by him for the dismissal of the appeal, but I regret to say with respect that I have been unable to agree with the answer given by him in respect of the last of the three questions, for which special leave was granted, namely, the locus-standi of the Corporation to dispute the validity of the impugned orders made by the Government. As regards the two other questions, I agree with the conclusions reached by him, but I think, I should very briefly, give for such conclusions, my own reasons, which are a bit different in certain respects from those of my learned brother. I have not recounted the facts of the case, as they have been set out with proper details in the judgment of my learned brother.</u>

<u>49. The first question, for the consideration of which special leave has been granted, is whether the order of release made under article 15(3) of the President's Order No.16 of 1972 on 24-1-76 was lawful.</u>

<u>50. On this question Mr. Pal learned Counsel for the Corporation has contended firstly, that having regard to the provisions of article 15 of the President's Order No.16 of 1972 and the rules framed thereunder there was no proceeding under the said article which was to be initiated within three months of the date of the commencement of the Order before the prescribed authority, i. e the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub Divisional Officer within whose Jurisdiction the property was situated and as such there could be no valid order under article 15 of the said Order and secondly that in any event the properties in question having been vested in the Government by virtue of provisions of President's Order No.16 of 1972 the Government was not competent in any view of the matter to make the impugned order of release, which purports to divest the Government of such properties.</u>

51. The impugned order appears to have been made by the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> which is not the prescribed authority within the meaning of article 15 (1) of the Order. The order does not also indicate that it was made in any proceeding under article 15 nor does it disclose the basis of the decision conveyed by it. No materials have been placed before the Court to show that there was any proceedings under article 15 of the Order or there was any investigation within the meaning of clause (3) of the said article in which a decision was reached that the assets of the Company were not liable to be taken over as abandoned property. Such a decision is essential, because in the absence of such a decision the prescribed authority has no jurisdiction to release the property.

<u>52. A proceeding under article 15 presupposes the taking over of a certain property as abandoned property. On the promulgation of President's Order No.16 of 1972, all properties which were abandoned properties within the meaning of article 2 of the Order vested in the Government of Bangladesh. The Government has no right to release the property which has vested in it as an abandoned property but the prescribed authority under article 15 can release the property only when it comes to a finding that the property to be released, though treated as an abandoned property, was not really an abandoned property and as such it did not vest in the Government. The impugned order does not show that it was the result of Such a finding nor does it appear to have been made by the prescribed authority in a proper proceeding under article 15. In the circumstances, the contention of the learned Counsel that the impugned order cannot be treated to be valid order under article 15 seems to be a force.</u>

<u>53. But this answer does not finally dispose of the question, as the question still remaining to be answered is whether the order of release can be said to be otherwise lawful, if the properties released were not really abandoned properties. Learned Counsel for the Corporation has submitted that article 15 read with article 16 is the only remedial provision for release of a property taken over as an abandoned property, no matter whether it was really an abandoned property or not and that there having been no such proceeding as contemplated in article 15 the Government has no jurisdiction to release such a property.</u>

<u>54. I am not prepared to accept such an extremely mechanical proposition which looks merely for the form, rather than the substance of a matter. A property taken over as an abandoned property will not ipso facto vest in the Government. Under article 4 of President's Order No.15 of 1972 all abandoned properties within the meaning of article 2(1) of the Order vested in the Government of Bangladesh on the commencement of the Order. If any property, which has been taken over and treated as an abandoned property is not in fact an abandoned property within the meaning of the Order, it has certainly not vested in the Government. The Government has not acquired any right or authority in respect of such a property. In such a circumstance, the Government must be deemed to be not in lawful occupation of such a property and shall be, under the general law, accountable to the rightful owner for depriving him of the profits and gains of the property, subject to the provisions of article 23 of the Order which gives legislative protection to the Government and any person for anything done in good faith under the Order and the rules framed thereunder. It is an inherent duly of every person in a State governed by the rule of law to refrain from doing an act which is contrary to law and so it is also his duty to dissociate from, or purge himself of, any illegal action with which he may have unknowingly or inadvertently associated. This duty is all the more incumbent upon the Government, the executive organ of the State, which has the supreme duty of enforcing the rule of law. So if it is found that a property which was not an abandoned property but through some mistake or misconception was taken over as an abandoned property and that under the law in force it has not vested in the Government the Government has certainly on a discovery of such a mistake or misconception, the right, may the duty, to restore the property to the rightful owner forthwith, independently of any positive provision of law in this regard. So if it can be shown that the assets of the Respondent's firm were never abandoned properties and has never vested in the Government under any law, the impugned order of release may be taken as a valid and lawful order of release, although it was wrongly described to have been made under article 15(3) of the Order.</u>

<u>Now let us see if the assets of the Respondents firm were abandoned properties within the meaning of resident's Order No.16 of 1972 and as such vested in the Government of Bangladesh.</u>

55. On 26-12-71, there was an Acting President's Order 1-35/71/13, under which the Ministry of Commerce could take over control and management of certain Industrial and Commercial concerns. On 30-12-71 there was another Acting President's Order which was merely an amending Order, by which the words "the Ministry of Commerce" in the earlier Order were substituted by the words "the Ministry of Commerce and the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> and Natural Resources." On 3-1-72 another President's Order being Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 which was styled as the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 was promulgated. The relevant provisions of article 2(1) of this Order are to the following effect:

<u>"2. (1) where the owners, directors or managers or majority of the owners, directors or managers of any Industrial or Commercial concern have left Bangladesh or are not available to control and manage the concern, or where, in the opinion of the Govt. of Bangladesh the Owners or directors of any Industrial and Commercial concern cannot be allowed, in the public interest to control and manage the concern, the Govt. of Bangladesh may take over its control and management or appoint a Management Board or Administrator or direct any autonomous or semi-autonomous or any other authority to take over its control and management.</u>

<u>Under article 3 of the Order, the Management Board, Administrator, Autonomous or Semi-Autonomous body or the authority controlling or managing any industrial or commercial concern under this Order shall exercise powers and perform duties under the direct supervision and control of the Government of Bangladesh.</u>

56. By article 6 of the Order, the Acting President's Order dated 26-12-71 was repealed and, notwithstanding the repeal, all <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s issued under the repealed Order shall be deemed to have been issued under the relevant provision of this Order. On 28-2-72 the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 was promulgated. In Article 2(1) of this Order the following properties were enumerated as abandoned properties:

<u>(a) any property belonging to a citizen of an enemy State.</u>

<u>(b) any property taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972.</u>

<u>(c) any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabout are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property.</u>

<u>On the commencement of this Order, all those properties which have been defined as abandoned properties in article 2(1) of the Order vested in the Government of Bangladesh.</u>

<u>57. Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 was not repealed by this Order but it has been contended at the Bar that despite the absence of any repealing provision the Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 was virtually abrogated by this new Order, which has laid down elaborate procedural provisions for the management of abandoned properties including those which may have been taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. This contention was advanced without noticing that the categories of the properties which can be taken over under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 are not the same as those which have vested in the Government and are controlled and managed as such under the provisions of President's Order No.16 of 1972 Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 relates to only industrial and commercial concerns and under the said Order the Government can take over the control and management, not only of the concern whose owners, directors and managers have left Bangladesh or are not available to control and manage the concern, which is in such a case, an abandoned property within the meaning of article 2(1) of President's Order No.16 of 1972, but also the concern whose owners, directors or managers, in the opinion of the Government, cannot be allowed in the public interest to control and manage the concern. The field of operation of the two Presidential Orders referred to above having not been the same, there seems to be no reason to take the view that there has been repeal of the earlier Presidential Order by necessary implication, even though there is no positive legislative provision in that respect.</u>

<u>Apart from the fact that it is a protected legislation under article 47(2) of the Constitution and has been specifically mentioned in the First Schedule to the Constitution there has been an amendment of this Order as late as on 15-12-72 by President's Order No.151 of 1972 which has been given retrospective effect from 3-1-1972. By the said amendment, clause 2(A) was added to article 2 of the Order, which has provided that the Government may from time to time publish for general information lists of industrial and commercial concerns taken over under the said Order. Had the Acting President's Order been repealed on 28-2-72 on the Promulgation of President's Order No.16 of 1972 the exercise of legislative power by way of amendment with regard to the said Acting President's Order could not have been possible.</u>

<u>So, in my opinion, it is not correct to say that Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 has been repealed by President's Order No.16 of 1972, by necessary implication.</u>

58. Now let us see whether the assets of Respondent's firm in question had really vested in the Government as abandoned properties under President's Order No.16 of 1972. As it has already been noticed that if the said assets did vest in the Government under article 4 of President's Order No.16 of 1972, the order of release made by the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> on 24-1-76 could not have been made with lawful authority, but if it can be shown that the said assets did not at all vest in the Government and the Government's act of taking over the control and management of the same did not lead to any such legal consequence, there seems to be no impediment in the way of the Government in making the order releasing such assets. The case of the appellant Corporation as sought to be made out is that properties were taken over under Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 and they had thereafter vested in the Government under the provisions of President's Order No.16 of 1972.

59. It appears that, by <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 purported to be made under what has been described as Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71, the management of M/S Masood Reza & Co., the firm of the Respondents, was taken over by the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> until further order. As we have seen, the Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 was merely an amending Order, by which the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> and Natural Resources was given concurrent powers along with the Ministry of Commerce for the purposes of Acting President’s Order dated 26-12-71, which, of course, authorised such taking over. But on 3-1-72 the said Acting President Order dated 26-12-71, was repealed by article 6(1) of Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 and article 2(1) of the Order empowered the Government of Bangladesh to take over the control and management of certain Industrial and Commercial concerns. It may be contended that reference to Acting President's Order dated 3-12-71 in the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 was clerical or accidental mistake. There is no doubt that such a reference was patently mistaken as on 7-3-72 there was no such Order in force as Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 and ordinarily such taking over purported to be made under a non-existing law cannot be regarded to be lawful. It may, however, be argued that when on the date of such taking over the Government had the necessary jurisdiction, albeit under different legislation, to take over the control and management of such a concern and the Company was, as a matter of fact, taken over and managed by the Government for several years, the Court may hold that the action was taken under the right law, which may be read in the impugned <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> in place of the mistaken reference.

60. We do not find any particulars in the impugned <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> which might throw some light on the persons and the grounds which may have induced the authority to take such action. It appears, however, that the impugned <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 was issued in modification of an earlier <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 18.2.72, which again was made in exercise of the powers under Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 and the modification of a <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 31-12-71. On a reference to the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 31-12-71 it is found that the said <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> was also made in exercise of the authority given under Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 and under the said <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> a number of industrial units were taken over. By the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 18-2-72, the management of M/s. E. Pak. Traders, Tejgaon Industrial Area, was taken over and by the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 the list of the concerns, the management of which were taken over, was purported to be further enlarged and the Respondent's firm was sought to be added to the said list. Reference to Acting Present's Order dated 30-12-71 in all those <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s seems to be obviously a mistaken one, based on some misconception. It seems that the effect of the amendment introduced by Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 in Acting President's Order dated 26-12-71 being that the powers conferred by the later Acting President's Order could also be exercised by the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> and Natural Resources, it was perhaps thought that as the said <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> were being issued by the <u>Ministry of Industries</u> they should necessarily be under Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71, Having regard to facts of the case, it may very well be taken that reference to Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71 in the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> in question may have been an obvious mistake for Acting President's Order dated 26-12-71 as amended by Acting President's Order dated 30-12-71, but as Acting President’s Order dated 26-12-71 had already been repealed by Acting President's Order Mo.1 of 1972, such reference may at best, be treated to be a mistake for Acting President’s Order Mo.1 of 1972.

61. We have already noticed that Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 has not been repealed and in spite of the promulgation of President’s Order No.16 of 1972 there are and certain areas where the said Presidential Order has no application but Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 may very well apply, namely, the case where, in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh, the owners and the directors of any Industrial or Commercial concern cannot be allowed, in the public interest, to control or manage the concern. As regards the other contingencies contemplated under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972, namely, when the owners, directors and managers or majority of the owners, directors or managers have left Bangladesh or are not available to control or manage the concern have lost their significance so far as Acting President's Order No.1 of 1973 is concerned, after the promulgation of President's Order, No.16 of 1972 as they are covered by the provisions of the said Presidential Order, whereunder such concerns vested in the Government of Bangladesh on the promulgation of the said President' Order. The <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 cannot be read, in any view of the matter, as one under President's Order No.16 of 1972. Had it been so, there was no question of its management being taken over, as under article 4 of the Order all the properties would vest in the Government and they would be administered, controlled and managed and disposed of in accordance with the provisions of that Order. Having regard to the fact that Acting President's Order dated 26-12-71 was repealed by Acting President's Order No.1 of 172 and that it is provided therein that all the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s made under the repealed Order shall be deemed to have been made under the new Presidential Order, the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> dated 7-3-72 can at best be read as one under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972. If the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> be taken to be one under Acting President's Order No.1 of 1972 it must have been issued on the ground that the owners, director, or managers of the concern, in the opinion of the Government of Bangladesh, could not be allowed to control and manage the concern in the public interest. In such a case the properties were taken over for the control and management, but they did not vest in the Government and there seems to be no legal bar to the restoration of the concern to its owner i.e. if the Government is of opinion that in view of the changed circumstances, it is no longer necessary in the public interest to retain the control and management of the concern.

62. The answer to the second question also depends upon the fact whether on the placement of the Respondent’s firm under article 10(1) of President's Order No.27 of 1972, all the shares of the Respondents firm stood vested in the Government of Bangladesh under article 4 of the said Order. Under the said article, all the shares of the scheduled industrial enterprises or, as the case may be, the industrial enterprises placed under the Corporation by an order under clause (1) of article 10 shall stand vested in and allotted to the government. The respondent’s firm was not a scheduled industrial enterprises. The question, therefore, is whether it was lawfully placed under the Corporation under clause (1) of article 10 so that the legal consequences as contemplated in article 4 of the Order did follow. The Government may, by a <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> under article 10(1) place an industrial enterprise, which had vested in the Government under President's Order No.16 of 1972 or was owned and managed by a Statutory Corporation. Obviously, the Respondent’s firm was not one of any of the two categories mentioned above, and as such it could not be lawfully placed under the Corporation under article 10(1) of the Order.

<u>63. It has been contended, however by the learned Counsel for the Corporation, that in view of the clause (IA) of Article 10, which was added by President's Order No.153 of 1972, any Industrial enterprise if placed under a Corporation by an order notified in the Official Gazette under sub-clause (d) of clause (1) of article 10, whether it answers the description given therein or not, shall be deemed to have always been vested in the Government and no such order, as made under the said provision, shall be challenged on the ground that the industrial concern had not vested or was not liable to be vested in the Government. It appears that the contention of the learned Counsel could have been of much force, if the Respondent’s firm was an industrial enterprise. The provision of clause (1A) is attracted in case of an industrial enterprise which may be placed under a Corporation by an order under article 10(1) (d) of the Order. The Respondent’s firm being admittedly a commercial concern and not an industrial one, the provision of clause (1A) has no application in this case. Had it been an industrial enterprise, it would have been in my opinion, very difficult to avoid the operation of the said clause. Mr. Pal has contended that, even if it was a commercial concern, it is ancillary to, and has become an essential part of, the industrial enterprise managed by the Corporation and that in the circumstances of the case it may be deemed to be an industrial enterprise. There appears to be absolutely no reason to give an extended meaning to the term 'industrial enterprise' as used in President's Order No. 27 of 1972, which was promulgated, as the title, preamble and the enacting provisions of the Order indicate, for the nationalisation of certain industrial enterprises and for the establishment of Corporations for the control, supervision and co-ordination of such nationalised industrial enterprises.</u>

<u>64. The third question relates to a consideration solely on the basis of which the judgment of the learned Judges of the High Court Division appears to have been rested. It appears that their Lordships were impressed at one stage with the reasonings of Denning. J. as given in the decision in the case of Robertson Vs. Minister of Pensions. (1948) 2 All. E. Reports 766: 1 K. B. 227, where it was held that an assurance given by the War Office, which was an agent of the Crown was binding upon the Minister of Pensions, which was another agent of the Crown, by virtue of the principle of estoppel. The relevant observation of Denning, J. at pp 770-771 of the Reports was to the following effect:—</u>

<u>"The department (War Office) itself is clearly bound and as it is but an agent for the Crown, it binds the Crown also, and as the Crown is bound, so are other departments, for they also are agents of the Crown. The War Office letter therefore binds the Crown and through the Crown, it binds the Minister of Pensions. The function of Minister of Pensions is to administer the Royal Warrant issued by the Crown and he must so administer it as to honour all assurances given by or on behalf of the Crown?"</u>

<u>Miscellaneous</u>

<u>65. The principle of estoppel as has been enunciated in the Robertson's case may have some kind of application where the legality of the order or act, sought to be enforced or given effect to, is not in question. But if such an order or act assailed as one without lawful authority, the principle of estoppel is hardly applicable in such a case, as there cannot be any estoppel against a Statute. It does therefore appear that the House of Lords did not accept the principle in a case where the legality of an act was in question, when it had an occasion to consider it in the case of Howell Vs. Fatmouth Boat Construction Ltd, (1951) 2 AII. E Reports 278, where Lord Simonds referred in his speech to the principle laid down in the Robertson's case and made the following comments at page 280 of the Reports:</u>

<u>"My Lords, I know of no such principle in our law nor was any authority for it cited. The illegality of an act is the same whether or not the actor has been misled by an assumption of authority on the part of Government officer however high or low in the hierarchy. I do not doubt that in criminal proceedings would be a material factor that the actor had been thus railed if knowledge was necessary element of the offence, and in any case it would have a bearing on the sentence to be imposed, but that is not the question. The question is whether the character of an act done in fact of a statutory prohibition is affected by the fact that it has been induced by a misleading assumption of authority. In my opinion, the answer is clearly: No."</u>

66. The learned Judges of the High Court Division do not appear to have been correct in expressing the view that the observation of Lord Simonds, as quoted above, had relevance in a criminal case, and as such it did not diminish the persuasive value of the Robertson's case. What the noble Lord wanted to convey in the said observation is that in a criminal case a representation made by a department of the Crown contrary to law may affect in certain cases the question of mens rea of an offender and may also have some bearing on the question of sentence, but that cannot induce a Court of Law to accept an act as lawful, which is, in fact, unlawful. In the instant case their Lordships, however, have not applied, the principle of the Robertson's case on the view that the Corporation was not a Government department nor the Government itself, but have mainly based their decision on the view that the Corporation, as constituted under the President's Order No.27 of 1972 was bound by the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> issued by the Government.

67. Their Lordships seem to be of the view that inasmuch as the Government being the sovereign authority has made a pronouncement in the shape of a declaration by way of a <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> and a citizen seeks to enforce it, a statutory Corporation constituted under President's Order No.27 of 1972 which operates, according to the provisions of the said Presidential Order, subject to the superintendence and control of the Government, cannot take the stand that it is not bound by the Govt. <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>. Learned Counsel for Respondents Nos.1 to 3 has submitted, in support of the decision of the High Court Division, that the corporation being in the position of an agent vis-a-vis the Government and subject to its superintendence and control is not competent to challenge the validity of the Government <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> and is bound to comply with it.

<u>68. The only reasoning underlying the decision of the High Court Division and also the submission of the learned Counsel seems to be, although it has not been so explicitly spelt cut in the judgment, that an agent, whose actions are subject to control and superintendence by the principal, is not entitled to question the validity of an order given by such principal and is bound to carry it out, no matter whether the order is lawful or unlawful.</u>

<u>69. This proposition is, on the face of it, untenable. In a society governed by law, everybody is required to act accordingly to law and not to do a thing which is contrary to law. It is no doubt the duty of an agent to conduct the business of his principal according to the direction given by the principal, but it is no part of his duty to carry out a direction which is not according to law. If the principal gives an order to his agent which is not lawful, the compliance with such an order amounts to an unlawful act which, according to the basic law of the society, he is not bound to do. Even if there is a contract or engagement between them that whatever order or direction will be given by the principal stall be obeyed unquestioningly, such a contract or engagement shall not be enforceable in a Court of law, as it is void so far as the unlawful order is concerned, being contrary to law and against public policy. The general relationship between the principal and his agent, or master and servant, is regulated by the law of contract, which does not countenance such a proposition. So, if in a case of disobedience by an agent or servant of his principal's or master's order, the principal or master goes to a Court to enforce his order can it be said that the agent or servant, whose duty is to carry out the order of his principal or master, is estopped from pleading that the order is unlawful and, therefore, not enforceable. A Court of law may compel an agent or servant to do an act, which according to its judgment is lawful, if it is not otherwise barred, but a command of a principal or master cannot be deemed to be ipso facto lawful. It is a fundamental principal of judicial procedure in this country that a Court must be satisfied as to the enforceability of such a command after giving a proper opportunity to the person against whom the mandate of the Court has been sought, to substantiate his plea, if any. It is imperative for the Court to permit a person, against whom an order is sought, to show cause against such an order and in showing such cause the said person is certainly entitled to bring to the notice of the Court that the order which it is going to pass will be contrary to law. This is in conformity to the rule of natural justice which is naturally attracted in such a case. If, of course, there were a valid legislation disentitling an agent or servant to plead against an order sought to be made against him and compelling him to confess judgment in an action brought by his principal or master, the position might have been different. But we are not aware of any such legislation abrogating the rule of natural justice in such a case nor the decision of the learned Judges has been based upon any such law. Indeed, cases are not few where public servants, who are subject to the control of, and are bound, by the terms of their service, to carry out, the directions given by the Government, take recourse to the Courts of law for restraining the Government from enforcing certain orders against them, which, in their opinion, are unlawful, and Courts will not be within their powers to dismiss the servant's actions on the view that the set /ants are bound to obey the orders of their masters, right or wrong; but, on the other hand, they are required to decide the question of enforceability of the orders on their merits.</u>

<u>70. It has been argued that as the Corporation, which has been constituted for the purpose of control, supervision and coordination of certain industrial enterprises including these which may be placed under the Corporation by an order under article 10(1)(d) of President's Order No.27 of 1972 has no concern with the decision of the Government to place an industrial enterprise under it under the aforesaid provision and has no interest in such an enterprise except the duty of its control, supervision and co-ordination, if has no locus standi to question the decision of the Government to withdraw the said enterprise from its control and supervision, particularly in view of the fact that the Corporation is to act, according to the provision of the Presidential Order, subject to the superintendence and control of the Government.</u>

71. The contention, that the Corporation being the agent of the Government and having had no concern with the questions of placement of an enterprise under it or its withdrawal is bound by the <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u>s issued by the Government, leads us to the consideration of the nature of the functions of the Corporation and its position vis-a-vis the Government in relation to an industrial enterprise placed under it under Article 10(1) of the Order. In my opinion, its position is not that of an agent required merely to carry out the directions of the Government in respect of such an enterprise, but it’s position is that of a juristic person functioning in accordance with the provisions of law as contained in President's Order No.27 of 1972. The Government of the country which is the executive organ of the State undoubtedly exercises immense power for the administration of the affairs of the State. But the exercise of such powers must be subject to the law of the country. The Government is an abstract concept but its functions are carried on by a number of officers in various departments in accordance with the laws relating thereto. Now the provisions of President's Order No.27 of 1972 have laid down the procedures for nationalisation of certain industrial enterprises and for administration and management of such enterprises. Under the said Presidential Order, the Corporation as well as the Government have been allocated certain general and specific duties, which are to be performed in accordance with the provisions of the said Order. According to clause (1) of Article 11, the general direction and administration of the affairs and business of the Corporation shall vest in a Board of Directors which may exercise all powers and do all acts and things which maybe exercised or done by the Corporation and under clause (2) of the said article the Board shall be subject to the superintendence and control of the Government and shall be guided in the discharge of its function by such general or special instruction as may from time to time be given to it by the Government. Under article 13 the Chairman, and any other Director shall exercise such powers, perform such functions and discharge such duties as may be prescribed by rules or regulations made under the Order. Under article 17(1) the function of a Corporation is to control, supervise and co-ordinate, subject to any regulation made in this behalf, the activities, business and affairs of infer alia, the industrial enterprises placed under it by an order under clause (1) of article 10 and to establish and develop new industrial enterprises within their respective fields. Under clause (2) of the said article the Corporation shall have to exercise such powers as may be prescribed by rules or regulations made under the Order in respect of such industrial enterprises and under clause (3) thereof the Corporation shall in respect of such enterprises also exercise such of the powers of the Government as the Government may, by <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> in the Official Gazette, delegate to the Corporation. Under article 22 the Corporation is to furnish to the Government such returns and statements as the Government may from time to time require. Under article 24 the Government may by <u><u>NOTIFICATION</u></u> in the Official Gazette make rules for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of the Order and under article 25 the Board of Directors may with, the previous approval of the Government make regulations to provide for all matters for which provision is necessary or expedient for the purpose of giving effect to the provisions of this Order.

<u>72. From the provisions referred to above it is clear that the Corporation is not, in the strict sense, an agent of the Government, but that all the actions of the Corporation in respect of an industrial enterprise placed, under article 10(1) (d) and also those of the Government in relation to such an enterprise are to be controlled and regulated by the provisions of the Order and the rules and regulations made under it. The Government may be the sovereign authority, in the sense that it is the supreme executive authority of the state, subject to whose control and superintendence, the Corporation discharges its functions in accordance with the provisions of the Order; nevertheless, it shall have to act according to law with respect to the enterprise which had been delivered to its care for the administration and management of the enterprise in accordance with the provisions of the Order, and, in my opinion, it will not be correct to say that it is a matter of no concern to a Corporation whether an enterprise which had been placed under it for administration and management is lawfully taken away from it or not, only because it did not participate in the Government's initial decision of placing the enterprise under it. The duty of the Corporation to administer and manage the enterprise in accordance with the provisions of the Order arises only after the placement of the enterprise under it and it having been deeply involved in the affairs of the enterprise since then, it will not be correct to say that what happens to the said enterprise is a matter of no concern to the Corporation. The Corporation has been invested with a legal personality, as it appears from article 10(2) of the Order, which provides, inter alia, that the Corporation shall be a body corporate, having a perpetual succession and shall by its name sue and be sued, and there can therefore be no doubt that such a Corporation has the necessary legal competence to raise a question as to the legality of an act which seeks to affect its scheme of administration and management of the enterprise which was purported to have been lawfully entrusted to it for such administration and management. When such a question is raised, the Court is bound to give its decision on the question in the light of the law applicable thereto. The Corporation also has its duties and responsibilities under the said Presidential Order and is accountable for all of its actions. If in course of discharging its duties which are regulated by laws the Corporation comes across an order of the Government which, in its opinion, is not in accordance with the provisions of the Older nor any other law, it will be its duty not to implement such an order but to place the matter before the appropriate authority for proper decision in the matter.</u>

<u>73. There is, however, another aspect of the case. When the jurisdiction of the Court of law has been invoked under Article 102(1) of the Constitution to make an order directing the Corporation to restore the Respondents firm to Respondents No.1 to 3 in compliance with the Government order of release of the enterprise on cancellation of its placement under the Corporation and the Court has called upon the Corporation to show cause why such an order should not be made in such a case, the Corporation has the bounden duty apart from the question of its powers and duties under the said Presidential Order, to state before the Court why it has not complied with the Government order and the Court is bound to decide upon the legality and enforceability of the Government order after giving a hearing to the Respondent Corporation.</u>

<u>74. The duty of the Court has been very clearly spelt out in the provisions of Article 102 of the Constitution under which the judgment under appeal was pronounced. Under the said provision, the High Court Division can make an order requiring the Corporation to act in accordance with the Government order of release and cancellation of placement of the Respondent’s firm, only when the Court judicially decides that the said orders are lawful and the Corporation 'is required by law' to act in accordance with the said orders. It will not suffice to say that it is a Government order and the appellant Corporation, which operates under President's Order No.27 of 1972 is subject to the control and superintendence of the Government and is therefore bound to carry it out, because the High Court Division is enjoined by the law as incorporated in Article 102 of the Constitution, to come to a decision that the Corporation 'is required by law" to restore the disputed firm to the Respondents. If the Corporation acts frivolously in raising untenable objections to the Government orders, it is for the Government to whose control and superintendence it is subject, to take appropriate action consistent with the rules of business applicable to the case. It relates to the internal management of the Corporation and the Court has nothing to do with it.</u>

<u>75. On all these considerations I do not think that there is any legal bar preventing the Corporation from raising, in an appropriate Court of law, a question as to the legality of an order affecting its administration and management of an enterprise placed under it under</u> <u>Article 10(1) of the Order, even though the said order is purported to have been made on behalf of the Government which exercise a kind of control and superintendence in accordance with the provisions of the said order.</u>

76. But as I have already held that the assets of the Respondent's firm did not vest in the Government and that as such the order of release made by Government cannot be said to be to be unlawful. I concur with the opinion of any learned brother Mr. Justice Munim that these appeals should be dismissed.

Order of the Court.

The appeals are dismissed.

End.
