full_judgment:
Fazle Munim, J.-In this petition under Article 102 of the Constitution the validity of a Notification dated 11.10.72 taking over the Petitioner's Industries and Public Notice published on August 25, 1974, inviting sealed tenders to sell out the Industries as an abandoned industrial unit has been challenged. Of the two petitioners, petitioner No.1 which is a Company incorporated ill the then East Pakistan in 1959, and the petitioner No. 2 who is a citizen of Bangladesh was functioning as the General Manager of the Company but was subsequently ousted forcibly by some people who managed to get an order from the Government taking over the industry in November, 1972. Facts of the case shortly stated, arc as follows:-

The paid up capital of the Company is Rs, 2, 75,000/-. The shares of the Company were held by the members of the family in the following ratio:-

1. Mr. Batual Bai-8.750 shares

2. Mr. Sajjad Hussain- 12.500 shares

3. Mr. Saifuddin-3.750 shares

4. Mr. Sabbir Hussain-2.500 shares

All the share-holders who belong to Dawoodi Bohra Community have been permanently residing at 43E, Cantonment Bazar, area Dacca and the directors in the Company till 1971 were as. follows:-

1. Mrs. Batual Bai wife of Mr. Sajjad Hussain.

2. Mr. Sajjad Hussain.

3. Mr. Saifuddin.

Mrs. Batual Bai is the wife of Mr. Sajjad Husain and Mr. Sabbir Hussain is the s/o of Mr. Sajjad Hossain. Mr. Sajjad Hossain and Mr. Saifuddin arc full brothers. The Petitioner No. 2 is the own nephew of Mr. Sajjad Hussain and Mr. Saifuddin. The Company is a family business under a joint family system and the petitioner No. 2 always lived with the family and still resides at 43E, Cantonment Bazar Area, Dacca. The petitioner No. 2 used to work in the interest of the factory of the Company at 158, Tejgaon Industrial Area right from the inception of the Company as a family property and used to look after the general interest of the family in the business. In 1971 the wife of Mr. Sajjad Hussain fell seriously ill and he left the country with his wife for treatment. But the other Director Mr. Saifuddin remained in the country Through. Soon after the liberation of Bangladesh a delegation of Dawoodi Bohra-Community of Dacca met the Acting President Syed Nazrul Islam and pledged their loyalty and allegiance to the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. The said public allegiance was also published in the "Morning News" and "Bangladesh Observer" on 7.1.72. All the four share-holders of the Company originally migrated from India and was domiciled in the then East Pakistan and are permanent residents and citizens of Bangladesh although Mr. Sajjad, Hussain and his family remained stranded in Pakistan due to the policy of Pakistan Government and could not return despite willingness.

2. After the emergence of Bangladesh the management of Mesrs. A. T. J. Industries, which I will call the Company, was taken over by the Government on 31.12.71.  On this day, Mr. Saifuddin, the Director of the Company was both present in Bangladesh, and managing the affairs of the Company. The Notification concerned which was not originally annexed to the petition but subsequently produced before us is as follows:-

"GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S

REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH

MINISTRY OF INDUSTRIES

NOTIFICATIONS

No. 186-SL-3Ist December, 1971 the exercise of the authority given by the Acting President's Order No. Sec-X1/1M/35/71/17, dated  the 30th the December 1971, the Ministry of Industries is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders, the management of the different industrial units mentioned in Groups 'A" to 'F' including all the properties and assets wherever located in Bangladesh, and to appoint the Management Board indicated under each group to operate the Mills and generally conduct all their affairs, including operation of bank accounts : GROUP 'F' (11)-TEJGAON Industrial Area. Miss. A. T. J. Industries Ltd. 158, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca-1 Against this taking over, a representation was made on behalf of the Company praying for its release as the said industries-could not be treated as abandoned property because all the share-holders were Bangladesh nationals. Having being satisfied by the representation and the supporting documents in support the Government passed the following order on 15.2.72 releasing the industries :-"Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh Ministry of Industries & Natural Resources, Bangladesh Secretariat, Dacca. No. 1A(96)72-242 dated 15. 2. 72.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM

As per Notification No. 186-SI dated 31.12.71 the management of M/s. A. T. J. Industries Ltd. 158, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca was taken over by the Government and was placed under the Management Board. It has now been decided by the Govt. to release the unit in favour of its owner subject to future govt. overall industrial policy. The owners are allowed to operate the unit including normal operation of Banking accounts.

Sd-/- K. A. Zaman,

Secretary

Ministry of Industries"

This order was followed up by another order subsequently passed on 3.3.72 by which the management of the Company was directed to be handed over to Mr. Saifuddin, one of the Directors, who was in Bangladesh and who was operating the Mill. This order is as follows:-

GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH MINISTRY OF INDUSTRIES & NATURAL RESOURCES, 58, DILKUSHA COMMERCIAL AREA, DACCA.

OFFICE MEMORANDUM

IN CONTINUATION OF THIS Ministry's No. IA(96)72-242 dated 15th February, 1972 the management of M/s. A. T. J. Industries Ltd., 158 Tejgaon industrial Area, Dacca may be handed -tier to Mr. Saifuddin, Director of M/s. A. T.J. Industries Ltd., 158, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca who is now available in Bangladesh to operate the Mill, with immediate effect.

Sd/- M. A. Rahim Mia

for Secretary

Ministry of Industries."

In pursuance of the aforesaid orders the management of the Company was made over to Mr. Saifuddin under the following memorandum :-

Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh Ministry of Industries & Natural Resources Directorate of Commerce Industries, 58, Dilkhusha Commercial Area, Dacca. Memo No. Cehm/72 Dated 3. 3. 72 In pursuance of the directives contained in Office Memorandum No. 1A (96)72-41(4) dated 3. 3. 72 issued by the Ministry of Industries and Natural Resources Government of People's Republic of Bangladesh, which imply the dissolution of the Management Board of M/s. A. T. J. Industries Ltd. 158, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca constituted under Notification No. 186-S1 dated 31. 12. 71 issued by the aforesaid Ministry, I; do hereby hand over the management of the firm to its Director, Mr. Saifuddin, today in the forenoon.

Sd/- Mir Muhammad Ali

Deputy Director of Industries

Planning & Development.

I do hereby take over the management of M/S. A. T. J. Industries, Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca from Mr. Mir Muhammad Ali, Deputy Director of Industries (P & D).

Sd/- (Saifuddin)

Director,

A. T. J. Industries Ltd."

After the release of the Industrial units the Company began to function smoothly. On 14th April, 1972, Mr. Saifuddin appointed the petitioner No. 2 to supervise and manage all the business of the Company. The letter of authority is as follows:-

"A. INDUSTRIES LIMITED

Manufacturers of Rubber Goods.

Specialist in Manufacturing Footwear & Rubber Sheets, Importers & Exporters Office: 158 Tejgaon Industrial Area Dacca the 14th April, 1972.

I authorise my nephew Mr. Abbasbhoy S/o Mr. Kurban Hussain to supervise and manage all the work of my above factory. M/s. A. T. J. Industries Ltd. Tejgaon Industrial Area, Dacca. I also give him full authority to run the factory as may be deemed necessary.

Sd/- (Saifuddin)

Director.

M/s. A.T. J. Industries Ltd."

In September, 1972, Mr. Sajjad Hossain and his wife executed a general power of Attorney constituting and appointing the petitioner No. 2 as their lawful Attorney to manage the affairs of the Company. The Power of Attorney has been annexed to the Petition and marked "E" In the meantime Mr. Sajjad Hossain and the members of his family who were in Karachi affirmed affidavits before the Notary Public in Karachi declaring that they were citizens of Bangladesh and owed allegiance to the Government of the People's Republic of Bangladesh. Photostat copies of the Affidavits have been annexed to the petition and marked 'D' D-1 and D-2.'

3. Most unfortunately, but not quite unexpectedly, a group of miscreants entered the premises of the Company on 28th May, 1972 and took away both the sale proceeds of the day amounting to Taka 54,451/- and also Kidnapped Mr. Saifuddin, the Director of the Company, Inspite of the best efforts of his family members and the petitioner No. 2, Mr. Saifuddin has remained untraced till today. In the circumstances which arose out of the kidnapping of Mr. Saifuddin, the petitioner No. 2 took over the complete charge of the Company despite some opposition from the people around him. The petitioner No. 2 got co-operation from the Jatiya Sramik League which issued a certificate allowing him to resume the duties as General Manager of the Company. A photostate copy of the certificate has been annexed to the petition and marked 'G'. Thus while the petitioner No. 2 was acting as General Manager, the Collector of Customs and Excise also accepted his authority to deal with the affairs of the Company and allowed all the clearances of the Company on his signature. A copy of the older of the Assistant Collector of Customs and Excise which has been annexed to the petition and marked 'fib is as follows :-

"Governments of Bangladesh  Office of the Assistant Collector of Customs & Excise, Dacca Division-II.

C. No. IV/F(3) Rub-Excise /66 dated

To The Superintendent Customs & Excise, Dacca.

Sub:- Assessment at clearance of goods manufactured by M/s. A. T. J. Industries, Ltd.

Ref :- Your C. No. IV/R-1(ii) Plastic/66/ 3588 dt. 4. 7. 72 and 3600 dated 5. 7. 72.

In consideration of documentary evidence furnished by Mr. Abbas Ali in support of the authority letter 14. 4. 72 issued by Mr. Saifuddin Director of the firm authorising him to factory and the Affidavit dated 4. 7. 72 furnished by Mr. Abbas Ali, it is hereby ordered that clearances of M/s. A. T. J. Industries Ltd. may now be allowed by the Excise officers in the signature of Mr. Abbas All until otherwise directed.

Sd/- A. M. F. K. Khan, Chowdhury

Assistant Collector,

Customs & Excise, Dacca II/-Dv."

4. With the kidnapping of Mr. Saifuddin some complications arose inasmuch as a case being Tejgaon P. S. case No. 1749(5) 72 under sections 364/380/120B B. P. C. and P. 0. No. 50 of 1972 was instituted. An employee of the Company named Abu Jafar was arrested. The said Abu Jaffar was, however, subsequently enlarged on bail but the case is still pending against him. A copy of the forwarding letter and the order sheets granting him bail has been annexed to the petition and marked 'I' and 'I-1'. ...Though the petitioner No. 2 was being frequently threatened and on several occasions was stopped on his way to the factory, he was carrying on the operation of the mill till the following notification dated 11. 10. 72 was issued by the Deputy Secretary, Ministry of Industries. Under their notification the Company including all its assets and properties were taken over by the Government:-

"GOVERNMENT OF THE PEOPLE'S REPUBLIC OF BANGLADESH MINISTRY OF INDUSTRIES (INDUSTRIES DIVISION)

No. IR-XV-15/74 dated 11. 10. 72

NOTIFICATIONS

In pursuance of powers under Articles 4 and 5(2 ) (a) (b) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 'and the, made thereunder, the Ministry of industries is pleased to take over with immediate effect and until further orders M/s. A. T. J. Industries, Limited, 158, Tejgaon Industrial area, Dacca including all its properties and assets and to authorised Mr. Abu Zafar, Manager of the unit to run it. He shall operate the mills and generally conduct all its affairs including operation of Bank Accounts subject to the Control and super-vision of the Divisional Management Board, Dacca City and adjoining area.

Sd/- M. S. Islam

Deputy Secretary.

No. IR-XV-15/72/401(7) dated 11. 10. 72 Copy forwarded for information and necessary action to:-

1. Mr. Abu Zafar, Manager of M/s. A. T. J. Industries Ltd.158, Tejgaon Industries Area, Dacca. He is requested to submit a report to this Ministry at an early date on the action taken in light of the above order 5. He is further requested to submit regular weekly reports to this Ministry on the prescribed performs.

2. The Commissioner, Dacca Division and Chairman, Divisional Management Board, Dacca.

3. M/s. A. T. J. Industries 158, Tejgaon Industries Area, Dacca.

4. The Director-General, Industries Depart-meet, 58, Dilkhusha C. A. Dacca with reference to this Memo No. IPB/2319, dated 31. 8. 72.

5. O. S. D. Government printing press, Tejgoan, Dacca with a request to publish it in the next issue of the Gazette.

6. Master file.

Sd/- A. F. M. Noorul Islam.

11/10/72.

SECTION OFFICER.

5. Not only the order of taking over the Company was surprising but the order authorising the aforesaid Abu Zafar to operate the Mill as Manager was equally, if a not more, surprising. Having had no other alternative, the petitioner No. 2 handed over the unit to the said Abu Zafar on 18. 10. 72. Subsequent to the taking over of the Company under the aforesaid order, several representations were made to the Government including one before the Ministry of Industries on 15. 11. 72 giving all the necessary details and all the copies of the documents in support of the ownership and management of the Company. A copy of the said representation before the Ministry of Industries has been annexed to this petition and marked 'L'. Nothing tangible, however, happened on the representations made by the petitioner No. 2 as well as his lawyer.

6. So far as Mr. Sajjad Hussain and his family members are concerned, it has been claimed that the Ministry of Home Affairs, Government of Bangladesh, being satisfied that Sajjad Hossain is a Bangladesh national allowed his representation by the order dated 14th June, 1973. A copy of the Government Order has been annexed to the petition and marked 'P'. Mr. Sajjad Hossain who could not come earlier to Bangladesh due to the continued serious illness of his wife, has now arrived on a passport granted by the Government of Bangladesh which was issued to him on 5th January, 1975 by the Bangladesh Embassy in Kabul.

7. Against this back ground Mr. Moudud Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner contended that:-

(1) The Company which is registered in Bangladesh cannot be considered 'abandoned property' within the meaning of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control and, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 and as such could not be taken over by the Government on 11. 10. 72.

(2) That once the Government released the said Company by its order dated 15. 2. 72, it had no power to retake it, as has been done in the present case, and

(3) In the absence of a show cause notice enabling the Company to explain its position, the properties and assets of the said Company could not have been taken over.

8. As regards the first contention, the learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that so far as the first order dated 31. 12. 71, under which the management of the Industrial unit belonging to the Company, was taken over, is concerned, it merely shows that it is not the Company which was taken over but only its property and assets were taken for a limited purpose, namely, for the purpose of managing and operating them and also the Bank account. Nowhere the order shows that the shares of the Company (which indicate its ownership) were taken over by the Government, but the legal position which arose from the order is that though the Company management of the properties and assets were taken over by the Government for the time being, the ownership of the Company was not disturbed and it remained intact. On the other hand the Company, being a distinct legal entity which is separate from and different than the entity of the shareholders of the Company was very much present in Bangladesh on the relevant date, because it was registered in the territory which subsequently formed the State of Bangladesh. In support of the proposition that with the formation of a Company and its incorporation under law, no individual shareholder of the Company remains the owner of the properties and assets of the Company the learned Advocate referred to, the case of Solomon Vs. Solomon (1897) A. C. 22."

9. Since, however, the first order of taking over on 31st December, 1971 was subsequently rescinded on 15. 2. 72 there is no need to consider its legality any more than will be required in connection with the consideration of the question whether the properties in question taken over under this order could be considered as abandoned property within the meaning of the Abandoned Property (Control and Disposal) Order, 1972.

10. In order to consider whether the properties and assets of the Company which were taken over (under Bangladesh Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial and Commercial Concerns) Order No. 1 of 1972, (Acting President Order No. l of 1972) could be treated as abandoned properties within the meaning of the Abandoned Property Order (President's Order No. 16 of 1972), it is necessary to refer to certain provisions of this Order. Article 2(1) of the Order provides as follows:-

"(1) 'Abandoned Property' means any property owned by any person who is not present in Bangladesh or whose whereabouts are not known or who has ceased to occupy, supervise or manage in person his property, including'.

'Explanation:-"Person who is not present in Bangladesh includes any body of persons or company constituted or incorporated in the territory or under the laws of a State, which at any time after the 25th day of March, 1971, was at war with or engaged in military operations against the People's Republic of Bangladesh".

This Article deals with the definition of abandoned property Article 4 provides that:-

"On the commencement of this Order, all abandoned properties in Bangladesh shall vest in the Government and shall be administered, controlled, managed and disposed of, by transfer or otherwise, in accordance with the provisions of this Order"

This Article vests the abandoned property in the Government which is empowered to do all acts mentioned therein in relation to such property.

11. Since also the question has been raised whether the properties taken over by the Government under the impugned order were merely properties and assets of the Company or shares in such company the provisions of Article 8 of Order l6, 1972 are necessary to be quoted. It provides as follows:-

"8(a) the Government shall be deemed to be the registered holder of such shares and, notwithstanding anything in the memorandum or article of association of the Company or in any agreement or instrument, shall have the rights in the matter of making a requisition for the convening of a meeting or of presenting a petition to the Court under the provisions of the Companies Act, 1913 (Act of 1913) or under any other law or under the articles of association or in any other matter as the person whose shares have vested in the Government had immediately before such vesting, and

8(b) the Government shall have the power to acquire, at its option, all or a portion of the remaining shares in such Company in the prescribed manner or such terms as it deems fit. "

Irrespective of the question whether the properties taken over were .shares or the physical asserts of the Company which we shall representaly consider, we may proceed to consider whether there existed the necessity to serve a show cause notice before the order to take over was issued. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that there is such a necessity particularly when the order is in respect of a person's right property. In a case recently decided by LIS, to which I was a party, M. R. Khan Vs. Bangladesh writ petition No. 189 of l973 (1975) 27 D.L.R. 602 which is precisely on the point, namely, whether an order affecting right to property can be made without giving its owner a prior opportunity of being heard. The answer we gave was in the negative. The learned Advocate for the petitioner relied upon M/s. Speed Bird Navigation Vs. Bangladesh (1975) 27 D.L.R. 170, in which he appeared, to establish the same point. In this case the court had to consider the question:- Whether the assets and business of the petitioner firm were taken over by the Government under the Bangladesh (Taking over of Control and Management of Industrial "and Commercial Concerns) Order, 1972 (Acting President's Order No. I of 1972) and whether the said assets and business of the petitioner firm could be rightly regarded as abandoned property within the meaning of Article 2 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control Management and Disposal) Order, 1972) (President's Order 16 of J 972) and vested in the Government under Article 4 of the said Order? This decision is, however, more concerned with another aspect which is also relevant to the determination of the present case, namely, the formation of opinion by the Government as to whether the absence of the owner is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh.

<u>12. The wording of Article (2) of the Abandoned Property Order (President's Order No. 16 of 1972) implies the necessity to ascertain : (1) whether the owner of the property in question is present in Bangladesh (2) Whether his whereabouts were or were not known or (3) whether it was being supervised or managed by the owner in person If, upon ascertaining these things it appears that the owner of the property is absent but it is being properly occupied, supervised or managed, it cannot be treated as abandoned property. Again, if the owner is absent from Bangladesh leaving the property uncared for the Government is required to form an opinion that his residing outside Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh which empowers the Government to treat the property as abandoned, but if the Government has formed a contrary opinion, the property cannot be treated as abandoned property. Could the ascertainment of the questions referred to above be done unilaterally by the Government without serving a show cause notice on the owner of the properties concerned. There may by hundred and one reasons why the owner of a property might not have been present in Bangladesh at the relevant time and his absence from Bangladesh could under no circumstances be viewed as prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh unless the necessary opinion has been formed by the Government. If the atmosphere prevailing ill the Country for a couple of months following the emergence of Bangladesh be recalled and judicial notice may be taken of the uncertainly which forced some people to go in hiding, this was, of course, natural in the context of events that proceeded the emergence of Bangladesh. Many an owner might even have in such circumstances, lacked the courage to make their presence in Bangladesh known. Again, due to the unsettling effect of the change over many others might have temporarily been unable to occupy, supervise or manage their property in person. What can possibly be expected in the normal circumstances and peaceful conditions of society cannot be the yardstick to judge of the behavior of the people in an abnormal condition. Due to these circumstances the Government's obligation was all the more imperative to afford such owner an opportunity of being heard before their properties were taken over. If after the service of any notice to show cause against the taking over of any properly as abandoned property, the owner did not appear or respond to such a notice, the Government was at liberty to take over such property as abandoned property. In saying so, we do not import any limitation into the language of Article 2 of the Abandoned Property Order which is not there, the implications showing the necessity of serving a show cause notice are so obvious and appear so clearly from the wording of the Article that we are compelled to construe it accordingly.</u>

13. We now turn to the principal question raised in the case, namely, whether the properties taken over by the Government could be treated as abandoned property. It is felt that whether any show cause notice was served upon the owner or not, there are no materials in record to show that the Government formed an opinion either about the ownership of the property or whether the absence of even the supposed owner, the shareholders and not the company, (which must be considered to be the owner of the Company's assets and properties) was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The learned Advocate for the petitioner submitted that the Government proceeded on the wrong assumption that the property taken over by it belonged to the individual share-holders, some of whom were absent on the relevant date when the properties and assets were ordered to be taken over on 31.12.71. The properties and assets taken over by the Government did. it was submitted, belong to the Company which was not absent from Bangladesh within the meaning of Article 2 of the Abandoned Property Order, such property cannot be said 10 have been owned by the individual shareholders, some of whom, of course, were not present in Bangladesh on the date the properties in question were taken over. Secondly, even if some of the shareholders of the Company might have been away from Bangladesh, the Government did not form any opinion before the taking over was ordered whether, assuming that they were the owners of the properties in question, their absence from Bangladesh was prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. I entirely agree with following observations in M/s, Speed Bird Navigation Co. vs. Bangladesh (1975) 27 D.L.R. 170. The observations are as follows;-

"On the considerations set forth above it is clear that the definition clause is to be read as a whole in the light of the title and the preamble and also as an integral part of the Presidential Order. Whenever any question arises as to whether the property of an absentee owner can be taken to be an abandoned property it shall have to be seen if there is the necessary opinion of the Government as to the purpose of his absence. In the absence of such an opinion the property of an absentee owner cannot be regarded as abandoned property."

<u>14. In this connection Mr. K. Z. Alam, the learned Deputy Attorney General, drew our attention to the provisions of Article 4 and Article 8 of the Abandoned Property Order. With reference to the former Article, he submitted that since under its provisions the vesting of the ownership in the Government is automatic, there is no necessity to make an order showing that the Government had previously formed an opinion whether the absence of the owner from Bangladesh is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. This submission seems to me like putting the cart before a horse. For, how could the Government decide that a particular property as abandoned, assuming that its owner is absent from Bangladesh, unless it forms an opinion that his absence is prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. The logic of the circumstances is such that no property can be treated as abandoned property unless the Government has formed an opinion about the nature of absence of it owner and unless the formation of such opinion is established, the concomitant result would be that the property cannot be viewed as having vested in the Government as abandoned property.</u>

<u>15. Secondly, as was submitted by the learned Deputy Attorney General, since all the shares in the Company vested in the, Government under Article 8 of the Abandoned Property Order, the Government became the owner of the Company itself and as such the Government may take over its properties and assets as has been done in the present case, This position cannot so readily be conceded because the difficulties mentioned in the preceding paragraphs will stand in the way of the Government becoming the owners of the sharers. If the shares were considered to be abandoned property, the Government was equally under the obligation to notify its owners that they have become abandoned property due to their absence from Bangladesh, which absence is considered by the Government to be prejudicial to the interest of Bangladesh. No materials were produced before us to establish that the above requirements of law were fulfilled by the Government. Moreover, none of the impugned orders, namely, the order dated 31.12.71 and 11.10.72 respectively show that the properties taken over were shares in the Company. There is nothing before us to show that the Government first proceeded to take over the shares in the Company and then took over the properties belonging to the Company. It straight away dealt with the physical properties and assets of the Company, as if they became owner-less or were left uncased for. Moreover, there is no indication as to what the Government decided with respect to the shares which belonged to Mr. Saifuddin, one of the directors of the Company.</u>

16. In order to show that the vesting of the abandoned property was automatic and no express order was necessary, the learned Deputy Attorney General referred to the pro- visions of rule 182 of the Defence of the Pakistan Rules, 1965 and also the provisions of Order 22 of the Civil Procedure Code. He also referred to the case of Guru Das Saha Vs. The Deputy Custodian, Enemy Property (L. B.) East Pakistan and ors (1968) 20 DLR 683 in P.L.D. 1969 (Dac) 841. In view of the language employed in the Abandoned Property Order, and which I have just considered, it will be difficult for me to accept that the provisions of rule 182 or Order 22 of the Civil Procedure Code are relevant to construe the provisions of the Abandoned Property Order as to enable the .Government to make an order in the manner as has been done by it.

<u>17. Apart from the objections regarding the nature of the properties in question and the corresponding authority of the Government to treat them as abandoned property, the learned Advocate for the petitioner raised another substantial question as to the power of the Government to cancel or revoke the earlier order or release dated 15.2.72 and making an order treating the properties in question as abandoned property. There are no provisions in the Abandoned Property Order, which empower the Government to revoke the earlier order of release passed by Itself. It is true that under section 21 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 an authority which has the power to make an order has also the power to revoke or unmake it. If the circumstances mentioned above did not intervene between the order of release on 15.2.72 and the order of revocation on 11.10.72 there might have been some justifications to uphold the power to revoke an earlier order. Since It has now been established that neither the Company whose ,properties and assets were being taken over was absent from Bangladesh nor did the Government take the shares of some of the shareholders who were temporarily absent from Bangladesh and since also it is seen that those shareholders were making serious attempts to get back to Bangladesh and particularly when they succeeded in getting the required permission from the Government of Bangladesh to come back here as the nationals of Bangladesh and since further no opinion was formed by, the Government that their absence from Bangladesh was prejudicial to the interest of the Country, it would, indeed, be stronger to say that the power to revoke the earlier order of release has been rightly or properly exercised. If the Government claims to have exercised its inherent power to revoke an earlier order passed by itself, this Court has Jurisdiction to see whether in the particular facts and circumstances of the case the power has been justly exercised. Since the order of release created a legal fight in favour of the petitioners, the same could not be revoked in order to destroy It. Vide Pakistan U. M. H. Farukhi, (1969) 21 DLR S. C. 238 P.L.D. 1969 S. C. 407.</u>

<u>18. It has been painful for us to see the opinion expressed by the Section Officer of the Ministry concerned which, of course, was also endorsed by the Secretary and which ultimately led to the order of revocation, as will be seen from the earlier order of released, the Secretary of the Ministry of Industries made the order. The latter order of revocation passed on 11.10.72 was passed by the Deputy Secretary to the same Ministry which is preceded by the opinion of the Section Officer just mentioned above. He says "It is not understood how the unit was released to a person who holds only 10 per cent share". This has been quoted in the affidavit-in-opposition. We shall not be guided, it is true, by this sort of opinion but we were amazed to see the impertinence of the remark by an officer subordinate to the Secretary regarding the correctness of his opinion. Be this as it may, in the absence of any express provisions in the Abandoned Property Order itself empowering the Government to revoke an order of release which was passed after due consideration of the objection placed before it by the appropriate person and the lack of materials to show that in doing so the Government had ample justifications, we cannot but hold that the impugned order dated 15.10.72 has been passed without lawful authority and is, therefore, of no legal effect. If the Company is the owner of the properties and assets which were ordered to be taken over, which the Company is, as we have already held above, and, further, if it be that the shares of the Company were not taken over by the Government, no order to this effect has been produced before us, and finally when the Government itself has allowed the shareholders to come back to Bangladesh as the nationals of Bangladesh, the Government should not have passed the impugned order.</u>

<u>19. Illegality also seems to have attached to the order of revocation due to another important principle. Since the earlier order passed in favour of the petitioner released the property, it was obligatory upon the Government to have afforded the person concerned, whether it be the Company or the shareholders of the Company, the opportunity of being heard whenever its or their right to property was going to be affected by the proposed order. The Government is required to act judicially or, in other words, it must act on the principle of natural justice which requires it to notify the person whose right to .property was going to be affected by its order.</u>

20. Mr. K. Z. Alam the learned Deputy Attorney General, was vehement in his objection regarding the locus standing of the petitioner No.2. As he was neither a Director nor a shareholder Of the Company be should not have been impleaded as a party nor was be empowered to affirm the petition under Article 102 of the Constitution. In order to show that the petitioner No.2 did not have valid authority to affirm the petition under Article 102, the learned Deputy Attorney General referred to the Power of Attorney which was executed by Mr. Sajjad Hossain and his wife in Karachi on 17th September.1972 empowering him to do various acts, such as prosecuting any suit or application before any Court or defend any action on behalf of the Company. A photostat copy of the power of attorney which has been annexed to the petition and marked as 'E', does not show that it was stamped as required under the Stamp Act, for being acted upon in Bangladesh. He also referred to the letter of authority given by Mr. Saifuddin, one of the directors of the Company on 14th April, 1972. It will be seen from the letter itself that the petitioner No. 2 was empowered to run the factory as its Manager.

21. In addition to these documents showing the authority of the petitioner No.2, Mr. Moudud Ahmed, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, referred to the resolution of a meeting of the Board of Directors, which is annexed to the affidavit-in reply and marked 'X' to show that the petitioner No. 2 was appointed General Manager of the Company on 1. 6.1 72 with immediate effect. By this resolution he was authorised to do all acts and things as may be necessary to run and supervise the affairs, or the operation of the Company. He, further, pointed out that whether the petitioner No. 2  had any authority to present this petition under Article 102 of the Constitution on behalf of the Company can be challenged only by any other shareholder of the Company, the Government cannot be said to have become the shareholder of the Company. He referred to Articles 51 and 55 of the Articles of-the Association of the Company and also the provisions of Order 29, rule (I) of the Code of Civil Procedure. The learned Advocate relied upon Messrs. Allen Brothers V.S Aruri Mal Khanna A.I.R. 1925 (Lahore) 338, and All India Reporter, Ltd. Bombay with Branch at Nagpur and another Vs. Ramchandra Dhondo Datar, A.I.R. 1961 (Bombay) 292. In the latter case it was observed as follows:-

"In the case of companies the plaint can be signed by either a Secretary or a Director or other principal officer under 0.29, R. I., Civil Procedure Code, or by any person duly authorised by the Company under 0.6, R, 14. The words "duly authorised" in 0.6,

R. 14, need not be restricted to mean authorised by proper written authority or by power of attorney."

He further submitted that the Government had power to dissolve the Board of the Directors under Article 8(2) of the Abandoned Property Order, but since the Government had not done so, the Government did not become the shareholders of the Company.

<u>22. Besides these documents showing the authority of the petitioner No. 2, the learned Advocate for the petitioner, submitted that since Mr. Sajjad Hossain is now in Bangladesh and filed 2 affidavits in reply and also the supplementary affidavit on two different dates ratifying the act of the petitioner No. 2. valid objection can be taken as to the maintainability of the petition. For this proposition he relied on A.I.R. 1961 (Bombay) 292 referred to in the preceding paragraph. No contrary decision was shown to us to refute the proposition advanced by the petitioner's learned Advocate. In the aforesaid circumstances the maintainability of the petition would seem more plausible than doubtful. In addition, the presence of Mr. Sajjad Hussain, the Managing Director of the Company, during the hearing of the petition is an additional factor which contributes to its maintainability.</u>

23. For the reasons stated above, we are of the opinion that the impugned order i.e. Notification dated 11.10.72 public Notice published on 25.8.1974, inviting sealed tenders to sell out M/s. A. T. J. Industries Limited as an abandoned industrial unit are declared to have been passed without lawful authority and the industries including its properties, both movable and immovable, assets and Bank's account are being held by the Government without lawful authority. We direct that the said Company (A. T. J. Industries Ltd.) and its assets including Bank accounts be immediately handed over to Mr. Sajjad Hossain, the Managing Director of the Company.

In the result, the Rule is made absolute We however make no order as to costs.

Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.—I agree.

End.

full_judgment:
Md Abdur Rashid J: Both the appeals were presented by the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner at Comilla against the decree dated 29-7-98 passed by Subordinate Judge, Court No.1 at Comilla in Title Suit No. 58 of 1997, which decreed the suit.

2. Respondent No. 1 as plaintiff on 3-9-97 instituted the suit for specific performance of a contract dated 16-1-95 for sale of the suit land along with shops thereon as described in schedule-1 (Kha) to the plaint and also for possession thereof.

3. Plaint case, in short, is that the land comprising of 11 plots as described in schedule-1 to the plaint measuring about 35.35 decimals consisted of an industrial unit, namely, Rupkatha Cinema Hall at Comilla. In 1977, the Ministry of Industries took over possession of said Rupkatha cinema hall as abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972 through the Deputy Commissioner at Comilla. Pursuant to the disinvestment policy, on 25-5-79 said Ministry. invited tenders for sale of said Rupkatha cinema hall and the plaintiff along with others took part in the bid. Quotation of the plaintiff was accepted as the highest bid. Upon deposit of 20% of the quoted price as down payment, on behalf of said Ministry a deed of agreement was executed for the sale of the cinema hall at Taka 31,15,000 and on 26-10-79 an authorised officer on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner at Comilla delivered possession of the cinema hall to them. After receipt of the rest of consideration of Taka 31,15,000, a Senior Assistant Secretary on behalf of the Ministry, executed and registered a sale deed being No. 2726 dated 12-6-94 transferring 22.92 decimals of land only along with cinema hall building and other adjuncts thereto.

4. Further case of the plaintiff is that an area of 12.43 decimals of land of plot Nos. 210,209,208 and 203 with eight shops thereon as described in schedule 1-(kha), which was part and parcel of said cinema hall, was left out from the tender notification, and also the deed of agreement and consequently, from the deed of sale. Then, the plaintiff made an application to the Ministry of Industries mentioning said omission and expressed his desire to purchase said left out land with the shops. The Ministry accepted his prayer and the value of schedule-1 (Kha) land was settled at Taka 3,38,182 and on 25-2-93, the plaintiff deposited said amount in favour of the Ministry of Industries. Then, defendant No. 1 asked the plaintiff to pay value of the structures of said schedule property. Value of the structures was on 16-6-93 determined through an Executive Engineer (Building) at Taka 6,33,256. As directed, the plaintiff deposited 25% of the valuation Taka 158,328 as down payment and the Ministry of Industries upon receipt of the money on 16-1-95 made an agreement with plaintiff to transfer said schedule 1-(Kha) property and allowed three equal instalments to pay rest of the price. But it did not deliver possession. On 30-8-95 the plaintiff also deposited first instalment of Taka 1,58,314.

5. Then, the Ministry started to avoid executing and registering necessary sale deed in respect of schedule-1(Kha) in spite of receipt of Taka 6,54,770. On 11-8-97 the plaintiff came to know from the officials of the Ministry that they would not give him any sale deed. Hence, the plaintiff was constrained to institute the suit.

6. Defendant No.4, Government of Bangladesh, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla alone contested the suit by filing a written statement. Its case, in short, was that after original owners left the country, schedule-1 (kha) property became enemy and ultimately, vested in the Government. The Deputy Commissioner, Comilla on behalf of the Ministry of Land was in control and management of said shops of schedule 1 (kha) by granting lease on receipt of lease money from eight lessees since 1977. Some of the lessees were tenants under the original owners. The Ministry of industries never took over possession of said property as abandoned property. Schedule-1(Kha) was not part of the industrial unit, Rupkatha cinema hall. The Deputy Commissioner as district Administrator never handed over possession of said property to the Ministry of Industries. The Ministry of Industries never granted lease to any of the lessees. The lessees never ever admitted the Ministry of Industries as lessor of said 1-(kha) property. Determination of the value of the property by any order of said Ministry or payment of any money on the basis of such determination must be held to be without any lawful authority and jurisdiction. The Ministry of Industries was never in management and possession of the schedule 1 (kha) property. The agreement as claimed by the plaintiff with the Ministry of Industries must be held to be illegal and not enforceable in law. The lessees shopkeepers were still in possession peacefully.

7. On the pleadings following issues were settled:

a.	whether the suit was maintainable in the present form;

b.	whether the plaintiff was entitled to get a decree for specific performance of the contract as prayed for; and

c.	to what relief, if any, the plaintiff was entitled to

8. In support of his case, the plaintiff. examined him alone as PW 1 while said defendant examined 4 witnesses. Plaintiff adduced a copy of registered kabala No. 2726 dated 12-6-94, one agreement dated 16-1-95 and three receipts, which were marked as Exhibits-1 to 5.

9. By impugned decree, learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit. Hence the appeal.

10. Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan, learned Senior Advocate for the appellant in First Appeal No.425 of 1998 submitted that the plaintiff having miserably failed to prove that scheduled 1-(kha) shops were ever pall of the Rupkatha cinema hall and was left out from the tender notification, first agreement for sale of the cinema hall and in the absence of any proof that the Ministry of Industries ever took over possession of said property, learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in holding that schedule-1(Kha, property seemed to be abandoned property and not vested property.

11. He submitted that the plaintiff having full knowledge from the very beginning that the schedule-1(Kha) shops was never treated as industrial unit and never a part of the industrial unit, namely, Rupkatha cinema hall, taken over and transferred as an abandoned property by the Ministry of Industries, obtained the agreement dated 16-1-95 on false representation from the Ministry of Industries and learned Subordinate Judge erred in law in granting a decree for specific performance of such agreement.

12. He submitted that after the original owners left the country, schedule-1(Kha) vested in the Government as non-resident property and the Deputy Commissioner on behalf of the Ministry of Land granted lease of said property to different shopkeepers who were in. possession as lessees on payment of lease money and usual rents and the Ministry of Industries having made the agreement dated 16-1-95 in the absence of any authority and the plaintiff having obtained the agreement on false representation, such agreement must be held to be not enforceable in law. In support, he cited a decision of the House of Lords in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction Ltd, [1951] 2 All England Reports 278 and that of the Supreme Court of India in Delhi Cloth and General Mills Ltd vs Union of India, AIR 1987 SC 2414.]

13. He also read the Rules of Business and submitted that under said Rules administration of industrial units was assigned to the Ministry of Industries while vested and non-resident property including shops, etc to the Ministry of Land. He also read article 7 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order 1972 and article 9 of  The Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over possession) Rules, 1972 submitted that the shops could never be subject for the Ministry of Industries and any agreement obtained from such ministry in respect of such shops could not be enforceable in law and, as such, the learned Subordinate Judge fell in serious error in granting specific performance of such agreement.

14. Mr AJ Mohammad Ali, appearing in other appeal, submits that the plaintiff contracted to buy schedule-1(ka) property comprising of the Rupkatha cinema hall at a consideration of Taka 31,15,000 vide agreement dated 26-10-79 but got the kabala executed and registered by the Ministry of Industries showing a price of Taka 4,06,240 only in the sale deed. Such a plaintiff could always misrepresent and, in fact, through misrepresentation to said Ministry of Industries in making them to believe that the suit shops of schedule-1(Kha) belonged to said ministry, got an agreement executed on 16-1-95 and such agreement obtained through misrepresentation cannot be enforceable in law.

15. On the other hand, Mr Mahmudul Islam, on behalf of the plaintiff, took us through the record and submitted that defendant No.4 miserably failed to prove that the suit shops vested in the Government as nonresident property, as the trial Court found.

16. He submitted that in 1977 no property could lawfully vest in the government as non-resident property and, the control and management by the Deputy Commissioner of the suit shops must be held to be on behalf of the Ministry of lndustries.

17. He also took us through the topography of the suit shops and the deed of sale dated 12-6-94 Exhibit-1 and submitted that the plaintiff purchased 4.5 decimals of land with the verandah, booking counter and the main entrance covered by the roof of the southern building of the cinema hall and the land measuring 12.34 decimals with the suit shops thereon covered by the same roof must be held to be the integral part of the cinema hall and was left out from the said transaction; and with the taking over of possession of the cinema hall, the Ministry of Industries took over possession of the suit shops as well. The Ministry of Industries, therefore, did not commit any mistake in entering into an agreement with the plaintiff to sell the suit property and the learned Subordinate Judge did not commit any mistake in granting a decree for specific performance of the contract.

18. Whether or not the learned Subordinate Judge was justified in decreeing the suit in the facts and circumstances of the case and on the evidence on record is the main issue before us.

19. The plaintiff instituted the suit for specific performance of a contract dated 16-1-95 for sale of the suit land measuring 12.34 decimals along with eight shops thereon as fully described in schedule-1(Kha) mainly against the Ministry of Industries. Said ministry was made defendant No.1 represented by a senior secretary. The secretary and a deputy secretary of said ministry were made defendant Nos. 2 and 3. Again the Government of Bangladesh represented by the Deputy Commissioner at Comilla was made defendant No.4. Said defendant No.4 alone contested the suit. None of the Ministry, however, appeared and contested the suit.

20. Main case of the plaintiff is that he agreed to purchase the Rupkatha cinema hall at a consideration of Taka 31,15,000 and deposited twenty percent of said consideration as down payment and upon receipt of said amount, on 26-10-79, the Ministry of Industries made an agreement to transfer; and delivered possession of said cinema hall. The RDC on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner at Comilla put him into possession. Then, on behalf of said ministry, one deputy secretary on 12-6-94 executed and registered a sale deed being No. 2726 transferring 22.92 decimals of plot Nos. 211, 212, 206, 207, 202, 204 and 205 along with the cinema hall building with third class booking room, manager room, proprietor room, representative room, night guard room and latrine at the west of the cinema hall and 4.5 decimals of parts of plot Nos. 203, 208, 209 and 210 with the verandah, booking counter and the main entrance covered by the roof of the southern building of the cinema hall.

21. Besides said land of 22.92 decimals, the structures were described in the schedule to the deed of sale as follows:

1. cinema hall building measuring in detail 5250 square feet;

2. third class booking room, manager room, proprietor room, representative room, night guard room and latrine at the west of the cinema hall measuring 1131 square feet and

3. 4.5 decimals of parts of plot Nos. 203, 208, 209 and 210 with the verandah, booking counter and the main entrance covered by the roof of the southern building of the cinema hall measuring 1534 square feet.

22. As stated above, on 2.6-10-79 the plaintiff got possession of said cinema hall with the aforesaid structures on the basis of an inventory made by the RDC on 23-10-79. On 3-9-97 the plaintiff instituted the suit claiming that an area of 12.43 decimals of land of plot Nos. 210, 209, 208 and 203 with eight shops thereon as described in schedule 1 (kha), which was part and parcel of said cinema hall was left out from the tender notification dated 4-4-79, the deed of agreement dated 26-10-79 and from the deed of sale dated 16-1-95.

23. In order to succeed in the suit, the plaintiff was required to prove that said schedule-1(Kha) property was part and parcel of the industrial unit, namely, Rupkatha cinema hall and left out of said tender notification, agreement and sale deed. Burden, therefore, is upon the plaintiff to prove that he did not obtain the agreement dated 16-1-95 from the Ministry of Industries without making any misrepresentation to get a sale deed in respect of said schedule-1(kha) properties and said ministry had the authority to make the agreement.

24. The plaintiff in support of his plaint case deposed as PW 1 that defendant No. 1 was the Ministry of Industries represented by one senior assistant secretary and defendant Nos. 2 and 3 the secretary and deputy secretary of said ministry. Defendant No. 4 Government of Bangladesh represented by Deputy Commissioner, Comilla was made proforma defendant. The suit property comprised of 11 plots. The Rupkatha industrial unit comprised of 35 decimals of land of said 11 plots. In 1977, the Government took over the cinema hall as abandoned property and managed through the Ministry of Industries, On behalf of said Ministry, the Deputy Commissioner Comilla controlled and managed said property. Pursuant to the tender 16 persons participated. As the bid of the plaintiff for Taka 31,15,000 was highest it was duly accepted. He deposited 20% of the quoted price as down payment and an agreement was executed on 25-2-79 and possession of the cinema hall was handed over to him by the RDC as representative of the Deputy Commissioner. Main entrance to the cinema hall, ticket counter, manager-room, waiting verandah covered by the same roof were also handed over to him. On receipt of Taka 31,15,000, a senior assistant secretary of the Ministry of Industries on 12-6-94 executed and registered the sale deed transferring the cinema hall. The property of schedule-1 (Kha) was inseparable part of schedule-1(ka) and was omitted or left out from the tender notification, the agreement and the deed of sale.

25. Then, he applied to the Ministry of Industries for purchase of said schedule-1(Kha) property and the price was settled at Taka 3,38,142. On 25-2-93 he deposited said amount of Taka 3,48,142 vide receipt Exhibit 2. Then, price of the structures of said schedule-1(kha) property was determined at Taka 6,33,256. On 22-12-94 he deposited Taka 1,58,318 as twenty five percent of the price as down payment vide receipt Exhibit 3. Then, on 16-1-95 on behalf of defendant No. 1 an agreement for sale of said schedule-1(kha) property was executed, Exhibit-4. The agreement stipulated that rest of the money was to be deposited in three equal installments. Upon receipt of the remainder, said ministry would execute and register necessary sale deed in term of the agreement. The ministry did not hand over possession of said schedule-1(kha). On 30-8-95 he further deposited Taka 1,16,950 with interest in favour of the ministry vide receipt Exhibit 5. In total, he paid Taka 6,54,770. When he went to deposit rest of Taka 3,1.6,628, defendant No. 1 declined to receive further amount and declined to hand over possession of said property. Lastly, on 11-8-97 said ministry refused to execute and register necessary sale deed in respect of said schedule-1(Kha) property. He therefore, instituted the suit for specific performance of the contract dated 16-1-95.

26. In cross-examination, he stated that he did not file any paper evidencing that the Ministry of Industry ever took over possession of said schedule-1(kha) property. He also did not file any order of said Ministry of Industries evidencing treating said property as abandoned. He could not say at what date the suit property was taken over as abandoned property. He also did not file the inventory of taking over and making over of the first schedule property by the Ministry of Industries. He also did not file any paper to show that the Deputy Commissioner took over possession on behalf of the Ministry of Industries of the suit property. He did not see any government decision about disinvestment of first schedule property. On 25-10-79 possession of schedule-1(ka) property was delivered to him and on 26-10-79 the agreement with the Ministry of Industries for sale of schedule-1(ka) was executed. Price of schedule-1(ka) was settled at Taka 31,15,000 and within 9 years of the agreement, he deposited the entire money. On 12-6-94, the sale deed was executed and registered in his favour in respect of schedule-1(ka). There were seven plots in schedule-1(Ka) land which was transferred to him by the sale deed. Land of schedule-1(Kha) was outside the tender notification, the agreement and registered deed of sale and was also outside the schedule of disinvestment of the abandoned property. He informed said ministry about the omission in 1980. (No evidence was, however, produced in support). He did not file any paper evidencing disinvestment in respect of schedule-1(kha) property. He was in possession of the main entrance, special counter, first class counter, viewers waiting room on the verandah measuring about 4.5 decimals of land. In the rest eight decimals, there were 8 shops. None was evicted from said 8 shops measuring about .0793 decimals. He was not aware as to whether said schedule-1(kha) was leased out as abandoned property. Said 8 shops were leased out by yearly basis. He did not produce any paper to show that the property of schedule-1(kha) was disinvested. The Deputy Commissioner was leasing out the property of schedule 1(kha) since 1977. He was not aware as to whether the Deputy Commissioner leased out property of schedule-1(kha) as vested and non resident property. He did not inform the Ministry of Industries that the Deputy Commissioner leased out. He did not know who the abandoned owners of the land were. Original owners of schedule 1(kha) migrated to India long back. Schedule-1(kha) property was owned by the vested property authority and situated at centre of the Comilla town.

27. On the other hand, defendant No.4 examined one Prodip Kumar Raha as DW 1, He stated that there were 8 shops on the suit land. Those shops were there for last 50 years. Original owner Uttor Chand Khetry leased out 5 shops and Ramchand Khetry leased out rest 3. Names of the tenants of Uttor Chand Khetry were (1) Narayan Saha, Bastra Niketan, (2) Jogesh Chandra, Tritul Bastralaya, (3) Mrinal Chandra Bhattarcharjee, Bengal Works, (4) Late Taruni Mohan Raha, his father, Khadi Ghar, (5) Late Jagannath Majumder, Satya Store and Boikunta Babu. Tenants of Ram Chanda were (1) Baikuntha Babu, Roy Brothers, (2) Jogen Paul, Paul Brothers and (3) Anil Das, shop of betel leaf. They were tenants under the old landlords. Out of old tenants, three of them were still possessing. Rest 5 tenants got lease from the government. He knew that Rupkatha cinema hall was sold as abandoned property. The 8 shopkeepers obtained lease from the government in 1977 and they were still continuing as such. Said shops were never abandoned property. The original owners of said shops migrated to India long ago and their property vested in the government as enemy property and the Ministry of Land was managing and controlling the suit shops.

28. In cross-examination, he stated that Uttor and Ram Chand Khetry were the owners of the cinema hall. The viewers of the cinema hall used to go through the main entrance between the shops. Main entrance, first class counter, special counter and the shops were covered by same roof. After the shops vested in the government they took lease as vested property. He denied that the suit shops were part of the cinema hall.

29. Aftabuddin Ahmed was examined as DW 2. He corroborated DW 1 that there were 8 shops. Uttar Chand and Ram Chand Khetry were the original owners. There was a shop under the name of Aftab Brothers. He got possession of said shop in 1967 from Baikuntha. He paid rents to Ram Chand Khetry. Ram Chand Khetry and Uttor Chand Khetry went to India and schedule-1(kha) property became enemy. They 8 shopkeepers took lease from the office of Deputy Commissioner in 1977 as vested property. They took lease of those shops which the plaintiff knew.

30. In cross-examination,. he stated that Uttor Chand and Ram Chand Khetry were owners of the cinema hall and those shops. The entrance to the cinema hall and the shops were under the same roof. Behind the shops, there were a counter under the same roof.

31. DW 3 Swapan Kumar Podder also corroborated DW 1 and DW 2 that there were 8 shops. They were doing business since 1953. Original owners were Uttor Chand Khetry and Ram Chand Khetry. They went to India. They took lease as enemy property. The Ministry of Industries never gave them any notice claiming the property as abandoned property. He denied that said shops were part of the Rupkatha Cinema Hall.

32. DW 4 Fazlur Rahman deposed as VP Toshilder. He deposed on behalf of the Deputy Commissioner Comilla. He stated that original owners were Uttor Chand and Ram Chand Khetry. There were 8 shops for more than 35 years. Present lessees were tenants under the original owners. They granted lease vide VP Case No. 114 of 1977. The suit shops were never handed over to the Ministry of Industries as abandoned property. Nor the Ministry of Industries ever gave any notice treating the property as abandoned property. Lessees were never tenants under the Ministry of Industries. The agreement created in respect of said shops was illegal and void. He denied said shops were part of the cinema hall. The Ministry of Industries had no authority to make an agreement. Original 8 files of leasing out the schedule-1(Kha) property were tendered in evidence.

33. In cross-examination; he stated in 1995 he joined the office. He denied that the Ministry of Industries had the authority of making an agreement in respect of schedule-1(kha).

34. From close scrutiny of the above testimonies and the sketch map, we find that eight shops of schedule-1(kha) are situated at the south of the cinema hall facing the main road Kandirpar in the centre of Comilla town. The shops are standing on an area about 12.43 decimals of land of plot Nos. 203, 208, 209 and 210. Behind the shops, there was a verandah, booking counter and main entrance to the cinema hall on 4.5 decimals of said four plots. The main entrance passed through the middle of the shops. The shops along with said structures were covered by same roof and this building is situated on the south of the cinema hall separated by an open space.

35. The cinema hall was an industrial unit and, as such, in 1971 the Ministry of Industries took over possession of the cinema hall as an abandoned property. The Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Industries) Rules, 1972 defines 'industry' meaning any abandoned industry within the meaning of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972. The plaintiff failed miserably to prove that said shops were ever treated as part of the industrial unit, cinema hall.

36. There is of course evidence that the owners of the shops were owners of the cinema hall. What was the nature of the ownership, proprietorship or corporate could not be ascertained for want of evidence. But this much is clear that with the taking over possession of the cinema hall, the Ministry of Industries did never take over possession of said schedule-1(kha) property and never ever tried to treat said property as abandoned property. Evidence, on the other hand, particularly of DW 1 to DW 4, overwhelmingly proves that the Deputy Commissioner managed and controlled said property as vested and non-resident property.

37. Mr Mahmudul Islam strenuously argued that as the land measuring 4.5 decimals of plot Nos. 203 and 208 to 210 with the booking counter and the main entrance to the cinema hall thereon and said shops described in schedule-1(kha) were covered by the same roof, said shops must be held to be part of the cinema hall. With the taking over possession of the cinema hall with the above structure and entrance, etc, possession and control of the shops were also deemed to have been taken over by the Ministry of Industries, he claimed.

38. Such submission did not appeal to us in any way. First, not only under the same roof but also in the same house, there may be existence of more than one industrial unit. Similarly, there may be shops and/or clubs, etc in the same building along with an industrial unit. With the taking over possession of the industrial unit, possession of such shops and/or clubs would not vest in the Ministry of Industries.

39. Secondly, if the facts were not so, then the plaintiff did not take 25 years to come up with such claim. On 26-10-79, the plaintiff admittedly got possession of the structures as adjuncts to the cinema hall on the basis of an inventory. During his possession of the cinema hall, he never ever complained about said schedule-1(kha) property. In 1997, he instituted the suit claiming that said schedule-1(kha) property was part and parcel of the cinema hall and with the taking over of possession of the cinema hall, the Ministry of Industries got the control of said shops as well as abandoned property. He, however, failed to produce all iota of paper to support his claim. There is, therefore, no escape from the conclusion that it was the discovery of the plaintiff as an afterthought in order to grab said schedule-1(kha). The evidence on record proves that the existence of the shops in question was distinct and separate from the cinema hall.

40. The positive defence case is that schedule 1(kha) property vested in the Government as non-resident property and the Deputy Commissioner was managing the property, as such, by leasing out since 1977. Learned Subordinate Judge rejected such case.

41. It is on record, original owners Uttor Chand Khetry and Ramchand Khetry were the owners of said shops. Both of them admittedly migrated to India long back. When they actually left the country could not be ascertained. They belonged to minority Hindu community. In all likelihood, they might have migrated to India before Bangladesh came into being. If not so, and had they been in Bangladesh after the creation of Bangladesh, there would have not been any dearth of evidence on their departure. If they migrated to India before the prescribed day, then said shops became enemy by operation of law and for that no order was necessary to declare them enemy. Enrollment of enemy property was necessary for management of such property till final decision was taken. It is true that no property could become enemy and then, vest in the Government after 16 February, 1969 when Ordinance I of 1969 came into force at the earliest on 27 November, 1976 when Ordinance XCII of 1976 came into force at the latest. But once a property became enemy by operation of law before that prescribed day, taking possession and control of such property by the Deputy Commissioner in 1977 cannot be said to be illegal and invalid.

42. The learned Subordinate Judge, therefore, missed the relevant law and fell in serious error in rejecting the defence case that schedule-1(kha) property became enemy with the migration of the original owners long ago and then, vested in the Government. He also committed serious error that said property seemed to be abandoned property and not vested property as the defendants failed to prove that the property vested lawfully in the Government as non-resident property, against evidence on record.

43. Under rule 2(c) of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Industries) Rules, 1972, "industry" means an abandoned industry.' Such restrictive definition does not include shops. Under the Rules of Business, administration of industrial units was placed under the Ministry of Industries while vested and non-resident property including shops in the Ministry of Land. Shops, therefore, could not be claimed to be placed in the management and control of the Ministry of Industries.

44. We find the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla representing Government of Bangladesh presented both appeals through two Deputy Attorneys-Generals. How on earth there could be two appeals by same authority against the same decree. Latter appeal was presented by Mr A J Mohammad Ali, learned Additional Attorney- General. We were looking for hearing from anyone of the Ministry of Industries. Mr Mohammad Ali brought all the relevant files from the ministry and informed us that he could not find a single piece of paper evidencing said ministry ever took over possession and/or control of those shops or treated them as abandoned property.

45. But on 13-3-04 an affidavit of facts on behalf of the Ministry of Industries was sworn by one Prasanta Kumar Das as an Assistant Secretary of said ministry and filed by an Assistant Attorney-General. She filed the affidavit without any authority from said ministry, In the affidavit, number of papers were annexed, The deponent claimed that the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla took over possession of Rupkatha Cinema Hall holding and was in possession of the land in question on behalf of said ministry, He did not stop there, At paragraph 10, he further claimed that the shops standing on plot Nos, 203, 208, 209 and 210 were under the same roof. So, those shops were part and parcel of the cinema hall. Said shops were also under the management of the District Management Board headed by Deputy Commissioner, Comilla. It must be mentioned that none of the papers supports his claim.

46. Pursuant to the affidavit, the Deputy Commissioner, Comilla promptly filed an affidavit sworn by the ADC (Rev), Comilla annexing number of letters including one dated 21-3-04 of the Deputy Commissioner addressed to Mr Abdul Wadud Bhuiyan. In the letter, the Deputy Commissioner informed him that the disputed shops were never under the management and/or control of the Ministry and the shops were all along being managed as vested property. At the instruction of Ministry of Land, the Deputy Commissioner was managing the shops as vested property.

47. So, this is the position of the Government of Bangladesh. We wanted to know the actual position from the standpoint of the Ministry of Industries but it failed us. In view of the evidence on record, such affidavits are of no help. Nor woe should act upon such affidavits.

48. Another pertinent question may arise, as the property vested in the Government, and the Ministry having made an agreement for sale of said property on behalf of the Government and received money pursuant to such agreement, why the plaintiff would not be entitled to a decree for specific performance.

49. In similar situation, Mr Denning LJ in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction Ltd, [1950] 1 All England Reports 542 expressed himself more forcefully,

"Whether the Government officers, in their dealings with a subject, take on themselves to assume authority in a matter with which the subject is concerned, he is entitled to rely on their having the authority which they assume. He does not know, and cannot be expected to know, the limits of their authority and he ought not to suffer if they exceed it. That was the principle which I applied in Rebertson vs Minister of Pensions and it is applicable in the present case also."

50. In appeal therefrom in Howell vs Falmouth Boat Construction Ltd, [1951] 2 AII England Reports 278, the House of Lords, however, reversed Mr Denning. On 'behalf of the House, Lord Simonds opined.

"My Lords, I know of no such principle in our law nor was any authority for it cited. The illegality of an act is the same whether or not the actor has been misled by an assumption of authority on the part of a Government officer, however, high or low in the hierarchy. I do not doubt that in criminal proceedings it would be a material factor that the actor had been thus misled if knowledge was a necessary element of the offence, and in any case it would have a bearing on the sentence to be imposed; but that is not the question. The question is whether the character of an act done in face of a statutory prohibition is affected by the fact that it has been induced by a misleading assumption of authority. In my opinion, the answer is clearly: No".

<u>51. On the doctrine of promissory estoppel, the Indian Supreme Court held in Delhi Cloth & General Mills Ltd vs Union of India, AIR 1987 SC 2414-</u>

<u>"It is, however, quite fundamental that the doctrine of promissory estoppel cannot be used to compel the public bodies or the Government to carry out the representation or promise which is contrary to law or which is outside their authority or power. Secondly, the estoppels temps form equitable doctrine. It, therefore, requires that he who seeks equity must do equity. The doctrine, therefore, cannot also be invoked if it is found to be inequitable or unjust in is, enforcement."</u>

<u>52. We could not find any reason to differ with the above principle of law on the limitation of the Government functionaries in dealing with subject on behalf of the Government. An authority not empowered by the Rules of Business or otherwise to deal with any subject and/or represent the Government cannot act on behalf of the Government and any action by such authority, how high or low in the hierarchy, cannot bind the Government. An act done by assumption of authority, however, by misrepresentation or inducement or ignorance, cannot be enforced in law. Mr Mahmudul Islam, however, did not press his case on the doctrine of estoppel.</u>

53. We are of the view that the Ministry of Industries had no authority to deal with schedule-1(kha) property in any way far less to make any contract and/or receive any money pursuant thereto to transfer such property and the plaintiff led them to believe that they had such authority and obtained the agreement dated 15-1-95 through false representation. When the Ministry understood their position, they took their hands off the matter and declined to execute and register the necessary deed of sale as per requirement of the plaintiff. The agreement dated 16-1-95 for sale of schedule-1(kha) property, therefore, cannot be enforced in law.

54, In the above view of the matter, the learned Subordinate Judge committed serious error in decreeing the suit and such decree cannot be sustained in law.

55.  Appeals, therefore, succeeds.

56. In the result, both the appeals are allowed with cost. Impugned judgment and decree are hereby set aside.

57. The suit is dismissed. The Ministry of Industries is now obliged to return the money received in respect of schedule-1 (kha) property to the plaintiff.

Send down the LCR at once.

End.
