case_source: (From the judgment and Decree dated 29-6-67 & 1-8-67 passed by the Dacca High Court in S.A. No. 1081 of 1961)
full_judgment:
The Judgment of the Court was delivered by D. C. Bhattacharya, J.—This appeal by special leave at the instance of one of the plaintiffs of a suit for a declaration of title to and recovery of possession of a certain property is against a judgment of the Chief Justice of Dacca High Court, sitting singly, allowing a Second Appeal and dismissing the plaintiff's suit. It raises the question as to whether under the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act, (Act xv of 1856) a Hindu widow forfeits her right to her deceased husband's property on her remarriage.

2. The predecessor-in-interest of the appellants along with respondent No. 13 brought the suit for recovery of possession of a property on a declaration of their title thereto. The disputed property belonged to one Ramchandra. Malta, who died several years ago, leaving behind a widow named Jagadaya Mallani, who inherited her husband's property as his sole heiress. A few months after the death of her husband the said widow having remarried one Bokhan Malla, the property she inherited from her previous husband, according to the plaintiff's case, stood forfeited and devolved on one Akaluram the reversionary heir of the said property. Akaluram thereafter settled a part of the property with respondent No. 13 and sold the rest of the property to the predecessor of the appellants. The said lessee and the purchaser, having been resisted in their attempt to take possession of the disputed property by the defendants on the pica of title alleged to have been acquired by the said defendants from Jagadaya Mallani, instituted the suit for recovery of possession.

3. The defendants sought to make out a case in their written statement firstly that there was no remarriage of Jagadaya Mallani with Bokhan Malla but she lived with him as his concubine and secondly, that there having been a custom of remarriage in the community to which the Mallas belonged, there was no forfeiture of the property she inherited from her husband on account of remarriage.

4. It was argued at the trial Court on behalf of the defendants, relying upon a Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Bhola Ungar Vs. Mst. Kausilla. A.I.R. 1932 All 617 that even if remarriage of Jagadaya was proved the provision of the Act IV of 1856 had no application to the facts of the case, as there was evidence to show that there was a custom of remarriage among the Mallas. The trial Court, however, in its judgment noticed that when the case of Bhola Umar vs. Mst. Kausilla came back to the Division Bench for disposal after the Full Bench had laid down the law as aforesaid in A.I.R. 1932 All 617, the Division Bench (Young and Niyamatullah, J J.) in explaining the decision of the Full Bench held in the said case, as reported in 1937 All 230, that the practice of widow remarriage after the Act had come into force should be referable to that Act unless it could be shown that the practice was an ancient custom, and remitted the case to the trial Court for the necessary finding, on taking evidence, whether there was such a practice of remarriage before the Act of 1856 had come into force. The learned Munsif also noticed the case of Sontala Bewa Vs. Bateswari Das 27 C.W.N, 669: A.I.R. 1924 Cal 68 in which it was held by a Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court that section 2 of the Act applied not only to the widows who could not marry before the passing of the Act but also to those who were not so precluded from remarrying either by law or by custom. On a consideration of the evidence on record and relying upon the decision referred to above, the trial court came to the finding that there was no such evidence as showed that the custom of remarriage had been in vogue among the Mallas before the enactment of the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act, 1856 and as such held that the provision of section 2 of the Act was available in her case.

5. On appeal, the learned Additional District judge who beard the appeal affirmed the finding of the trial Court that there was no evidence to show that the custom of remarriage was prevalent among the Mallas before the promulgation of the Act and taking notice of a Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court in the case of Saudamini Roy Malakar vs. Narendra Chandra Barman, as 4 D. L. R. 492, dismissed the appeal holding, that both under the Act as well as under the principle of Hindu law, a Hindu widow by her remarriage forfeited her right to her husband's property even if remarriage Was allowed under the custom of her caste.

6. A Second. Appeal against the said judgment being heard by the learned Chief Justice of the Dacca High Court was allowed and the suit was dismissed. Learned Chief Justice, however, does not appear to have noticed the Division Bench decision of his own Court as reported in 4 D.L.R. 492 and also the preponderant view of all the High Courts of the sub-continent excepting that of Allahabad, but have laid down, solely relying upon the reasonings given in the Full Bench decision of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Bhola Umar Vs. Mst. Kausilla, the proposition that section 2 of the Act did not apply to a case where remarriage of the widow had taken place in accordance with the custom of the caste to which she belonged. It was also not noticed in the Judgment of the High Court that, according to the Allahabad view, the evidence or proof of the custom of widow remarriage should be referable to the prevalence of such custom before the Act came into force and that the specific finding of trial Court, as affirmed by the lower appellate Court was that there was no such evidence or proof. The said finding was not, however, set aside by the High Court which allowed the appeal merely on the basis of the existence of such a custom, as has been found by the learned Chief Justice himself on the assessment of the evidence in Second Appeal.

7. Special leave to appeal was granted in this case, by the Supreme Court of Pakistan to consider the question, whether under the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act, 1856 a Hindu widow, by remarriage forfeited her right to her husband's property even if such remarriage was allowed by the custom of her caste, as there was divergence of judicial opinion on this point.

8. It should be pointed, at the outset, that, so far as the Dacca High Court was concerned, a Division Bench of the sail Court consisting of Shahabuddin, C.J. and Faiaz Ali, J, has given a well considered judgment on this question in the case of Saudamini Ray Malaker Vs. Narendra Chandra Barman, 4 D.L.R. 493 after reviewing all the conflicting authorities and accepting the view of the High Court of Calcutta, Bombay, Madras and Lahore and dissenting from the view of Allahabad High Court. The judgment of the learned Additional District Judge which was reversed by the High Court was, as a matter of fact, specially referred to the said Division Bench decision of the Dacca High Court. It seems a bit strange that the said decision, which appears to have been binding upon the learned Chief Justice, escaped his notice at the time of delivery of the judgment. However, special leave to appeal was granted for considering this question in view of the divergence of judicial opinion. We have, therefore, tried to examine this question closely afresh,

9. Mr. Gholam Rabbani, learned counsel appearing on behalf of the appellant, has cited before us several decisions and texts in support of the rule of forfeiture of a widows interest is her deceased husband's property on her remarriage, even if her remarriage is according to the custom of her caste and Mr. Yasin learned Counsel, has, on the other hand, addressed us on behalf of the respondents in support of the contrary view.

Md. Birendra Nath Chowdhury, learned Counsel on being requested by the Court, has appeared in this case as an Amicus Curiae and has made his submissions on the basis of the decided cases and treatises relating to the Hindu Law in support of the rule of forfeiture.

10. The controversy as to whether, notwithstanding the provision of section 2 of the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act, 1856, a Hindu widow in whose caste or community there is a custom of widow remarriage or the one who contracts a valid remarriage under any law, loses her interest in her previous husband's property on her remarriage is about a century old. The earliest decision on the point appears to be one of Madras High Court in the case of Murugayi Vs. Viramakali (1877) I.L.R. I Mad. 226 where a Division Bench of the said Court, relying upon Smriti Chandrika' which lays down that a Hindu widow inherits the property of her husband as the surviving portion of her husband, and also taking note of the enquiries embodied in Steele's Hindu Castes that it was a practice of a wife or a widow among the Shudra caste of the Deccan on remarriage to give up all the properties to her husband's relations, held that the widow who had remarried must be regarded as no longer surviving her husband and as such not entitled to lay any claim to the properties left by her husband. This case appears to have been decided solely on the principle of Hindu Law and no reference appears to have been made in this decision to the Act of 1856. After the aforesaid Madras decision, came the first of the series of the decisions of the Allahabad High Court, namely the case of Har Saran Das Vs. Nandi and another (1889) I.L.R.11 Ali 330, which referring to the preamble of Act XV of 1856 held that the Act was passed for enabling a person to remarry who could not remarry before the Act was passed and that section 2 of the said Act did not, therefore, apply to persons who were allowed by the custom, to which they were subject, to remarry.

11. The first important case in which the Calcutta High Court had to deal with Act XV of 1856 and overruled an earlier decision of the said Court, namely, Gopal Singh Vs. Dhungazee (1864) 3 W.P. 206 is the Full Bench decision in the case of Matungini Gupta Vs. Ram Rutton Roy (1891) I.L.R. 19 Cal 289. It was, of course, not a case of a widow who had a customary right of remarriage but the case of one who remarried a Brahmo under the provisions of Act III of 1872 making a declaration that she did not profess Hindu religion. The question raised was whether section 2 applied to the case of a widow who renounced the Hindu religion at the time of her re-marrige and she forfeited her interest in her first husband's estate.

12. Wilson, J., in his referring judgment with which the majority of the Full Bench (Prinsep. J, dissenting) agreed, expressed the view that the forfeiture of the widow's estate on her remarriage was in accordance with the principal of Hindu Law, in the following passage of his judgment at page 292 :

"That view is clearly expressed in the Text of Vrihaspati which Jimutavahana makes the basis of his reasoning on the subject of a widow's estate (Dayabhaga XI, 1) : "of him whose wife is not deceased half the body survives. How then should another take his property while half his person is alive. This is difficult to reconcile with a right in a widow, who ceases to be the wife or half of the body of her late husband, and becomes the wife and half of the body of another man, to keep the estate of her late husband. The view that on principle a second marriage determines a widow’s estate is strengthened by the fact that where second marriages were sanctioned by custom, the further rule seems almost always to have followed, that such remarriage entailed a forfeiture of the first husband's estate. See the cases cited in Mayne's Hindu Law, section 512, and in West and Buhler Bk 1, Ch. 2, s. 7, Q.1 (3rd Ed. P 420) ; and again the adoption of the rule of forfeiture on second marriage in the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act (XV of 1856) seems to be an indication that the Legislature considered that rule to be in accordance with the principles of Hindu Law."

13. Gurudas Bannerjee, J., another refer ring Judge, in his separate judgment explained the principle of Hindu Law in the following manner:

"The widow's right of succession is based, according to the Dayabhaga, on the ground that she is half the body of her deceased husband, and is capable of conferring by her acts spiritual benefit on him. The widow takes her husband's estate, not because of past relationship, not because she was the wife of the deceased, but because, of the continuing. relationship, because she is still the patni housewife) of the deceased. This is abundantly clear from Chapter XI, section 1 of the Davabhaga, and in particular from paragraph 2 of that section, and if that is  so, it follows, as a necessary consequence, that the estate of a Hindu widow can last only so long as she continues to be the wife and half the body of her deceased husband ; that is, only so long as the relationship, by reason of which she inherits, continues, and the estate must be held to determine when she must cease to be the wife of her late husband and half his body by marrying another person. In other words, the Hindu widow's estate must be taken to be an estate during widowhood. This view has been recognized in the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act (XV of 1856), section 2, which declares that a widow remarrying loses all her rights in her deceased husband's estate.

14. Petheram C. J. (with whom all the , judges of the Full Bench, excepting Prinsep, J. agreed) in course of a short judgment agreed with the referring judges and stated his view in the following words :

"Section 1 no doubt relates to marriages between Hindus, but section 2 includes all widows who are within the scope of the Act, that is to say, all persons who being Hindus become widows and it must follow from this that if any such widow marries she is deprived by that section of the estate which she inherited from her Hindu husband. The words are clear-"All rights which any widow may have in her deceased husband's property by inheritance to her husband ;" the estate which a Hindu widow took upon her husband's death in his property is an estate which she takes by inheritance to him, and such estate is expressly determined by that section.

My answer to the question is, that by marriage the widow forfeited her estate in her first husband's property in favour of the next heir."

15. The case is which the Calcutta High Court had to consider this question as to forfeiture of a widow's inheritance to her husband on her remarriage, which is sanctioned by custom to which she is subject, was of Rasul Jahan Begum vs. Rain Saram (1899) I.L.R. 22 Cal '589 which expressed strongly in favour of the opinion that section 2 of the Act was applicable to such a case and noted its dissent from the view of Allahabad High Court taken in Har Saran Das vs. Nandi in the following words :

"It does not appear that the true position of the Hindu widow inheriting an estate of her husband was considered in that case."

16. The Bombay High Court in one of its early decisions in the case of Parekh Ranchor vs. Bai Vakhat (1886) I. L.R. 11 Bom 119 held that, on an interpretation of section 2 of Act XV of 1856 the said provision did not apply to the case of a widow in whose caste there was a custom of widow remarriage and remanded the 'case for a finding, if according to the custom of her caste, the property inherited from her first husband would be forfeited on her remarriage.

This view appears to have been over-ruled by a Full Bench of that High Court in the case of Vitto vs. Govinda, I. L. R. 22 Bom 321 which based its decision simply on the interpretation of the provisions of Act XV of 1856.

17. Farran, C. J., in giving a lucid exposition of his view in his referring judgment, made the following observation;

"Section 2 of Act XV of 1856, read by itself and without reference to the circumstances under which it was enacted, plainly extends to all Hindu widows irrespective of the caste to which they belong and to the special customs of such caste It reads like a law of universal applicability;

All rights and interest which any widow may have in her husband's property shall upon her remarriage cease and determine as if she had then died.

It would be difficult to use more general words, and in our opinion there is no sufficient indication afforded by the preamble or other provisions of the Act that the legislature intended to use them in a restricted sense--

18. The view of the learned Chief Justice with respect to the differing view of the Allahabad High Court, as stated in the following passage of his aforesaid referring judgment, may be appropriately quoted:

“In the judgment of the Court in Har Saran Das vs. Nandi (I.L.R. 11. All 330) it is said that the Act was not intended to apply to persons like Mst. Nandi, who could before it have remarried without thereby forfeiting the property inherited by them from their first husband. The answer to this appears to be two-fold:

(1) That it is an assumption without basis to attribute that absence of intention to the legislature; it is equally probable that they intended to assimilate the Hindu Law in this particular in all castes and to make the law as administered accord with the true principles of Hindu Law—Murugayyi vs. Virama Kali (1 Mad 224) and (2) that it is not allowable to cut down the express provisions of a law by a consideration of the supposed intention of the Legislature in passing it."

19. Ranade, J. after noticing the variation between the preamble and enacting clauses of the Act, expressed the following view on behalf of the Full Bench:

"It appears to me that the variation between preamble and the enacting clauses was not the result of an oversight but that the legislature deliberately used the mere general words in section 2 of the Act, because it found that while the custom of prohibiting remarriage obtained in certain castes and did not obtain in others in the matter of forfeiture by the widow of her all interest in her first husband's estate, there was no such divergence."

20. The Allahabad High Court, in two of its Division Bench decisions, namely, Ranjit vs. Radharani I. L. R. 20 All 476 and Khuddo vs. Durga Prasad I. L. R. 29 All 122, merely followed the earlier decision in Har Saran Das vs. Nandi, after noticing that Calcutta and Bombay High Courts had taken different views on the matter. In the case of Mula vs. Pratab, I. L. R. 32 All 489, Stanley, C. J. and Banerji, J. however, followed the earlier rulings of the Court with the following observation:

"This has been the course of rulings in the Court, and, although personally we may have hesitation in accepting this view adopted in those rulings, we think, we are bound by the unanimous course of decisions in this Court.

21. The question which arose in the case of Vitta Taya Ramma Vs. Chata Kandu Sivayya, I. L. R. 41 Mad. 1078, was whether a Hindu widow who became a Mohammadan and contracted a valid marriage according to Mohammaden Law forfeited her right in Hindu husband's property. It was conceded in that case that her conversion did not per se affect her right, which was saved by Act XXI of 1850. A view contrary to that expressed in  Murugeyyi vs. Virama Kali I.L.R. 1 Mad 226 having been pronounced in Choudappa vs. Narasamma (1917) 23 M. L. T. 81. the case of Vitta. Taya Ramma was referred to a Full Bench, the majority of which held (Sheshagri  Ayyar, J, dissenting) that the remarried widow would lose her right in her first husband’s property according to the provisions of section 2 of Act XV of 1856, Wallis, C.J. expressed the majority view in the following words at pages 1090-91 of the Report:

“But whatever may have been the rule in archaic times when remarriage was permitted, I think considering the ideas which in later Hinduism underlay the prohibition of Hindu remarriage as far possible and the encouragement of Sati that the retention by a widow of her deceased husband's estate is altogether incompatible with her renunciation of her status as a widow and I respectfully agree with the view of the Bombay High Court in Vitto Vs. Govinda that the invariable rule among so many castes in the Deccan that remarriage when permitted entailed the forfeiture of the first husband's estate is merely an illustration of that essential incompatibility, which was again recognised by the legislature was it enacted Act XV of 1856."

22. Learned Chief Justice proceeded further to state his conclusion as to the interpretation of the Act in the following words:

"Having regard to the generality of the language, the fact that the section was, in substance, though not in form, declaratory and the incongruity which would result from holding remarriage by the widows of Hindus to persons of another religion to be outside its scope. I think the more extensive and beneficial construction should be adopted."

23. The Patna High Court also expressed a similar view in the case of Mst Suruj Jotekuer vs. Mst. Attar Kumari I.L.R. 1 Pat. 706: A.I.R. 1922 Pat 378, following the decisions of the Calcutta and Madras High Courts.

24. A Division Bench of the Calcutta High Court appears to have taken notice of the differing view of the Allahabad High Court in the case of Sontala Bewa vs. Badaswari Dasi I.L R. 50 Cal 727, A.I.R.1924 Cal 98, 27 C. W. N. 669 and stated that the consensus of the judicial views of the Calcutta, Madras and Bombay High Courts were contrary to the view of the Allahabad High Court on the question of the interpretation of section 2 of Act XV of 1856 in the following words;

"The consensus of the opinion, so far as this Court and Madras and Bombay High Courts are concerned, is that the 2nd section of Act XV. of 1856 applies not only to widows who could not remarry before the passing of the Act but also to those who were not so precluded from marrying, either by law or by custom."

25. A single Judge of the Madras High Court after a review of the authorities of all the High Courts summarised very succinctly and clearly his conclusion in the case of Gajapathi Naidu and others vs. Jeevammal and others, A.I.R. 1929 Mad. 765, as to the state of law on the question respecting the construction of section 2 of Act XV of 1856 in the light of the said authorities in the following words:

"In view of the decision of this Court in Murugayee vs. Virama Kali, which has been followed both in this Court and in other High Courts ever since, the only conclusion to which I can come on the question whether sec. 2 Act XV of 1856 applies to a Hindu caste in which widow remarriage is permissible, is that it does. The reasons for this opinion are so well put in the referring judgment of Farran, C. J, and in the judgment of the Full Bench given by Ranade, J, in Vitto vs. Govinda that there is no need to repeat them. It is sufficient to say that if the rule of the general Hindu Law is, as it has been held to be, that even in cases of castes permitting remarriage the remarrying widow forfeits her interest in her first husband's property, the legislature must have had this clearly before it when enacting Act XV of 1956. This is also apparent from the first paragraph of the preamble where exceptions to the rule prohibiting remarriage are expressly referred to when, therefore, with this fact before it the legislature enacted section 2. by which Hindu widows on remarriage, are declared forfeit their interest in their first husband's property no new penalty or disability was being enacted, but statutory sanction was being given to what was then known to be the general Hindu Law. In short, what had been the general unwritten law of the Hindus was converted into an express and statutory enactment. On the question of construction, therefore, I am clearly of opinion that assuming that the firs defendant belongs to a caste where widow remarriage is permissible, her case would be within the forfeiture enacted by section 2."

26. The High Court of Lahore appears to have held is the case of Mst. Parj vs. Mahgta, A.I.R. 1930 Lahore 101, that according to the custom permitting widow remarriage to which the parties were subject the remarrying widow would forfeit her interest in her previous husband's property unless it was proved that there was a corresponding custom against such forfeiture and that the provision of the Act XV of 1856 would have no application to such a case.

27. In this state of judicial authorities of the Indian High Courts, a Full Bench of the Allahabad High Court had to review its exceptional stand on the question of interpretation of the provisions of Act XV of 1856, in the case of Bhola Umar vs. Mst. Kusilla, A.I R. 191.; All. 617, but after such review it decided to follow its own solitary course and reaffirmed its previous opinion. Sulaiman, C. J. in explaining the decision of the Full Bench formulated the principle underlying the construction of section 2 of Act XV in the following manner;

"In order to find out the true scope of the section one is compelled to look to the pro vision of that Act contained in section 1, as well as the preamble. No doubt, a preamble can never control or restrict the substantive provisions of an Act. It merely supplies a key to the interpretation of those sections or where there is any doubt as to the true scope of the provisions of that enactment, the preamble may be of some guidance. The Act was professedly passed with the object of removing all legal obstacles to the marriage of Hindu widows. The preamble stated that it was known Hindu widows, with certain exceptions, are held to be, by reason of their having been once married, incapable of contracting a second valid marriage and the off-spring of such widows, by any second marriage, are held to be illegitimate and incapable of inheriting, whereas many Hindus believed that this imputed legal incapacity, although in accordance with established custom, was not in accordance with the precepts of their religion and desired that the law should no longer prevent those Hindu widows who may be so minded from adopting a different custom. The Act was intended to relieve all such Hindus from this legal incapacity complained of and to remove all legal obstacles to the marriage of Hindu widows."

28. The learned Chief Justice sought to explain the rational of the view, held by the Allahabad High Court in its earlier decisions and also reiterated by the Full Bench, in the following words:

"The Allahabad High Court has accordingly held that the Act could never have been intended to apply and did not apply to those Hindu widows who by the custom of their caste had independently of the Act, a right to remarry. The point does not appear to have been emphasised in any of the previous cases nor does it appear to have been refuted in cases taking the contrary view that there is no option but to restrict the scope of section 2. That section cannot apply to all widows. It can only to a particular class of widows for whom the Act was intended. To ascertain that class one is compelled to look to the preamble, which shows that that class of widows consisted of those who were incapable of contracting a second valid marriage. This obstacle in their way was removed and their children were declared by enactment to be legitimate. The act was intended to render remarriage valid and legalize the legitimacy of children. It conferred a benefit on those who could not remarry, but at the same time imposed a restriction on them. It was not intended to deprive those who already possessed the right to remarry of whatever rights they enjoyed in their deceased husband's properties."

29. The learned Chief Justice criticised the decision of other High Courts on the ground that the said decision proceed “on an assumption of the prevalence of custom of forfeiture on remarriage" and on the supposed principles of Hindu Law to the effect that a widow inherited her deceased husband's property as her "surviving half of the body of her husband" and on her remarriage she ceased to be the surviving half of the body, which was, according to him, nothing but a picturesque metaphor," as was called by Sir Sheshagiri Ayyar in his dissenting judgment in Vista Tayaramma vs. Chata Kondu Sivayya I.L.R. 41 Mad. 1078. According to him, there was no such custom as to forfeiture of widow's right to her previous husband's property on her remarriage which was sanctioned by the custom of her concerned far as the United Provinces were concerned. As regards the principle of Hindu Law; the learned Chief Justice relied upon the decision of the Judicial Committee, in the unchastely case of Moniram Kolita vs. Keri Kolitan L.R, 7  I. A. 115 ; I.L.R. 5 Cal. 776, in holding that whatever injunctions there were in Texts like those of Vrihat Manu or Catyayana as to "keeping unsullied the bed of her lord" related to the right of succession to the property once it had vested and not to the retention of such property once it had vested in the widow.

30. Mukerji, J., in his concurring judgment in the said Allahabad Full Bench decision considered the question further and was of the view that the decisions of the other High Court did not give due importance to the preamble of the Act in considering the provision of section 2 of the Act. On the question of principle of Hindu Law the learned Judge observed that in the context of the conflicting Texts and the absence of any positive provision relating to forfeiture of a widow's interest in her husband's property on remarriage. it would indeed be bold" to lay down the only reason why a widow inherited under the Hindu law on the death of her husband was that she was one-half of her late husband's body not withstanding the Text of Jimuta Vahana wherein such a reason had been put forward. In any view of the matter, the learned judge thought it was not correct that the fine reasons which had been advanced from time to time by the sages on the basis of Hindu Law applied equally to the Shudras to which the parties belonged.

31. It is interesting, to notice that after the Full Bench had answered the question referred to it in the manner stated above, the case was laid before a Division Bench consisting of Young and Niamatullah, JJ. who in their decision, reported in A.I.R. 1937 All 30, took the view that the custom contemplated in the Full Bench decision must be an ancient custom prevalent before the Act XV of 1856 had come into force and expressed the said view, in the following words at page 231 of the Report :

"The practice of widow remarriage after 1856 in this community or in any other section of the Hindus may well be referable to the provisions of the Hindu Widows Re-marriage Act and would not necessarily be indicative of an ancient custom existing before the passing of the Act. Unless therefore, it is shown that the practice of remarriage is in pursuance of an ancient custom and not under the Act, the remarriage of a widow cannot be held to be under the custom of the caste."

32. There having been no such evidence on record in the said case, it was ultimately remanded to the Trial Court for findings on two issues under Order 41, rule 25 of the Code of Civil Procedure, namely, whether there had been any such ancient custom of widow re-marriage and whether, if there had been a corresponding custom, of forfeiture of widow's right to her previous husband's property.

33. The Allahabad High Court of Indian Jurisdiction appears to have been maintaining this position consistently, as it appears from the decision in the case of Union Bank Ltd vs. Mst. Ram Rati and others AIR 1954 All. 595, that a widow remarrying in the exercise of her customary right would not forfeit her right in her previous husband's property but that such a custom must be an ancient custom existing before the passing of the Act of 1856.

34. On the other hand, the other High Courts of Indian Jurisdiction, namely, Calcutta, Bombay, Madras, Madhya Pradesh, Nagpur and Orissa appear to have been maintaining their respective points of view by reiterating the proposition that a Hindu widow on remarriage would lose her right to her previous husband's property, both under the provision of section 2 of the Act XV of 1856 as well as under the general principle of Hindu Law, as will appear from the cases, namely, Lalit Mahan vs. Shayama Pada Das AIR 1942 Cal. 771 , Gurrupadappa Bassappa and others vs. Krishidappa Shivuba appa AIR 1954 Born 318 , Kishan Chatur Nal vs Arjun Shankar AIR Madhya Pradesh 429 , Mst Manabai vs Mst Chanclan Bai AIR 1954 Nag 284 , Hira Dei Badhu Sahu AIR 954 Orissa 172 , and Basappa and others vs Parwatamma and others AIR 1952 Hyderabad 99.

35. This point, however, seems to have lost all its importance since, so far as the Indian jurisdiction is concerned, after the passing of the Hindu Code 1956 where under the widows have been given absolute right of inheritance in the properties of their husband.

36. The Dacca High Court also appears to have examined this question, prior the instant case, in two of its decisions. A Division Bench of that Court (Shahabuddin, C J. and Faiz Ali J.) considered this question in the case of Saudamini Roy Malakar vs, Narendra Chandra Barman and another, 4 DLR 492 and after a review of the decisions of the different High Courts of the sub-continent has expressly dissented from the view of the Allahabad High Court and had expressed itself in favour of the view of the majority of the High Courts, in holding that under Act XV of 1856 and also under the principle of Hindu Law a Hindu widow by remarriage forfeits her right to the deceased husband's property, even if the remarriage is alloyed by the custom of her caste. In dealing with the reasonings of the learned Judges of the Allahabad High Court in the Full Bench Case of Bhola Umar vs. Mst. Kausilla, as the interpretation of section 2 of Act XV of 1856. Shahabuddin, C.J. in delivering the judgment of the Bench has made the following observation at page 503 of the Report:

"It is no doubt true that the preamble is a guide to the intention of the Legislature if there is any ambiguity with regard to the expressions used in the Act proper ; but we think that there is no ambiguity as far the expression 'any window's in section 2 is concerned. That being the case, the preamble of this" cannot restrict or extend the enacting portion."

37. On the question of the principle of Hindu law the learned Chief Justice has clearly stated that they agree with the view expressed by Wilson, J., on this point in his referring judgment in ILR 19 Cal. 289 and has observed as follows at page 506 of the Report:

"It is clear from the preamble to the Act that the intention of the legislature was to remove the disability which many Hindus felt to be not in accordance with the true interpretation of the precepts of their religion. That being so, legislature would never have imposed this serious disability with regard to the property of the deceased husband, had it not considered it to be in accordance with the precepts of Hindu Law. The decision of the Judicial Committee in 5 Cal. 776 that a widow does not forfeit her property inherited from her husband even though she becomes unchaste after inheriting it has been referred to by Mukerji, J., (in AIR t 932 All 617) in support of his view. But, as pointed out by Wilson, J. in 19 Cal. 289 at page 292. there seems to be a very broad distinction between misconduct on the part of a widow as a widow and her ceasing to be a widow."

The learned Chief Justice has added that on the principle of 'Stare decisis' also they would hesitate to disturb the view of the law which seems to have held the field for a long time in Bengal.

This view of the Division Bench was followed by a Single Judge of Dacca High Court (Nandi, J.) in the case of Rabia Khatun vs. Mahendra Chandra Mondal, 12 DLR 634.

38. On the analysis of the principles laid down in all these decisions referred to above, it appears that the question, whether a widow loses her right to her husband's property on her remarriage, which is sanctioned by the custom of her caste, has been approached mainly from two different stand points, namely, the one relating to the principle of Hindu Law and the other being solely a question of interpretation of the positive provision of section 2 of Act XV of 1856.

<u>39. All the High Courts of the Indian sub-continent except that of Allahabad have taken the view that under the general principle of Hindu Law, a widow entering into a lawful wedlock for the second time cannot retain the property of her previous husband. It is also the view of the said High Courts that the provision of section 2. of Act XV of 1856 which is not inconsistent with the general principle of Hindu Law is comprehensive enough to cover the case of a widow, whose remarriage is sanctioned by the custom of her caste and that she also forfeits her right to her previous husband's property on her remarriage by virtue of the said provision. On the other hand, the basis of the Allahabad view, as has been elaborated in the Full Bench decision in Bhola Umar vs. Kausilla, is that there is no direct and specific authority in any Text of the Hindu legal literature prescribing forfeiture of a Hindu widow's right to her husband's property on her remarriage. According to this view, whatever texts have been relied upon in support of the contrary view relate to actual succession of a widow to her deceased husband's property but do not deal with the question of the forfeiture of her right after it had vested in her on the death of her husband. On the question of the applicability of section 2 of the Act, it has been held by the said High Court that the preamble of the Act has restricted the scope of the Act which is limited only to those widows who were debarred, by virtue of their custom, from contracting a valid marriage.</u>

40. Let us examine these two propositions, one relating to the principle of Hindu Law and the other concerning interpretation of the provisions of Act XV of 1856 one after the other.

41. When we look for some positive provision of Hindu Law in the ancient Texts we are confronted with certain difficulties, as the legal system of the Hindu presents a changing pattern, in keeping with the changes in the socio-economic conditions of the community. The question which is facing us involves two aspects of legal relation the right of a Hindu widow to inherit her husband's property and her right of remarriage.

<u>42. Vedic literature, as has been observed by Dr. Mares Chandra Sen Gupta in his Tagore Law Lectures, 1950 'Evolution of Ancient Indian Law" at page 12, has very little to say about the proprietary right of wives. She was however not incapable of acquiring properties despite a saying of Mann that woman could hold no property, but her property was naturally small, ornaments, domestic utensils and the like. In different Texts of Smriti literature, several kinds of properties which might be owned by a woman were mentioned as Stridhan, which were, mainly, gifts and presents and did not include any inherited property. Women did not figure in the scheme of inheritance yet. The preservation of the family entity appears to have been the main concern of the early exponents of law and the law of primogeniture seems to have held sway in the early stages. Subsequently ancestral property was regarded as a sort of corporate property of the agnatic descendants of the ancestor and propinquity of blood was generally the basis of the law of inheritance. But gradually a change in the legal concept took place with the change in the religio-social ideas. Raj Kumar Sarbadhikari has described the evolutionary process in his "The Principles of Hindu Law of inheritance". Tagore Law Lectures, 1880 at pages 211-212:</u>

<u>"We thus see that the early legislators, the authors of the Dharma Sutras ignored the rights of women, and excluded them altogether from inheritance. But a change in the feeling is evident in the interval between the Dharma Sutras and the Metrical Smritis. Gleams of light were first described by Sankha who first introduced the religious spritit into the province of legislation. As the family knot became unloosened, the theory of spiritual benefits gathered strength and consistency Neither the last owner nor his father could have efficaciously performed sacrifices in honour of gods and ancestors, unless their wives assisted them; and it is but just, therefore, that the mother and the widow, through whose means both his father and himself were spiritually benefited, should share his estate after his death. It should never be forgotten that from the time of Sankha, religious principle which played. only a secondary part in regulating succession before him, became equal in importance to, if it did not supersede, the principle which recognised the preservation of the family as the first and highest aim of legislation. It was from the time of this legislator that the great struggle between the religious and communistic principles commenced, which ultimately resulted in effecting a compromise that gave to the Hindu world its present law of inheritance."</u>

43. None of the early legislators, viz, Goutama, Baudhayana, Apastambha or Vashistba" appear to have recognised the claims of women to inheritance. But after the efficacy of women's participation in religious obsequies for the spiritual benefit of the deceased had been recognised, as referred to above, the right of such women to the properly of the deceased also, by and by, received the recognition of some of the distinguished propounders of law, such as Briddha Manu, Vrihaspati and Katyayana as will be evident from the precepts quoted below: Briddha Manu:

"The widow of a childless man, keeping unsullied her husband's bed and persevering in religious observances, shall present his funeral oblation and obtain (his) entire share (Dayabliaga, IX 1, 7)" Vrihaspati:

"In scripture, in law; in sacred ordinances in popular usage, a wife is declared by the wise to be half the body of her husband, equally sharing the fruit of pure and impure acts:

"Of him whose wife is not deceased, half the body survives; how should another take the property while half the body of the owner survives:

"Although distant kinsmen although his father and Mother, although uterine brothers be living, the wife of him who dies leaving no male issue shall succeed to his share:

"Since she was previously espoused in due form, she must support the consecrated fire; and after the death of her husband the widow, faithful to her lord, shall take his wealth; this is a primeval law.

"Taking his effects, movable and immoveable, the precious and base metals, the grain, liquids and clothes let her cause the several sradd has to be offered in each month, in the sixth and at the close of the year."

Kalyayana:

Let the childless widow preserving unsullied the bed of her lord; and abiding with her venerable protector (i.e., father in law) enjoy with moderation the property until her death. After her, let the heirs take it."

<u>44. When in the 11th century Vijnaneswara sought to systematise the entire body of the Hindu Law into a complete Code, namely Mitakshara, on the basis of the Smritis as explained and developed through several centuries by various law givers, the above quoted sayings of Briddha Mann, Vrihaspati and Katyayana appear to have influenced his recognition of a childless widow's right of inheritance, as laid down in the following provision of Mitakshara:</u>

<u>"It is a settled rule that a wedded wife, being chaste, takes the whole estate of a man, who being separated from his co-heirs and not subsequently re-united with, them, dies leaving no male issue."</u>

<u>45. As is well known, different schools of law grew subsequently in different parts of India on the basis of the different commentaries of some distinguised jurists, such as Mithila, Benares, Maharastra and Dravida, wherein references to the sayings of Briddha Manu, Vrihaspati and. Katyayana on the question of a childless widow's right of inheritance were often made. Bengal however drifted away from. the main course and set up a different school of its own through "Jimuta Vahana who flourished during the 15th century and came with his Code, Dayabhaga, in which the following statement was made as to a widow's right of inheritance ;</u>

<u>"On failure of heirs down to the son's grandson, the wife being inferior in pretensions to sons and the rest, because she performs acts spiritually beneficial to her husband from the date of her widowhood (and not like them from the moment of birth) succeeds to the estate in their default. Since the wife rescues her husband from hell, and since a woman doing improper acts through indigence causes her husband to fail (to a region of horror), for they share the fruits of virtue and of vice; therefore the wealth devolving on her is for the benefit of the former owner, and wife's succession is consequently proper."</u>

46. From the history of the gradual evolution of a widow's right of inheritance to her husband's property, as has been generally referred to above, it is clear that the foundation of her such a right, as recognised by the Jurists, was her capacity to render spiritual benefits to her husband's soul by participating in various religious performances as the wife of her deceased husband. As has been clearly laid down by Jimuta Vahana, and quoted above, "the wealth devolving on her is for the benefit of the owner", and the right which a widow acquires to the Properly of her deceased husband is a peculiar one and is known in the modern legal parlance as a `widow's estate", which is to be contra-distinguished from her right of Stridhan.

<u>47. Jimuta Vahana explained the peculiar character of this right in Dayabhaga, Ch. TX, 1,56-59 after quoting the aphorism of Katyana, which has been cited above by us, in following manner :</u>

<u>"She shall enjoy her husband's estate during her life; and not, as with her separate property, make a gift, mortgage or sale of it at her pleasure. When she dies, it goes to her husband's heirs, and not to her own heirs. The heirs of the woman's separate property shall not take the succession to the exclusion of her husband's heirs. The heirs of her husband, who would have succeeded if the widow's right had never taken effect, equally succeed to the residue of the estate remaining after her use of it upon the demise of the widow in whom the succession had vested."</u>

<u>48. From the above Text it appears that a widow shall have a right of enjoyment of her husband's property, during her life time but shall have no right to transfer or encumber the property in any way, and after her death, the property shall go to the heirs of her husband, and not to her own heirs. The injunctions contained in other Texts require the widow to enjoy with moderation and lead a life of austerity, and in that sense, she has not even a life interest. On the other hand, she is not a tenant for life, but the property is vested in her and she is the owner of the property, subject to certain restrictions. She has the right to alienate the property absolutely for what is known as 'legal necessity', namely, for payment of husband's debts, for performance of acts which conduce to the spiritual welfare of the husband, for discharging obligations of her husband, for her own maintenance which is also an obligation of the husband and for the preservation of the estate. Mr. Justice Dwarkanath Mitter, reputed to be a distinguished Judge of the last century, described a widow inheriting the property from her husband because of the peculiar character of her ownership "a trustee for the benefit of her husband's soul" in course of his dissenting judgment in the Full Bench decision in the celebrated case of Moniram Kolita vs. Teri Kolitani 19 TAR 367 : 13 BLR 1 (FB) and expressed the view that inasmuch as, by reason of unchastity subsequent to her husband's death, she became incapable of performing effectively the religious services that were essential to the spiritual welfare of her deceased husband's soul she ceased to be capable of performing her trust, and as such she must have incurred the forfeiture of her estate. The majority of the Full Bench did not accept the view of Mr. Justice Mitter, nor did the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council sitting in appeal over the said decision of the Full Bench see eye to eye with him in regard to this exposition. Sir Barnes Pea-cock, a very distinguished Judge, who had a long tenure in Indian High Courts as a Chief justice in delivering the judgment of the Judicial Committee, reported in L.R. 7, I.A. 115, L.R. 5 Cal. 775, called the widow's estate "an anomalous one" but dismissed the characterisation of Mr. Justice Mitter as "somewhat fanciful analogy of trusteeship". The conclusion arrived at by the Judicial Committee respecting the interpretation of certain original Texts as to the legal consequences affecting a widow's right to property in the event of her non-performance of duty on ac-count of certain acts of unchastity, subsequent to her succeeding to her husband's estate may not perhaps be taken exception to. But, as Wilson, J. pointed out in his referring judgment in the case of Matungini Gupta vs. Rum Ration Roy, there is an essential difference between a misconduct as a widow and her ceasing to be a widow. We may say, with great respect, that the reasonings of Mr. Justice Mitter and his characterisation of a widow’s estate, if considered in the context of a widow's complete disavowal of marital ties and her ceasing to be the wife of the deceased, may not have been regarded to be as fanciful as what was so considered by Sir Barnes Peacock.</u>

49. The concept of a widow's estate is peculiar to Hindu Law, which has evolved, as has been indicated earlier, in course of religiosocial development of the Hindu society, as a result of the recognition of the importance of the doctrine of spiritual benefit in the law of inheritance and of the capacity of the widow to render spiritual benefit to the soul of the deceased husband. The sole reason for giving her the right of inheritance to her husband's property, according to the Texts cited above, is the spiritual benefit she may render to the departed soul as his wife. Acts of unchastity by a woman, which may be of different grades, may not amount to disavowal of her marital relationship and defacto abandonment of her character as the widow of the deceased husband. It may be a venial and expiable offence. The decision of the Judicial Committee in the Unchastity case may be quite good for such acts of unchastity. Mr. Golap Chandra Sarkar Shastri in his 'A Treatise on Hindu Law' (7th Edition, 1936) has, therefore, stated at page 662 that the proposition laid down in the said Privy Council decision is "true only in a qualified sense." Citing the Texts of Parasara and Yajnavalkya on unchastity at page 664 of his Treatise, the learned author has observed:

"The above Texts were not before the Courts in the Unchastity case. They show that unchastity alone is a light offence (but) it becomes very grave if followed by conception and that then a widow's right to her husband's estate must cease."

50. The concept of civil death in the case of person becoming outcaste in consequence of commission of sinful acts was not unknown in the ancient Hindu society and it was not inconceivable in the said society that a widow who, by leading an openly unchaste life, abandoned her character of a widow could be regarded as an outcaste and socially dead. The judicial Committee, however, did not examine the said aspect of the question in the Unchastity case.

<u>51. In the case of widow's estate, however, there are instances when a widow can bring about her own civil death by her own voluntary acts. As for example, in a case where a sonless widow who has inherited the estate of her deceased husband has taken an adoption, her widow's estate shall cease and the adopted son shall be invested with the right to the said property from the moment of the adoption. Similarly a widow by an act of surrender or by relinquishing her all interests in the inherited property in favour of the entire body of the nearest reversioners may efface herself out and thus accelerate the vesting of the property in the said reversioners. It may be pointed out that this doctrine of relinquishment has been developed by judicial decisions as a logical deduction from the nature of the widow's right.</u>

52. It is interesting to notice here the following observation of Sir Ashutosh Mookerjee as member of the Full Bench in the case of Debi Prasad Chowdhury vs. Gopal Bhagat ILR 40 Cal. 721 at pages 771-72 on an interpretation of a Text of Jimuta Vahana, which has been cited above:

"As a matter of fact, the theory of relinquishment is foreshadowed in the Dayabhaga, Chapter XI, section I para 59, where Jimuta Vahana lays down that the persons who would be the next heirs on failure of prior claimants succeed to the residue of the estate remaining after her use of it, upon the demise of the widow in whom the succession had vested, in the same manner as they would have succeeded if the widow's right had never taken effect. The words used by Jimuta. Vahana 'Jatadhikaraya Patnya Adhika Ra Pradhwangsehpi Bhogabistang Dhanag Grihiyu' ("if her right ceases or never takes effect") are comprehensive enough to include, not merely the case of the death of the widow, but all cases where her right ceases ; in other words, the reversioners take the estate not merely when the widow dies, but also when her title is extinguished, for instance, by renunciation, remarriage or the like."

53. On the question of widow's remarriage there appears to have been no mention of it in the Vedas, nor in the Grihya Sutras, that is, the aphoristic rules framed by condensing the Vedic rules and rituals relating to domestic matters like birth, marriage and death. In later days, however, a right of remarriage seems to have been recognised, not only in the case of a widow, but also in the case of a married woman under certain specified conditions as we find in the following Text of Narada and Parasara:

"Naste Mritc Prabrajite Klibe cha Patite Patow Panchaswapatsu Narinang Patiranyc Bidhiyate" Another husband is ordained for women in 'five calamities namely, if the husband be not heard of, or be dead, or adopt a religious order or be impotent, or become outcasted"

54. It has, however, been observed by Sir Gooroodass Banerjee in his Tagore Law Lectures, 1878 "The Hindu Law of Marriage and Stridhana" (1913) that remarriage of a widow has always been held to be prohibited by the Hindu Law in the following passage at page 54 of his Treatise:

"The Marriage of widows though permitted by Parasara and Narada has never been the practice among Hindus. It is reprobated by Manu and it is prohibited for the kali or the present age in the Puranas and other sacred writings. Accordingly, it has always been held to be prohibited by the Hindu Law,"

55. Dr. Nares Chandra Sen Gupta in his "Evolution of Ancient Hindu Law" Tagore Law Lectures, delivered about 72 years after Sir Gooroodas, appears to be of the view that in spite of the approval by Narada and Parasara the practice of remarriage of widow or other women did not become universal nor did it continue long but does not endorse the view or Sir Gooroodass that it had never been recognised by Hindu Law. It may be pertinent to refer to the following passage at page 115 of Dr. Son Gupta's Book:

"The next stage is marked by Vishnu who sanctions a Samskara (i.e., marriage rites) of a widow who is still under puberty. Yajnavalkya also grants samskara to a remarrying widow expressly without the limitation imposed by Vishnu. Narada's texts are even more explicit and indicate that even widows who were mothers could wed. It is not without historical significance that no texts except the texts of Vishnu and Yajnavalkya mention the Samskara of marriage in connection with wedding of widows and women of incompetent or deserting husband. This, as has already been mentioned, was inconceivable in early laws as embodied in Grihya Sutra which contemplates a Samskara only with a Kanya (virgin). Later law as it survives in Narada or Parasara gives a wide licence to wives in particular circumstances, and, in Narada, makes it her duty to consort with kinsmen. But they say nothing of Samskara. It would seem re-samskara of widows and other women never became universal, nor was it an institution which persisted long in such communities as recognised them. And it is clear that in later law a clean sweep was made of all texts that dealt with Samskara of widows when very rigid standard of chastity of women was reimposed. It would be quite natural to expect therefore that there should be no extant texts giving special rules with regard to Samskara of widows. It would however be wrong to suppose as Sir Gooroodass Banerjee seems to think that there were virtually no rules whatsoever….”

<u>56. We may refer here to a famous Treatise which gives us a glimpse of the Hindu society which flourished a few centuries before Christ and we find that during those days, widow remarriage was recognised and that on her remarriage a widow used to lose her right to her previous husband's property and even to her Stridhan in certain cases.</u>

57. The Treatise, namely, The Arthashastra of Kautilya, vol. I. the original Sanskrit Text together with the Bengali translation of the same by Dr. Radha Govinda Basak, which throws some light upon the law and social practice of contemporary India has been cited at the Bar. The Treatise is supposed. according to one view, to have been written sometime in 4th Century B. C. According to the other view, it was compiled long after the death of Kautilya, sometime between the 2nd and 4th Century A. D. Whatever may have been the exact date of its compilation, there is no doubt that it gives us some inkling of the Hindu society existing during the early Mourjya period of Indian history, where the legal sanction against the remarriage of a widow as was enforced during the Vedic days and also the subsequent days Grihya Sutra appears to have been withdrawn and the remarriage of a widow seems to be a recognised social practice. It is interesting to notice that the law relating to the right of a widow to her deceased husband's property as well as to her Stridhan has been stated in Part Chapter 2 pages 86-87, in the following manner ;

"Patidayang Bindamana Jiyet a. Dharxna Kama Bhunjita. Putrabati Bindamana Stridhanang Jiyeta"

As translated in Bengali by Dr. Basak at page 237:

"The wife marrying the second time shall be deprived of, that is, shall not be entitled to, the inheritance from her husband. If she has a virtuous life without remarrying she shall be entitled to enjoy the same.

If any wife having a son marries for the second time she shall no longer remain the owner of her Stridhan that is, she shall not retain any right thereto."

<u>59. As we notice the development of the Hindu law of inheritance through the ages and the evolution of a limited right of a widow to succeed to the property of her deceased husband, it seems to be clear that such a right is of peculiar kind, which is to be enjoyed by a widow, as the injunctions in the 'Texts indicate, for the spiritual benefit of her deceased husband and is terminable under certain circumstances during the life time of the widow, and is quite distinct from the ordinary notion of a proprietary right which is vested absolutely in an owner. The determination of such right on the remarriage of the widow, when she abandons her character as the wife of the deceased owner and thus becomes incapable of performing the religious rites for the welfare of the said owner is consistent with the written text as well as the principle underlying the law of inheritance referred to above and is in accord with the historical evidence of such an incident.</u>

<u>60. In course of history, however, the practice of widow remarriage fell into much disuse, and the practice of Sati i. e., concremation with the deceased husband's body or a life of asceticism, were encouraged for the widow. At the instance of: the great Reformer, Raja Ram Mohan Roy, the practice of Sati was abolished by legislation in 1829. The practice of widow remarriage was, by and large, discontinued except in certain limited groups of people. In the courts of law administered by the East India Company it was not recognised at all except those where the said right could be shown to have survived by custom. In this historical context Pandit Eshwar Chandra Vidyasagar having espoused the cause of the Hindu widows, particularly those who were deprived of their husbands during their childhood, the Hindu Widow Remarriage Act was enacted in 1856.</u>

<u>61. We have seen that the right of re-marriage which was conceded by the said Act to the Hindu widows was not something new in Hindu law. We have also noticed that the disentitlement of a Hindu widow on her re-marriage, to retain the property of her previous husband, as has been prescribed by section 2 of the Act, is consistent with the general principle of Hindu law and also with the social practices of Hindus when such marriages were in vogue.</u>

<u>62. The controversy which has been raised in regard to the interpretation of section 2 of the Act is, however, based upon the divergence of judicial views mainly as to the role of the preamble of the Act in the interpretation of the substantive provisions of the Act. Sir. Mohammad Sulaiman, the learned Chief Justice of Allahabad High Court, has very correctly—if we may say so with respect—stated in his judgment in the full Bench case of Bhola Umar vs. Mt Kausilla that the preamble of an Act cannot control or restrict the substantive provision of the Act and that it can be of some guidance if there is an ambiguity in the sections or some doubt as to the true scope of the provisions of that enactment, but appears to have curtailed or restricted the scope of the Act, solely relying upon the preamble thereof, in holding that the Act could never have been intended to apply and did not apply to those Hindu widows, who by the custom of their caste had, independently of the Act, a right to remarry. The reading of the enacting provisions of the Act does not bear such an interpretation. The learned Chief Justice has pointed out that the expression 'any widow' as used in section 2 of the Act, standing by itself would lead to an absurd construction, as it would include not only Hindu widows. but even Christian, Muslim, Parsi or Buddhist widows and that it is therefore necessary to restrict the scope of the Act, by invoking, the aid of the preamble, to those Hindu widows who did not have the right of remarriage at the time of the enactment. The learned Chief Justice of Dacca High Court also has adopted the same reasoning in the judgment under appeal before us.</u>

<u>63. This Court had to examine in one of its recent decisions, Messrs Amin Jute Mills Ltd vs. Bangladesh in the relative role of the preamble of an enactment in the interpretation of its enacting provisions, while construing the provision of section 1 (2) of The East Pakistan Urban Immovable Property Tax Act, 1957, which authorises the Government to extend the Act 'to such other areas as may be notified in the Official Gazette it was argued at the bar that the Title as well as the Preamble of the Act indicated that the intention of the Legislature was that the proposed tax should be imposed on immovable property lying in urban areas only and that as such the expression 'such other areas' as used in section 1(2) of the Act should be read as 'such other urban areas.' It has been pointed out in that decision that the Title as well as the Preamble are the parts of an enactment, and as such for a proper appreciation of a particular provision of the enactment, the general rule of construction is that the enactment should be read as a whole including the Title and the Preamble, each part throwing light on the other. But if the enacting provision is precise and clear, the preamble should not be used for cutting down or restricting its meaning, because it may so happen that notwithstanding the limited scope suggested by the recited facts in the preamble the Legislature may have deliberately gone beyond the recited facts and made more comprehensive provision. In the preamble generally certain facts are recited, which are the immediate occasion of the enactment. For its correct understanding, the contemporaneous conditions and state of law as well as the mischief which is sought to be remedied may be taken note of. In this connection the observation of Lord Davey in his speech in the House of Lords case of Powell V. The Kempton Park Race Course Company Limited (1899) A.C. 143 (H.L) at page 185 may be referred to :</u>

<u>“……the preamble is a key to the statute and affords a clue to the scope of the statute, when the words construed by themselves without the aid of the preamble are fairly capable of more than one meaning. There is however another rule or warning which cannot be too often repeated, that you must not create or imagine an ambiguity in order to bring in the aid of the preamble or recital. To do so would in many cases frustrate the enactment and defeat the general intention of the legislature. In may well be in this and other cases that the legislature taking the recited facts as the occasion of the enactment has deliberately used larger words to prevent the same kind of mischief in other forms."</u>

64. Similar is the enunciation made by Lord Normand in the ease of Attorney-General vs. Prince Ernest Augustus of Hanover, 1957 A.C. 436: 1957 (1) All. E. R. 49 (H. L) which is as follows:

"Where there is a preamble, it is generally in its recitals that the mischief to be remedied and the scope of the Act are described it is therefore clearly permissible to have recourse to it as an aid to construing the enacting provisions. The preamble is not however of the same weight as an aid to construction of a section of the Act, as are other relevant enacting words to be found elsewhere in the Act or even in related Acts. There may be no exact correspondence between preamble and enactment, and the enactment may go beyond, or it may fall short of the indications that may be gathered from the preamble."

<u>65. Regard being had to the rule of statutory construction with reference to the preamble of an enactment, as has been stated above it will be clear that if the provisions of Act XV of 1956 are read as a whole, there is no ambiguity or inconsistency in any of its provisions. The short title of the Act is "The Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act." which, in its longer title, is styled as an "Act to remove all legal obstacles to the marriage of Hindu widows." In the preamble it is recited that whereas the Hindu widows with certain exception are incapable of contracting a valid second marriage according to the law as is enforced in the courts and that the offspring of such widows by their second marriage are held to be illegitimate, whereas many Hindus believe that although this imputed legal incapacity is in accordance with the established custom, it is not in accordance with the true interpretation of the precepts of their religion and therefore desire that the civil law administered by the courts should no longer prevent such Hindus from adopting a different custom, and whereas it is just to relieve all such Hindus from the said legal incapacity and removal of all obstacles to the marriage of Hindu widows will tend to the promotion of good morals and public welfare, the enactment is made. The immediate cause of this enactment, as is recited in the preamble was, no doubt, to remove the legal incapacity of those widows who, according to the custom to which they were subject, were incapable of contrating a valid second marriage, but the enacting provisions as contained in sections 1, 2, 3, 6 and 8 have been framed, in general terms so as to include all sections of Hindu widows irrespective of the fact that some of them might have had a different custom permitting their remarriage, and none of the said provisions appear to be ambiguous, or inconsistent. A point has been made in the Allahabad judgment .as well as in the judgment under appeal that the expression 'any widow' having been used in section 2 of the Act without any qualification or limitation has introduced a kind of indefiniteness or uncertainty which has made it necessary to invoke the aid of the preamble for the purpose of restricting the meaning of the said wide expression. We do not think that the expression 'any widow' in section 2 is as indefinite or uncertain as that, if the provisions of the Act are read as a whole. Section 2 follows section 1, by which it is declared that no marriage of a Hindu woman whose husband was dead at the time of such marriage shall be invalid by reason of the woman having been previously married or bethrothed to another person. By section 1, as the sub-title of that section indicates, marriage of Hindu widows was legalized. The provision of this section appears to be precise and unambiguous, and it is not indicated the-rein that a certain section of Hindu widows who have the customary right of remarriage is to be excluded from the scope of this provision. This is a beneficial legislation, and the benefit of statutory right is sought to be conferred upon all sections of the Hindu widows, irrespective of the fact that a certain section may have a similar right under custom, as has been suggested in the preamble. Section 2 provides that all rights and interests which any widow may have in her deceased husband's property shall upon her re-marriage cease and determine. This section obviously prescribes the legal consequence as to the widow's right to her deceased husband's property which shall follow upon her remarriage. Section 2 is to be read along with the preceding section and although the expression, 'any widow' has been used in this section, it is clear that the legislature contemplated by the use of this expression, such widows as had been dealt in the preceding section. Section 3 which makes provision for appointment of a guardian of the children of the deceased husband on the remarriage of a Hindu widow is also clear and unambiguous and includes within its scope all Hindu windows as are contemplated in section 1. Similarly, sections 4, 5 and 7, where the expression 'widow' has been used, as in section 2, without any qualification, are to be read. We may leave aside section 4 and section 3 which are merely in the nature of saving provisions and do not create any new right of liability. But section 7 deals with the case of remarriage of a minor widow whose marriage has not been consummated. It makes the consent of her lawful guardian as mentioned therein obligatory for the purpose of her remarriage and declare any remarriage of a minor widow in violation of the said provision to be void and abetment of such remarriage a penal offence punishable with imprisonment. Here also the Legislature is referring to the remarriage of such widows, who are minor, as has been contemplated in section 1. Section 6 refers in its text to the ceremonies necessary for constituting a valid marriage of a Hindu widow and makes all those ceremonies, etc. which are performed for constituting a valid marriage of a Hindu female applicable to the case of a marriage of a Hindu widow. This provision also is clear and precise to cover the case of all Hindu widows without any exception.</u>

66. It has been supposed in the contrary view of the Allahabad High Court that section 2 has provided for a kind of disability from which a widow having the right of remarriage under the custom of her 'caste does not suffer. It has been pointed out above, while discussing the general principle of Hindu law relating to a widow's right of inheritance to her deceased husband's property, that the provision of section 2 is not inconsistent with the general principle of Hindu law of inheritance and has not introduced any new kind of disability, as supposed in the Allahabad view.

<u>67. We thus find on an examination of the provisions of the Act as a, whole along with its preamble and title that although the immediate occasion for making the legislation was the legal incapacity of those Hindu widows who .under the custom to which they were subject were incapable of contracting a valid Marriage, the legislature did not restrict the applicability of the enacting provisions to those Hindu widows only. It has gone beyond the limits of the recited facts in the preamble and it appears that, in order to introduce precision and certainty in the law of remarriage of Hindu widow, it has made more general Provisions, bringing within its scope all Hindu widows without any exception.</u>

<u>68. We have seen that the expression `Hindu' has been used only in sections 1, 3 and 6, and in the rest of the sections the said expression has not been used at all, but a general expression 'any widow' has been used. We have already indicated that despite the use of such a general expression, the legislature was referring in the said sections, particularly, sections 2 and 7, to such a widow as has been contemplated in section 1 of the Act. It may be pointed out that the use of a general expression without the epithet 'Hindu' is not without significance. In our opinion, the Legislature has deliberately used the general expression in section 2 to cover the case of a widow, who has inherited the property of her husband as a Hindu widow but may have ceased to be a Hindu by adopting a different faith at the time of her remarriage, as happened in the Full Bench case of the Calcutta High Court, Matungini Gupta vs. Ram Button Roy I.L.R 19 Cal 289 Where the widow remarried a Brahmo Under Act III of 1892 after renouncing her Hindu faith, and the Full Bench case of the Madras High Court. 'Vital Tayarama vs. Chatta Kandu Sirayya, I.L.R. 41 Mad 1078 where a widow became a Mohammedan and contracted a valid marriage under the Mohammedan Law. It has been rightly held in those cases that the provision of section 2 may be invoked in such cases. The observation of Petheram, C.J. in Matungini Gupta's case, as has been quoted above, may be usefully referred to in this connection. On an interpretation of the provision of section 2 of the Act, we have no manner of doubt that the said provision is not limited in its application to those widows only who had not the right of remarriage before the Act of 1856, but is applicable to all widows who had been married as Hindus and have succeeded to her husband's property as such.</u>

<u>69. On a review of the important judicial authorities having a bearing on the point in the light of the principle of Hindu law relating to a Hindu widow's right to the property of her deceased husband and the effect of her remarriage on such right and on an examination of the provisions of the Hindu Widow's Remarriage Act (Act XV of 1856) we are of opinion that a Hindu widow's right to her deceased husband ceases on her remarriage even though such remarriage is sanctioned under the custom of her caste, both under the general principle of Hindu law as well as under section 2 of Act XV of 1856.</u>

<u>The result, therefore, is that this appeal is allowed the judgment and decree of the High Court are set aside and the decrees of the Court below are restored, but there shall not be any order as to costs in this appeal.</u>

End.
