full_judgment:
Abdur Rahman Chowdhury, :—This rule is directed against the impugned action of the respondents in taking over an urban premises as an abandoned property under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972. Facts relevant for the disposal of the rule in brief, are that the petitioner entered into an agreement for the purchase of premises in question with one Anwarul Haque on 18.12.70 and pursuant to the said agreement paid a sum of Taka 50,000/- to the vendor as earnest money which was duly acknowledged in the agreement itself and pursuant to the said agreement the vendor delivered possession of the properly to the petitioner and since then he has been in possession of the said properly. It was further agreed between the vendor and the petitioner that after obtaining the necessary income tax clearance and other papers, the sale deed would be executed and registered on receipt of the balance of consideration money of Taka 25,000/- and in the event of failure or refusal to execute and register the sale deed the petitioner Would be entitled to get it registered through court. The vendor having failed to perform his part of the obligation, the petitioner was obliged to institute a suit for specific performance of contract in the first court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca on 1.4.74 being title suit No. 126 of 1974, wherein the vendor was made defendant No. 1 and the Government of Bangladesh was made defendant No. 2. The Government of Bangladesh appeared in the said suit through the Government Pleader and obtained several adjournments to file the written statement but ultimately did not file any. Thereafter the suit was decreed exparte in favour of the petitioner on 4.9.74 by the first Court of sub-ordinate judge, Dacca and defendant No. 1 (the vendor ) was directed to execute and register the same on receipt of the balance consideration money within 30 days in default of which the petitioner would get the sale-deed executed and registered through Court by depositing the balance consideration money in Court Certified copy of judgment and decree passed in the said suit has been annexed to the petition as Annexures `E' and `E-1'. The vendor, the defendant No. 1 having failed to comply with the direction of the Court, the Subordinate Judge executed and registered the sale deed on be-half of the vendor in the Sadar Sub-Registry, Dacca on 14.1.1975, certified copy of which has been annexed to the petition as Annexure It was further stated by the petitioner that while he was thus in peaceful possession of the premises in question, Mr. Aftabuddin, the then Deputy Secretary of the Government of Bangladesh forcibly evicted the petitioner from the premises on 15.1.75. It was further asserted by the petitioner that the petitioner produced before Mr. Aftalyuddin the certified copy of the sale-deed and the decree of the Court to establish his lawful ownership and possession in the property. That subsequently, the petitioner moved the authorities concerned by filing representations and also in person but failed to get any redress of his legitimate grievances. Being aggrieved, the petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

2. Respondent No. 1 contested the Rule by filing an affidavit-in-opposition wherein he denied the allegations made in the petition and asserted that it was an abandoned property which vested in the Government and as such the petitioner being an unauthorised occupant was rightly evicted.

3. Mr Moinul Hossain, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner has submitted that the properly in question by virtue of the court's decree rightfully belonged to the petitioner who was also in lawful possession of the same and the property was never declared as, an abandoned property and the petitioner eras illegally evicted from the premises in violation of the law. Mr. M. M. Haque, the learned Assistant Attorney General in reply submitted that the property having vested in the Government as an abandoned property, the court decree had no validity in the eye of law and the petitioner having no legal right to be in possession of the said property was rightly evicted by the respondents.

4. We have perused the petition, the affidavit-in-opposition, the affidavit-in-reply and the supplementary affidavit filed by the petitioner and have also considered the submission made by the learned Advocates in support of their respective cases.

5. In support of his arguments Mr. Moinul Hossain has drawn our attention to the supplementary-affidavit filed by the petitioner and the annexures 'V' and 'Z' to the said affidavit. It appears from the said annexures that the petitioner was served with a notice by the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (south), Dacca as early as 8.7.72 asking him to show cause why he should not be directed to surrender the property since it was an abandoned property. The petitioner duly showed cause on 15.7.72 wherein he asserted that he was in lawful possession of the property by virtue of a deed of agreement ( Annexure 'Y' ). Thereafter the Sub-Divisional Officer, Sadar (south) Dacca by his order dated 26.2.73 after considering the reply of the petitioner ordered that the premises in question be dropped from the abandoned list in favour of the petitioner '(Annexure 'Z'). This fact has not been denied by the respondent nor there is any assertion in the affidavit-in-opposition that the said order was set aside by the higher authority and the property in question was thereafter again included in the list of abandoned property. The petitioner thereafter instituted Title suit No. 126 of 1 974 in the First court of Subordinate Judge, Dacca wherein the vendor and the Government were made parties as defendants No. 1 and 2 respectively. The plaint of the said suit has been annexed to the petition as Annexure 'B'. It further appears that the Government Pleader entered appearance in the said suit by filling power, the certified copy of which has been annexed to the petition as Annexure .`C'. The Government of Bangladesh (defendant No. 2) thereafter took several adjournments for filing written statement, and the certified copies of the said applications for adjournments have been annexed to the petition as Annexures (4) but ultimately defendant No. 2 did not file any written statement and accordingly the suit was decreed exparte on 4.9.74. The vendor ( defendant No. 1) having failed to comply with the direction of the court, the sale deed was executed and registered by the court on 14.1.75, the certified copy of which has been annexed to the petition as Annexure 'F'.

6. The documents filed by the petitioner clearly show that the petitioner acquired valid title and possession of the premises in question by virtue of the sale deed which was duly executed and registered through court. Mr. M. M. Haque has, however, argued that since the property had already vested in the Government as an abandoned property under P. O. No. 16 of 1972, the decree passed in the said suit was a nullity in the eye of law. We find no substance in the contention of Mr. Haque. We wonder how on the face of the order passed by the Sub-Divisional Officer on 26.2.73. (Annexure 7') Mr. Haque can advance the argument that the property vested in the Government as an abandoned properly and that the decree could be treated as a nullity. Nothing has been produced before us to show that the order of the Sub-Divisional Officer excluding the premises from the list of an abandoned property by his order dated 26.2.73 was set aside by any higher authority'. Moreover, the plea that it was an abadoned property was not taken before the learned Subordinate Judge where it appears that the respondents took several adjournments to file written statement and contest the suit but ultimately they did neither. After having allowed the suit to be decreed exparte, we do not see how the respondents can now come up with the plea that the property in question vested in the Government as early as 1972. Having regard to these facts and circumstances and the materials on record, we are unable to accept the respondent's contention that the premises in question is an abandoned property.

7. Now coming to 'the second branch' of Mr. Moinul Hossain's argument that the petitioner was illegally evicted from the premises, it appears that the Bangladesh Abandoned Property Order, 1972 (P. 0. No. 16 of 1972) and the Bangladesh Abandoned Properly (Taking Over. Possession) Rules, 1972 lay down detailed procedure for eviction of an unauthorised occupant and taking over possession of the abandoned property. Article 7 of the Bangladesh. Abandoned Property Order 1972 (hereinafter called the order) lays down as follows:

"7(1) Where any abandoned property is not in possession of any person, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (or the authorised officer) shall take possession of the properly in such manner as may be prescribed.

(2) Where any abandoned property is in possession of any person, such person shall, within seven days of the commencement of this Order, surrender such property to the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (or the Authorised Officer).

(3) Where the person in possession of any abandoned properly fails to surrender such properly as he is required to do under clause (2), the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (or the authorised officer) shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the properly, within seven days of the service of the notice, to the person mentioned in the notice or to show cause against such surrender within the said period and, if he fails to do so, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate (or the authorised officer) shall take possession of the property in such manner as may be prescribed.

(4) Where the person on whom a notice is served under clause (3) shows cause, within the period specified in that clause, against the surrender of the abandoned property, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate or the authorised officer), as the case may be, shall after making such local enquiry as he may consider necessary and after giving the person an opportunity of being heard, pass such order as he deems fit."

8. Rule 3 of Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules, 1972 (hereinafter called the Rules) lays down the manner of taking over possession of abandoned property under Article 7 of the Order.

"3. Manner of taking possession of abandoned property under article 7(1). Where any abandoned property is not in possession of any person or a person surrenders any abandoned property under clause (2) of article 7 or in pursuance of a notice under clause (2) of an order under clause (4) of the said Article, the Deputy Commissioner or the S.D.M. shall pass an order in Form No. 1 and depute an officer for taking possession of such property.

(2) The officer so deputed shall affix an authoritative copy of such order on the notice board of the office of the Local Union Panchayat, Sahar Committee/Paurashava and where the property consists of immovable property another copy to some conspicuous part of such property.

(3) The order, may, if the Deputy Commissioner or Sub-Divisional Magistrate deems fit, be proclaimed by beat of drum in the locality in which the property is situated.

(4) The officer deputed to take possession for securing possession of the property including breaking open any lock or door; if necessary in making an inventory in duplicate, containing the full particulars of the properly, including machineries, installations, fixtures, fittings, stock-in trade, furniture, equipment’s, cash, bunions, ornaments, books, documents, papers, house-hold effects, standing crops, trees and all other things found therein.

(5) The inventory so made shall be signed by the officer himself and by two witnesses.

(6) On completion of these formalities, the possession of the property shall be deemed to have been taken by the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate.

(7) The officer shall submit a report to the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate about taking possession of the property in the aforesaid manner, along with both copies of inventory prepared by him.

(8) The notice referred to in clause (3) of article 7 shall be in Form No. 11 and shall be served on the person in possession or any adult male member of his family or, where none of them is available or they refuse to receive the notice, by affixing a copy of the notice to a conspicuous part of the residence of such person and also where the abandoned property consists of any immovable property on a conspicuous part of such immovable property in the presence of two witnesses.

(9) Where the person in possession fails to surrender the abandoned property or the show cause in pursuance of the notice under clause (3) of article 7 or where he shows cause, but fails to surrender the property in accordance with an order passed under clause (4) of that article, the Deputy Commissioner or the S.D.M. shall pass an order in Form No. III and depute an officer to take possession of the property by taking all steps necessary in that behalf, including evicting such person and for such eviction, such force may be used as may be necessary.

(10) the officer so deputed shall also publish the order, enter upon the property and prepare an inventory in the same manner as prescribed in Sub-rules (2)(3) and (4).

(11) After eviction and on completion of these formalities, the possession of the property shall be deemed to have been taken by the Deputy Commissioner on the Sub-Divisional Magistrate.

(12) The officer shall submit a report to the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate about taking possession of the property in the aforesaid manner, along with both copies of the inventory prepared by him".

9. Clause (3) of article 7 of the Order clearly lays down that where a person in possession of any abandoned property fails to surrender his property, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate or the Authorised Officer shall serve a notice on him in the prescribed manner requiring him to surrender possession of the property within seven days of the service of notice or to show cause against surrender within the said period and if he fails to do so the Deputy Commissioner or the S.D.M. or the Authorised Officer shall take possession of the property in such manner as is prescribed under the Rules. Clause (4) of article 7 lays down that where the person on whom a notice under clause (3) has been served, shows cause, the competent authority as mentioned in the said clause shall, after making such local enquiry, as he may consider necessary and after giving the person an opportunity of being heard, pass such order as he deems fit. Rule 3 of the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Taking over Possession) Rules 1972 lays down the manner of taking possession of an abandoned property under article 7 of the Order.

<u>10. Admittedly, no notice as required under article 7 of the order was served on the petitioner to be given an opportunity of being heard nor for that matter any of the procedure laid down in the order and the rules for taking over possession of the property, was followed and complied with. Under article 7(3) of the President's Order, the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate or any Authorised Officer was alone competent to serve the required notice and to order eviction of an unauthorised person from an abandoned property. It has not been denied in the affidavit-in-opposition that it was Mr. Aftabuddin, the Deputy Secretary who evicted the petitioner from the premises. There is no assertion on behalf of the respondent nor was anything produced before us to show that the said Mr. Aftabuddin was an Authorised. Officer as required under article 7 of the Order. We have, therefore, no hesitation in holding that Mr. Aftabuddin had no authority whatsoever to evict the petitioner and as such his action was wholly unauthorised.</u>

<u>11. It was evident from a perusal of the different provisions of the Order and the Rules that the legislature was fully conscious of the sacred rights of the citizens and to protect them from the high-handed and arbitrary action of the executive, various provisions were incorporated in the Order. These provisions were intended to afford an opportunity to a person to present his case and be heard in defence of his case. It is new well-settled that whether in administrative or in judicial matters the principles of natural justice, if consistent with the provisions of the statute, must be duly adhered to and complied with. In all proceedings whether administrative or judicial the principles of natural justice have to be observed, if the proceedings result in consequence affecting the person or property or other rights of the parties concerned. The general consensus of judicial opinion in this sub-continent appears to be that in order to ensure the elementary principles of fairness the person sought to be affected must, at least know the nature of the allegations made against him and that he should be given a fair opportunity of putting his case before the authority concerned. The object of the rules of natural justice is to secure justice and to prevent the miscarriage of justice. When a statutory provision can be read consistently with the principles of natural justice the courts are bound to see that the same has been observed and complied with. In the instant case, <u>Article 7 of the Order, in our opinion, enshrined the principles of natural justice and offered an opportunity to the person proceeded against to put his case before the authority concerned and he also had the right of being heard in person. This salutary provision of law was incorporated for the purpose of affording protection to the citizen against any arbitrary and highhanded action on the part of the executive. But, we are constrained to observe that in the instant case none of the provisions of law which were mandatory, was complied with in evicting the petitioner forcibly from the premises. Admittedly, the petitioner was not evicted by either the Deputy Commissioner or the Sub-Divisional Magistrate but by Mr. Aftabuddin the Deputy Secretary of the Government. Nothing has been asserted or produced before us to show that Mr. Aftabuddin was authorised to evict the petitioner as required under article 7 of the Order. It is singularly unfortunate that Mr. Aftabuddin, an officer of the rank of Deputy Secretary to the Government should have taken the law in his own hands and acted in such high-handed manner in utter disregard of the very law that he was supposed to be enforcing. He ignored the registered title-deed and even the decree of the court when those were produced before him by the petitioner. He did not comply with any of the mandatory provisions of law before evicting the petitioner from the premises in question. The allegations of arbitrary: action and high-handedness made on uncontroverted. Such action of the officers, if allowed to go unchecked, will bring slur on the good name of the Government. It shows how a law meant for the good of the country with safeguards for the protection of innocent citizens can become an instrument of oppression in the hands of irresponsible officers. Having regard to these facts and circumstances, we are constrained to hold that the impugned action of the respondents in evicting the petitioner from the premises in question was wholly unauthorised and illegal.</u></u>

12. In the result, the Rule is made absolute and the impugned action of the respondents in taking over the premises No. 20/1, Bahar Road, Block 'B' Mohammadpur Housing Estate, Dacca as an abandoned property and allotment thereof under the Bangladesh Abandoned Property (Control, Management and Disposal) Order, 1972 is hereby declared to have been done without any lawful authority and is of no legal effect. The respondents are directed to restore vacant possession of the premises in question to the petitioner expeditiously. The respondents shall pay costs to the petitioner which is assessed at 10 gold mohurs.

M. A. Khaliq, J.—I agree.

End.

parties:
Nayeb Ali and others ----------- Petitioners.
Vs.
Akhtar Rahman & others --------- Opposite parties.
full_judgment:
This Rule at the instance of the heirs of the pre-emptee is directed against a judgment of reversal in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

The pre-emptors claiming to be co-sharers of the holding, filed the application for pre-emption of the transfer made by Khhatijan in favour of pre-emptee Muktar Hossain by a registered kabala dated 19.8.67 for Rs. 1000/-.

2. The case was contested by the pre-emptee contending that the pre-emptors are strangers to the holding to which the land transferred appertains. The original jote recorded under C.S. khatian No. 21 was partitioned amongst the co-sharers and separate new jamas were created and the same were recorded in separate record of right. Opposite parties 17 and 18 claiming to be co-sharers to the holding by inheritance, prayed for pre-emption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

3. The learned Munsif on consideration of the materials on record rejected the pre-emptor's claim for pre-emption holding inter alia, that the tenants ledger, the Register No. 11 and the new record-of-rights 37-40 indicate that 4 separate jamas were created by splitting up the jote recorded in C.S. khatian No. 21. The learned Munsif in that view of the matter, held that "the original jote under c.s. khatian No. 21 do no longer exist after conversion of it into 4 new jamas, the petitioners have no co-sharership to the case jote which falls within the ambit of record-of-right No. 40. The O. P. 1 has purchased from Khatejan in whose name stands the R.O.R. jote No. 40 and the case land also falls within that R.O.R."

4. On appeal the learned Subordinate Judge reversed the decision of the learned Munsif and granted pre-emption in the following terms: "That the Misc. Appeal be allowed on contest with costs against the contesting respondents and exparte against the rest. The judgment of the learned Munsif is set aside. The petitioners are entitled to pre-emption along with O. P. 17 and 18". The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the jote recorded in C. S. Khatian No. 21 continued to exist and that there was no splitting up of the jama ass contended by the pre-emptee. According to the learned Subordinate Judge the creation of the 4 R.O. R. No. 37-40" cannot be treated as a regular partition by metes and bounds". The learned Subordinate Judge was of the view that the "presumption of jointness as recorded in C. S. Khatian can be rebutted only by a decree in a partition or a registered partition deed among the co-sharers or by an application under section 88 of the B. T. Act. But the O. P. No. 1 cannot produce any such paper. Thus it clearly proves that there was no partition by metes and bounds among the co-sharers of the e. s. khatian either by partition suit or by registered partition deed. 'Therefore the joint-ness of the jama recorded in C. S. khatian is still in existence."

5. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner contends that the learned Subordinate Judge acted with material irregularity in not recording a finding that the pre-emptor" is a person to whom transfer of the holding or the portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made u/s 90". According to Mr. Rahman, the court while allowing the pre-emption is required to record a finding that the preemptor had the right to purchase u/s 90 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The condition enjoined by the proviso to section 96(1), according to Mr. Rahman, is a requirement of law. In support of his contention he has referred to the case of Satya Ranjan Balder and others versus Surendra Nath Das and others reported in 13 D.L.R. page 338. Chowdhury C.J. and M. R. Khan, J dealt with the question in the following terms:

"Before he is entitled to get pre-emption he is to prove all the requirements under section 96 of the Act because the wording of the statute is no co-sharer shall have the right to purchase under this section unless he is a person to whom transfer of the holding or the portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under section 90."

<u>6. Mr. Nurul Hoque Bhuiya, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the pre-emptors contends that the pre-emptors satisfied the requirement by making an appropriate statement in paragraph 2 of the application for pre-emption. The assertion that section 90 is not an impediment to the pre-emptor's claim of pre-emption was not denied by the pre-emptee who contested the claim. According to Mr. Haque the learned Subordinate Judge was not required to record a finding on this question as it was not denied by the pre-emptee and that no evidence, on either side, was adduced on the question. True that the assertion made in the application was not denied by the pre-emptee and according to the rules of pleading, a fact not denied, may be taken as admitted but the fact remains that the learned Subordinate Judge while allowing the preemption did not direct his attention to this particular requirement of law. While allowing a pre-emption u/s 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act, the statutory requirements must be found to have been satisfied. These requirements have been specifically mentioned in section 96(1) of the Act and the proviso thereto. Mr. Nurul Haque, however, referred to the case of Abdur Rahman Vs. Baser Ali and others in 21 D.L.R. page 599 and relied upon a passage appearing in paragraph 13 at page 604.</u>

<u>"The last contention made by Mr. B. N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate for the petitioner is that the application for pre-emption must satisfy all the requirements u/s 96 of the Act before one can get an order for pre-emption in one's favour. He has referred to a case between Soya Ranjan Haider and another vs. Surendra Nath Das and others (8) in which it has been held that before an applicant is entitled to get pre-emption he is to prove all the requirements u/s 96 of the Act which says that no co-sharer tenant shall have the right to purchase under this section unless he is a person to whom transfer of the holding or the portion or share thereof as the case may be can be made -u/s 90 of the Act. I must say that this contention cannot prevail in the present case because there is no such averment in the present case that opposite party No. 1 Baser Ali has so much land that if the pre-empted land be added to it the quantity of land in his possession will exceed the prescribed quantity of land permissible under the law. No such question appears to have been raised in the courts below nor any objection was taken in the case itself but in the case cited above the objection was specifically taken and it was not proved otherwise, so the facts are not the same in the present case."</u>

<u>With due respect I must say that the burden to prove that the pre-emptor is entitled to get a pre-emption in his favour, is on the pre-emptor and as such he is required to prove that the land sought to be pre-empted, if allowed to pre-empt, will not exceed the ceiling. Therefore, it was not the burden of the pre-emptee to say how much land the pre-emptor had. The pre-emptor came to court for pre-emption and it is he who is to satisfy the requirements of law. He cannot steal a march over the silence of his adversary. Therefore the case referred to and relied upon by Mr. Nurul Haque is distinguishable in the facts and circumstances of the case. In the instant case the pre-emptor evidently asserted that section 90 is not an impediment in getting the pre-emption. Therefore, he discharged his part of the burden.  It was a duty of the court to record a finding to that effect. While granting an application for pre-emption, the court is required under the law to record a finding that pre-emptor is a co-sharer or a tenant holding contiguous land. In the absence of such finding the application for pre-emption cannot succeed. Similarly, in absence of a finding that a pre-emptor a person to whom transfer of the holding or a portion or share thereof, as the case may be, can be made under section 90" the application for pre-emption is bound to fail. The embargo contained in the provision to section 961 of the Act, if overlooked, shall ruder section 90 (1) of Act nugatory.</u>

<u>The judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge is conspicuously silent in this regard end accordingly is not maintainable.</u>

7. It was next contended by Mr. Rafiqur Rahman that the record of right raises a presumption of correctness at the time when it was prepared. There is also a presumption in favour of its continuity but such presumption is rebuttable. According to Mr. Rahman the pre-emptee has rebutted the presumption arising out of c.s. record-of-right by producing the 4 record-of-rights. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman submits that the learned Subordinate Judge acted with material irregularity in the exercise of jurisdiction in holding that it is only a decree in partition suit or a registered deed between the parties that partition by metes and bounds can be effected. A partition may be effected through court by a decree or by a deed between the co-sharers. Both have the same effect. Here the question is not of partition in terms of share between the co-sharers but the question is whether the jamaas evidenced by C.S. khatian No. 21 exists or it ceased to exist giving rise to four different khatians under new record of rights 37-40. Mr. Nurul Haque Bhuiya in support of the judgment of the learned. Sub-ordinate Judge submits that the learned Sub-ordinate Judge was not incorrect in the view taken by him. According to the learned Advocate a jama can be split up by an application under section 117 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act in addition to the manner referred to by the learned Subordinate Judge. True, the provisions for subdivision of a joint tenancy and distribution of rent thereof have been made in section 117(c) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. It appears that the lands of c.s. khatian No. 21 were recorded in 4 separate khatians on the basis of specific -possession of the heirs of Abdul, the original recorded tenant. The heirs of Abdul did not challenge such possession by amicable arrangement and they have been paying rent separately in terms of the separate khatians. Evidently the amicable arrangement does not amount to partition by metes and bounds. The question of possession according to share remains open to adjustment. This question may be conveniently decided between the parties in an appropriate suit. For the purpose of pre-emption it is evident that the 4 record-of-rights separately recorded the lands of the c.s. khatian No. 21. There is no dispute that the land sought to be pre-empted is covered by record-of-right 40 and it belonged exclusively to Khatian. In the circumstances it is difficult to conclude that the original c.s. khatian is still continuing. Mr. Rafiqur Rahman has also referred to the separate payment of rent in terms of the separate record-of-rights. This is another circumstance of actual splitting up of the jamas. In the circumstances the contention of Mr. Rahman is of substance.

8. It was lastly contended by Mr. Rafiqur Rahman that the order passed by the learned Subordinate Judge allowing preemption is misconceived as it did not satisfy the requirements of section 96, sub-section 6(1) and (b). The opposite party Nos. 17 and 18 are co-applicants for preemption u/s 96(4) of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. The learned Subordinate Judge allowed their claim along with that of the original pre-emptor. Under the law it was necessary to examine the respective claims of the applicant and the co-applicants.

9. Reference may be made to sub-section (6) of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act which runs as follows:-

"(a) On the expiry of the period within which an application may be made under sub-section (4), the court shall determine, in accordance with the provisions of this section which of the applications filed under sub-section (1) of Sub-section (4) shall be allowed. (b) If the Court finds that an order allowing the applications made under this section is to be made in favour of more than one applicant, the court shall determine the amount to be paid by each of such applicants and, after apportioning the amount, shall order the applicant or applicants who have joined in the original application under sub-section (4) to deposit the amounts payable by him or them within such period as it thinks reasonable; and if the deposit is not made by any such period, his application shall be dismissed."

The learned Subordinate Judge failed to direct his attention to this vital aspect of the case while allowing the pre-emption. This is another ground on which the judgment of the learned Subordinate Judge cannot be maintained.

For the reasons stated above there is substance in this Rule which must succeed.

In the result, the rule s is made absolute without any order as to costs. The judgment and order of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and those of the learned Munsif are restored.

End.

full_judgment:
This Rule has arisen out of an order passed by the learned Munsif, 1st Court, Dhaka, allowing an application for adjournment of hearing for addition of some co-sharers by inheritance as opposite-parties in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

2. Facts in short are that when the application for pre-emption was taken up for hearing and P.W.1 was being examined before the learned Munsif, at that stage the pre-emptor-opposite party filed an application that some co sharers by inheritance had not been impleaded in the proceeding and that they should be made parties for a decision of the case. The copy of the said application was served upon the purchaser-petitioner who raised objection against impleading of the co-sharers at that stage. The learned Munsif upon hearing the parties allowed the application for time for steps to add the remaining co-sharers in the proceeding. Hence this Rule at the instance of the purchaser-petitioner. 

3. Mr. B.N. Chowdhury, the learned Advocate appearing on behalf of the purchaser-petitioner submits that it was mandatory on the part of the pre-emptor-opposite parties to implead all co-sharers in the proceeding as they are necessary parties to the proceeding for proper and complete adjudication in accordance with law. He has submitted that addition of a co-sharer beyond the period of limitation cannot be allowed and the learned Munsif acted illegally and with material irregularity in granting the prayer for time to implead the remaining co-sharers. He has, further submitted that the proceeding having been started in 1975 the belated application for time to implead some remaining co-sharers in the proceeding is unsustainable in law and the impugned order allowing the same is illegal in as much as that the pre-emptor- opposite-party having not impleaded all co-sharers of the suit holding the application was not maintainable as the period of limitation for filing the application for pre-emption had long lapsed. The learned Advocate has further submitted that by granting adjournment to allow the pre-emptor-opposite-parties to implead the remaining co-sharers beyond the time has caused an injustice to the purchaser-petitioner in saving the application for pre-emption from it being dismissed. 

4. It appears that on the date of hearing of the application for pre-emption while P.W. I was being examined the pre-emptor-oppo-the parties filed an application stating that some co-sharers by inheritance had not been impleaded in the proceeding and that they should he made parties to arrive at a final decision of the case, and he prayed for one mouth's time for impleading the remaining co-sharers. The learned Munsif after hearing the patties adjourned the hearing of the case and allowed time for taking steps for the purpose. The provision under the sub-section 2 of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act as to impleading of all co-sharers of the holding as parties to the proceeding is obviously for the purpose of giving facility of pre-emption to the persons who have not exercised their right of pre-emption as provided under sub-section I of section 96 of the Act. It is however, mandatory on the part of the pre-emptor-opposite parties to implead all co-sharer tenants of the holding and the transferee, and if the pre-emptor is a contiguous owner of the land transferred all other owners contiguous to the land transfer-red and the transferee shall be made parties to the proceeding. This view has been finally set at rest by a decision of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh reported in 33 D.L.R, (A.D.) 113.

5. Now the question is whether a remaining-co-sharer can be added after institution of the proceeding under section 96 of the Act alien the application for pre-emption would (be barred by limitation. As has been referred to above the purpose of impleading of co-sharers is to provide opportunity of retable preemption to the persons interested in the holding. 

6. Under the provision of Order 1 rule 10 C.P.C. which in my view are applicable to the pre-emption proceedings, a party can be added as an opposite party at any stage of the proceeding unless it causes injustice to the ,other side and the inconvenience cannot be compensated sufficiently by cost. The impleading of a co-sharer under Order 1 rule 14 C.P.C. at any stage of the proceeding shall however, be subject to section 22 of the Limitation Act.

7. In the case reported in 33 DLR (A.D) 113 it appears that the pre-emptor after getting opportunity to implead the remaining co-sharers, having failed to amend the application by impleading the co-sharers in the proceeding, as pointed out by the purchaser the application for pre-emption thus failed. In the present Case, whether a remaining co-sharer who is a necessary party to a proceeding under sub-section (2) of section 96 of the Act can be added after the expiry of the period fixed for filing of the application for pre-emption. In my view such addition of remaining co-sharer is permissible under Order, 1 rule 10. C.P.C. even after the period of limitation for filing of application pre-emption has expired. No relief having been prayed against the remaining co-sharers who have not been impleaded earlier, impleading them before trial of the application can be allowed even after period of limitation fixed for filing of the application if the delay in not impleading them earlier is explained to the satisfaction of the Court. The Court shall in proper case refuse addition of parties in spite of opportunity and the delay is due' to latches and negligence on the part of the pre-emptor. In this connection the observation of the Appellate Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh may be referred to: 
8. the requirement as to making of parties is undoubtedly positive. It is the duty of the pre-emptor to implead the necessary parties, as I have already observed above that this requirement of law should be enforced keeping in view the pre-emptor, after getting an opportunity fails to amend his applica- • tion by impleading the necessary parties as pointed out by the pre-emptor and on evidence if it is found that the application suffers from defect of parties, in that event the application cannot succeed and must be dismissed". "In the instant case as I have already indicated above the pre-emptors got sufficient opportunity to remove the defect by impleading the persons named in the written objection but they failed to remove the defect, and, consequently, the application must be treated as not property constituted." 

9. From the aforesaid observations of the Appellate Division it appears to me that the question of addition of a remaining co-sharer in a proceeding under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act cannot, be said to be closed, and addition of a remaining co-sharer can, be allowed after the application for pre-emption leas been filed and the period prescribed for filing such application has lapsed. In the aforesaid decision of the Appellate Division the pre-emptor failed to amend the application by impleading the remaining co-sharer in the proceeding and it continued without him. In my view, the period prescribed for filing the application for pre-emption relates to vis-a-vis the pre-emptor and the purchaser. This view finds support in the decision of a single Bench of this Court reported in 19 D.L.R. (H.C) 655. I am further of the opinion that for the purpose of impleading a remaining co-sharer in a proceeding under section 96 of the Ad the period of limitation as provided in sub-section (I) of section 96 of the State. Acquisition and Tenancy Act in filing an application for pre-emption by a pre-emptor against a purchaser for pre-empting the latter's kabala shall not apply. 

This Rule, therefore, fails and it is discharged without any order as to .costs. 

End.

case_source: From the judgment and order dated 6 July 1983 passed by the High Court Division, Rangpur Bench, in Civil Revision No. 22 of 1983.
full_judgment:
Shahabuddin Ahmed, J.-In this appeal the simple question is whether a contiguous land-holder is entitled to pre-empt the land which has been transferred to co-sharer-tenants whose interest in the tenancy accrued by purchase.

2. This arises from Miscellaneous Case No.167 of 1978 in the Court of Munsif, Natore. The land in question was transfused by a katrala dated 29 July, 1976 to the appellants Nos.1 to 4; they are co-sharers of the vendor (respondent No. 2) in the tenancy by purchase. Respondent No.1 is a tenant having land contiguous to the land transferred He filed the Miscellaneous Case seeking pre-emption of the land under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. His claim was resisted by the appellants-transferees on the ground that their claim being higher in order of preference than that of the contiguous land-holder, the latter is not entitled to pre-emption. This contention was accepted by the learned Munsif who refused pre-emption. But on appeal the learned District Judge took the view that the transfer to a co-sharer by purchase is pre-emptible and that as the transferees, though co-sharers by purchase, did not join in the application for pre-emption, the contiguous land-holder is entitled to pre-empt the land, and on this view allowed the pre-emption. His decision was upheld by the learned Single Judge of the High Court Division at Rangpur by the impugned order dated 6 July 1983 in Civil Revision Case No.22 of 1983. Leave was granted by us to consider whether the pre-emption has been allowed on correct interpretation of section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act.

3. There is no dispute that a transfer to a co-sharer by purchase is pre-emptible, but the question is whether it is pre-emptible by a contiguous land holder. The learned Single Judge took the view that in this case the co-sharers by purchase namely, the appellants-transferees, did not join with the pre-emptor, contiguous land-holder, in the application for pre-emption, and as such, the latter is entitled to pre-empt the transfer made to the appellants-co-sharers. The harped Single Judge relied upon sub-section (4) of section 96 which provides for a co-sharer-transferee joining in an application for pre-emption already filed. But this sub-section must be read and considered along with other provisions of section 96 particularly, sub-sections (2) and (5). Sub-section (2) provides that in an application for pre-emption by a co-sharer tenant, all other co-sharer tenants shall be made parties; a contiguous land-holder is not a necessary party there. But if an application for pre-emption is made by a contiguous land-holder, all the co-sharer-tenants (whether by Inheritance or by purchase) and also all other tenants holding lauds contiguous to the land transferred, shall be made parties. This distinction between a co-sharer tenant and a tenant having the contiguous land has been again pronounced in definite terms and language in sub section (5). This sub section has set forth the prior rights to purchase under section 96. It is quoted below:

"(5) (a): If (i) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by inheritance and lii) a co-sharer tenant whose interest has accrued by purchase and (iii) a tenant holding land contiguous to the land transferred apply under this section and comply with the provisions herein contained, the applicant or applicants shall have the prior right to purchase under this section in the order in which they have been mentioned above." As appears clearly from sub-section 5 (1) (a), a co-sharer by inheritance gets the first priority and if he claims per-emption he will exclude all other claimants. If a co-sharer by purchase claims pre-emption, the claim of a contiguous land-holder stands superseded. Now in the instant case, the co-sharers by purchase already purchased the land, and no other co-sharer has come forward claiming preemption. The learned Single Judge observed that these co-sharer-transferees were required to claim pre-emption by joining in the application of the contiguous land-holder, but the learned Single Judge did not notice that even if these transferees had joined in the application for pre-emption the claim of the contiguous land-holder would have fallen through straightaway. It appears that the appellants-transferees are the only co-sharers in the holding, and it is they who already purchased the land. Since there was no other co-sharer in the holding, transfer to the appellants is immune from pre-emption by a contiguous land-holder, by necessary implication.

4. In this connection sub-section (10) of section 96 should be referred to. This provides that a transfer to a co-sharer in the tenancy whose interest has accrued otherwise than by purchase, such as, by inheritance, is not pre-emptible. This means, all other co-sharers by inheritance will be debarred from pre-emption by this sub-sec. (10). But in the case of transfer to a co-sharer by purchases; it is not so protected from pre-emption, and any other co-sharer, whether by purchase or by inheritance, may claim pre-emption. But it does not mean that pre-emption may be claimed by a contiguous land-holder when the land has been transferred to a co- sharer by purchase. The appellants need not have joined the pre-emptor-respondent, because to join in the application for pre-emption filed by a contiguous land-holder is unnecessary.

<u>5. The learned Single Judge has relied upon the case of Yakub Ali Mondal V Akher Ali Mondal 6 DLR 130 in which it was held that transfer to a co-sharer by purchase is pre-emptible. This proposition is not disputed; secondly, that case was decided under section 26F of the Bengal Tenancy Act which limited pre-emption to co-sharers only, either by pure chase or by inheritance; it did not extend the right of pre-emption to a tenant having land contiguous to the land transferred. As such the decision relied upon is of no assistance to the instant case where the claim of a contiguous land-holder is involved. The contiguous land-holder comes to the picture only when the co-sharer-tenants neither purchased the land nor claimed it by way of pre-emption but the land is sold to a stranger. Had, in the instant case, pre-emption been sought by a co-sharer by purchase, it would have been incumbent up on the co-sharer-transferee to apply to join in the application for ratable pre-emption. Reading section 96 as a whole it is found that if a land has been transferred to a co sharer and when no other co-sharer has claimed pre-emption, the transfer is immune, by necessary implication, to a pre-emption, by a contiguous land-holder. The question raised is found to have been correctly answered by the learned Munsif.</u>

6. In the result, the appeal is allowed, the impugned order of the High Court Division is set aside and that of the trial court is restored.

No order as to costs.

End.

case_source: (From the judgment and order dated 15th of March, 2010 passed by the High Court Division in First Appeal No.161 of 2006)
full_judgment:
Muhammad Imman Ali J. This civil appeal, by leave, is directed against the judgment and order dated 15.03.2010 passed by a Division Bench of the High Court Division in First Appeal No.161 of 2006 allowing the appeal.

2. The facts of the case, in short, are that respondent No. 1 as the plaintiff instituted Other Class Suit No. 3 of 2004 in the First Court of Joint District Judge, Mymensingh impleading the appellant and others as the defendants for declaration of his title to the land detailed in the second schedule to the plaint and for further declaration that the notice dated 24.12.2001 issued  by Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh (defendant No.1) in respect of the land detailed in the second schedule was void, illegal, collusive, without jurisdiction and not binding upon the plaintiff. The plaintiff stated, inter alia, that the suit land belonged to S.M. Rahmatullah and during Liberation War of 1971, he deserted the property and as such, the same was declared abandoned property under President's Order 16 of 1972. The suit property was included in the 'Ka' list of the abandoned properties prepared on 23.09.1986. The present appellant filed an application under Ordinance No. 54 of 1985 before the Court of Settlement for exclusion of the property from the abandoned properties list and the said application was registered as Case No. 1019 of 1992 before the Court of Settlement and the case was heard by the Court of Settlement, but the respondent-Government did not disclose the fact that the father of the applicant by practicing fraud made a claim that he got the property by way of auction purchase. Thereafter, the appellant on 10.12.1998 obtained an order from the Court of Settlement for excluding the property from the abandoned list. The appellant thereafter moved the High Court Division by filing writ petition for a direction upon the respondent-Government to restore the vacant possession of the suit property in his favour and obtained Rule Nisi in Writ Petition No. 5021 of 1999. The High Court Division by judgment and order dated 04.03.2001 made the Rule Nisi absolute and directed the respondent-Government to hand over the vacant possession of the suit property to the appellant. Pursuant to the said judgment and order, the Government on 24.12.2001 directed the plaintiff respondent to hand over possession of the suit property within 7 days from the date of receipt of the said notice. Subsequently, the plaintiff-respondent herein was evicted from the suit property.

3. The plaintiff-respondent stated that the Government took decision to dispose of abandoned properties and accordingly, the plaintiff applied for purchasing the suit property, and the appellant did not take any step to resist the sale of the suit property and the Government transferred the suit property to the plaintiff by a registered deed of sale dated 08.11.1990 for a consideration of Tk.1,01,091.00. Thereafter, the plaintiff took loan from respondent No. 5, National Bank Limited and constructed a semi pucca structure on the suit land by spending about taka 20 Lac. The respondent-plaintiff on going through abandoned property list and records of the Court of Settlement discovered that by judgment and order dated 10.12.1998 it released the suit property from the abandoned properties list. In Writ Petition No. 5021 of 1999, the High Court Division passed a direction upon the respondent-Government to hand over vacant possession of the suit property in favour of the appellant. The Deputy Commissioner, Mymensingh thereafter, on 24.12.2001 issued a notice upon the plaintiff directing him to hand over vacant possession and on receipt of the notice of eviction the plain-tiff preferred Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 226 of 2002 before this Division against the judgment and order dated 04.03.2001 passed in Writ Petition No. 5021 of 1999. The Government also preferred Civil Petition for leave to Appeal No. 2186 of 2001 before this Division against the said judgment and order dated 04.03.2001. In addition the plaintiff-respondent filed Writ Petition No. 3817 of 2002 challenging the decision of the Court of Settlement in Case No. 1019 of 1992 which had declared the suit property as not abandoned. The Rule issued in the said writ petition was discharged on contest on 14.06.2003, against which the plaintiff filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 963 of 2003 before this Division. By its judgment and order dated 27.08.2003 this Division dismissed both the petitions. The Government, was made party in the case before the Court of Settlement as well as in the writ petition filed by the petitioner and the Government had taken all necessary steps in support of the plaintiff’s case, but the Court found that the property was not abandoned property and accordingly, released the same in favour of the appellant.

4. The appellant herein, as defendant in the suit claimed that after disposal of the plaintiffs leave petitions by this Division, the plaintiff-respondent lost all sorts of claim over the suit property and the present suit was barred by the aforesaid judgment and, as such, the plaint was liable to be rejected.

5. The plaintiff-respondent filed written objection against the application for rejection of the plaint, stating that, the suit property was released illegally by the Court of Settlement in favour of appellant as he obtained the said order on the basis of some false and forged documents and that the Appellate Division did not dispose of the leave petitions on merit. The plain-tiff further stated that the points which have been raised in the present suit were not decided in the writ petitions filed by the appellant and the respondents.

6. The trial Court by its judgment and decree dated 23.4.2006 allowed the application and rejected the plaint of Other Class Suit No. 3 of 2004.

7. Being aggrieved, the plaintiff preferred First Appeal No. 161 of 2006 before the High Court Division and upon hearing the parties the High Court Division by its judgment and order dated 15.03.2010 allowed the appeal.

8. Feeling aggrieved by and dissatisfied with the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division, the appellant as petitioner filed civil petition for leave to appeal No. 09 of 2011.

9. Leave was granted on the following submissions of the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner:

"That the transferee (Plaintiff) from the Government had purchased the suit property during the pendency of the claim by the petitioner before the Court of Settlement and the judgment and order passed by the Court of Settlement having been upheld up to the Appellate Division, the transferee would rise and fall with the Government and as such, he has no cause of action to bring the suit. She further submits that the Government has no right to transfer the suit property as the Court of Settlement had deter-mined the character of the suit property to be not an abandoned property.

10. Mr. M.I. Faruqui, learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the appellant made submissions in line with the grounds upon which leave was granted. He further submitted that the plaintiff is seeking a declaration of title of property which has already been adjudicated up to this Division and hence the trial Court rightly rejected the plaint. He submitted that the High Court Division fell into error in finding that there were issues which would be raised in the present suit that had not been decided by the Court of Settlement or by the High Court Division in the writ petition. He submitted that the only issue in the suit is the plaintiff’s title which he got by way of purchase of the property from the Government. But this issue is already decided inasmuch as the Government had no title in the property because it had been decided up to this Division that the property was not abandoned and, hence, the Government had no title to sell.

11. Mr. Mahbub Ali, learned Senior Advocate appearing for the respondent submitted that that neither the Court of Settlement nor the High Court Division sitting in its writ jurisdiction can decide/ adjudicate the disputed question of facts as have been raised by the plaintiff therefore, the Civil Court is the only forum to redress grievances of the plaintiff as such, the appeal is liable to be dismissed. He further submitted that since, the case before the Court of Settlement was not filed within the stipulated period of limitation nor the original judgment of the Court of Settlement was found in the record therefore, judicial record was tampered with and fraud was practiced upon the Court of Settlement in having the property excluded from 'Ka' list and as such, without holding inquiry and trial and without thrashing out the allegations in the plaint it cannot be rejected. He further submitted that neither the High Court Division nor the Appellate Division decided the issues raised in the plaint on merit and the jurisdiction of the Civil Court is still open to thrash out the allegations. He submitted that the principles of res-judicata in writ matters, where decisions are made in a summary proceedings mostly on affidavits, it should not be applied with the same strictness as in disputes in suits or proceedings determined in Civil Courts. He submitted that since, the defendant-appellant obtained the judgment from the Court of Settlement suppressing the fact of the title and possession of the plaintiff in the suit property and willfully and deliberately did not make the plaintiff a party in the proceedings nor the Government disclosed the fact of selling the property to the plaintiff by registered deed dated 08.11.1990 and delivered possession to him therefore, in any way the judgment of the Court of Settlement was not binding upon the respondents. He submitted that Government action in contesting the writ petition as well as filing of Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2186 of 2001 feeling aggrieved only to the extent of imposing penalty at the rate of 20% interest on the rent in no way can be said to have been decided the matter finally rather, the conduct of the Government as well as the appellant in contesting the proceedings is clearly collusive one which are liable to be adjudicated in the Civil Court.

12. We have considered the submissions of the learned Advocates for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgment and order of the High Court Division and other connected papers on record.

<u>13. The property in question was listed as an abandoned property in the Gazette (Extra Ordinary) dated 23.9.1986 at page 9762 (70) Sl. No.9 in the 'Ka' list. Javed Alam son of the original owner, namely S.M. Rahmatullah (deceased) filed a case before the First Court of Settlement on 08.01.1987 for releasing the property from the list of abandoned properties. The case was subsequently transferred to the Second Court of Settlement and numbered as Settlement Case No.1019 of 1992. In due course after hearing, the abandoned property case was decided in favour of Md. Javed Alam by order dated 10.12.1998. Due to the inaction of the concerned authority in releasing the property and handing over possession to him, Md. Javed Alam filed Writ Petition No. 5021 of 1999. The Rule Nisi obtained by the writ petitioner was made absolute by judgment and order dated 04.03.2001 by which the Government of Bangladesh-respondent No. 3 was directed to comply with the judgment and order dated 10.12.1998 passed in Settlement Case No. 1019 of 1992 by evicting the unauthorised occupants and also to pay rent to the owner of the property with a direction to pay interest at 20% of the rent actually received by the Government in respect of the property in question from the date of unauthorised occupation till the date of restoration of possession thereof.</u>

14. The Government respondent, by filing Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2186 of 2001, did not challenge the legality of the decision of the Court of Settlement which had found that the property was not abandoned, but challenged the direction of the High Court Division to pay interest at 20% on the rent actually received by the Government from the date of unauthorised occupation till the date of restoration of possession. This Division disposed of the said civil petition maintaining the judgment of the High Court Division except the part wherein direction had been given to the Government to pay interest @ 20% per annum on the rent actually received from the date of unauthorised occupation till the date of restoration of possession, which was deleted. However, it was made clear that "the rent actually received by the Government from the date of unauthorized occupation till the date of restoration of possession should be paid to the respondent. The other part of the judgment i.e. making direction to restore vacant possession of the property in question to the respondent is maintained."

15. Thereafter, the Government released the property in question from the "Ka" list of the abandoned properties list by Gazette dated 02.12.2004.

16. It appears from the records that the present respondent A.F. Alfajuddin Ahmed filed Writ Petition No. 3817 of 2002 challenging the decision of the Court of Settlement dated 10.12.1998 passed in Settlement Case No. 1019 of 1992 claiming that he having been put into possession of the property in question by the Government was given the option to purchase the property, which he did by registered deed of sale dated 18.11.1990 and that all of a sudden he received notice dated 24.11.2001 directing him to hand over vacant possession of the property to Md. Javed Alam.

17. In due course after hearing the parties the Rule was discharged by reference to the judgment and order of this Division in Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 2186 of 2001 where it was held:

18. "The other part of the judgment, i.e. in making direction to restore vacant possession of the property in question to the respondents is maintained." The High Court Division also observed that it can-not interfere with the decision of the Court of Settlement passed in Settlement Case No. 1019 of 1992 since civil petition for leave to appeals filed by the writ-petitioner is pending before the Appellate Division.

19. We find from the records that Writ respondent A.F. Alfajuddin Ahmed had filed Civil Petition for Leave to Appeal No. 226 of 2002 and No. 963 of 2003 challenging the judgment and order dated 04.03.2001 and 14.06.2003 passed by the High Court Division in writ petition Nos. 5021 of 1999 and 3817 of 2002. By order dated 27.08.2003 both leave petitions were dismissed.

20. From the above facts and circumstances it transpires that the decision of the Court of Settlement in Settlement Case No. 1019 of 1992 was challenged both by the present respondent No.1, A.F. Alfajuddin Ahmed as well as by the Government and the challenges have been unsuccessful up to this Division and subsequently the property was released by the Government vide gazette notification dated 02.12.2004.

<u>21. It must be borne in mind that the claim of the writ respondent No.1 depends entirely on the success of the claim put forward by the Government with respect to the abandoned character of the property in question. We find from the records that the Court of Settlement, being competent to decide the matter of the abandoned character of the property, after due consideration of all evidence and facts presented in the case decided that the property in question was not abandoned. The Government was the competent party to challenge that decision. Any occupier of the property as tenant under the Government, within the scheme authorising the Government to manage the said property, has no locus standi to challenge the decision of the Court of Settlement. If the Government succeeds in establishing that the property was lawfully included in the list of abandoned properties, then only the question of transferring the property to the occupier will become relevant.</u>

<u>22. The effect of the decision of the Court of Settlement that the property was not abandoned is that the inclusion of the abandoned and, therefore, the Government had no authority to transfer the property. It is curious that the Government did not mention the sale of the property at any point in time during the proceedings before the Court of Settlement or indeed when the matter was pending before the High Court Division. When the Government came before this Division, only the direction of the High Court Division with regard to interest to be paid on the rental amount was challenged. In our view the decision of the Government to release the property from the "Ka" list of abandoned properties by Gazette dated 02.12.2004 has put a final seal on the matter. The abandoned character of the property having been established all the way to this Division and the challenges of the Government as well as the present respondent having been unsuccessful, there can be no doubt about the legality of the gazette notification dated 02.12.2004 and hence we find that the trial Court rightly rejected the plaint of writ-respondent No.1 under Order VII, Rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure.</u>

23. In view of the above discussion, we find that the judgment and order of the High Court Division is not in accordance with law and accordingly the impugned judgment and order is set aside and the judgment and decree date 24.03.2006 passed by the learned Joint District Judge, First Court, Mymensingh in Other Class Suit No. 03 of 2004 is upheld.

24. In the result the appeal is allowed, without however, any order as to costs.

End.

caseno: CIVIL PETITION FOR LEAVE TO APPEAL NO. 1710 OF 2011
lawyer:
A.J. Mohammad Ali, Advocate, instructed by Zainul Abedin, Advocate-on-Record ---------  For the Petitioner

case_source: (From the order dated the 6th of June, 2011 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 140 of 2008).
full_judgment:
MUHAMMAD IMMAN ALI, J :-This civil petition for leave to appeal is directed against the judgement and orders dated 06.06.2011 passed by the High Court Division in First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 140 of 2008 allowing the appeal thereby setting aside the order passed by the Additional District Judge, Third Court, Dhaka dismissing the Miscellaneous Case Nos. 110 of 1980 and 50 of 1966 by a single judgement.

02. Facts, relevant for disposal of the civil petition for leave to appeal are that 36 acre of land of Khatian No. 16 was recorded in the name of Ahmed Ali Dewan, Ismail Dewan, Abdul Dewan and Harmus Dewan as Charagi subtenant (চেরাগী মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী) I And 1.20 acres land of C.S. Khatian No. 21 was also recorded in the names of above mentioned as sub-tenant under the চেরাগী পীরসূত্রে মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী। With the above claim the respondent Ahmed Ali and other filed Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 and Kutub Uddin Dewan filed Miscellaneous Case no. 50 of 1996. The respondents had previously partitioned the said property vide Title Suit No. 981 of 1933 and obtained preliminary decree on 23.4.1934 which was made final on 21.2.1935 and their names were recorded in the S.A. Khatian accordingly. The possessive interest was shown as "Cheragi" in one khatian and "occupier as mutwalli" in another. Later on in R.S. Khatian No. 74, out of 1.20 acres of homestead land. 08 acre was recorded as mosque and the remaining 1.12 acres was recorded as the homestead of the petitioners. The land of C.S. Khatian No. 16 was recorded in the name of the petitioners under R.S. Khatian No. 167.

03. In spite of the above, one Fariz Uddin Miah filed a petition being No. 49/76 before the Waqf Administrator for enlisting 1.20 acres of the property within Khatian No. 21 as waqf property. The said petition was rejected declaring only. 08 acre of the property as waqf property and the remaining 1.12 acres as under personal ownership. Against the said order Fariz Uddin filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 352/76 before the District Judge, Dhaka, which was disposed of by order dated 30.10.1976. Against that order Osman Gani Dewan filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 21 of 1976 before the High Court Division, Which remanded the matter to the Wakf Administrator by order dated 22.8.1976. Thereafter, the Waqf Administrator included the whole property, i.e. 1.20 acres of land of khatian No. 21 as waqf property. Against that order Ahmed Ali Dewan filed Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 which was dis-missed on 20.08.1984 for want of tadbir. Against that order Ahmed Ali Dewan and others filed First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 183 of 1984 before the High Court Division which remanded the aforementioned Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 for disposal in accordance with law after taking evidence.

04. A huge number of cases, counter cases and appeals have been filed by various parties, the up-shot of which is as to whether the land, save and except the 08 acre containing Mosque, Graveyard and Mazar, has the character of wakq property or not, or whether the remaining 1.12 acres of land is secular property of the Dewan family. The Waqf Administrator declared the whole property as waqf property, against which Kutub Uddin Dewan filed Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 of 1985 before the District Judge, Narayangonj. By judgement and order dated 16.11.1989 the appeal was allowed declaring. 13 acre of land of plot No. 16 under Khatian No. 21 as waqf property and the reaming property as secular land of Dewan family. Against the Said judgement Miscellaneous Appeal No. 145 of 1999 was filed before the High Court Division.

05. The High Court Division in order to avoid conflicting decision, directed Miscellaneous Case No. 110 of 1980 and Miscellaneous Appeal No. 53 of 1985 which were re-numbered as Miscellaneous Appeal No. 50 of 1996, to be disposed of together.

06. Presently, the respondents claim that the suit land is 1.20 acres of land of dag No. 16 under Khatian No. 21 of Kutubpur Mouza and 36 acre of land of dag Nos. 142/143 of Khatian No. 16 in total 1.56 acres of land. The suit land originally belonged to Syed Kha and under him Ayesha Akter was in possession. The land of C.S. Khatian No. 21 was possessed by Ahmed Ali Dewan as Mutwalli as "Cheragi Madhasattadhikari". In this way Ahmed Ali Dewan and others also possessed the land of C.S. Khatian No. 16 Out of Dewan family, Ahmed Ali Dewan in 1955 created Wakf of 1.56 acres of land of aforesaid khatian and that was entered in E.C. No. 3083. In the Wakf property there is Mosque, Mazar, open space as field and homestead. On the other hand the petitioner claims that excepting. 08 acre of land, the remaining land is self acquired secular land. In the case both the parties examined one witness each and exhibited some documents as Exhibit 1-7 and Ka-Ga. The Wakf Administrator declared the property as Wakf property and the District judge affirmed the said order.

07. Mr. A. J. Mohammad Ali, Learned Senior Advocate appearing on behalf of the petitioner submitted that the High Court Division misdirected itself and erred in declaring 1.12 acres out of 1.20 acres of the suit property to be secular property of the Dewan Family and treating only. 08 acre as wakf property. The learned Advocate also submitted that the suit land is described in the record of rights as Cheragi Pir Suter Madhyasattadhikari (চেরাগী মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী) which manifestly demonstrates that it is a rent free grant for the purpose of defraying expenses of lighting lamps in the Mosque, Mazar and Dorga and as such the High Court Division was in error in holding that the property was being enjoyed as secular property. He further submitted that in Miscellaneous EC. No. 49 of 1976 (EC 3083) the Administrator of Waqf by order dated 24.5.1980 after detailed discussion of all the facts and circumstances and taking into account the meaning of the words Cheragi Madhyasattadhikari Chirosthai "(চেরাগী মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী)" and Cheragi Pir Dayal Mutwalli Sutre Madhyasattadhikari Chirosthai "(চেরাগী পীর দয়াল মোতওয়ালী সূত্রে মধ্যস্বত্তাধিকারী চিরস্থায়ী)" came to positive decision that the properties of two khatins are waqf by user and took the view that the entire property of C.S. Khatian Nos. 21 and 16 was Waqf property and that the enrollment of the property to EC case No. 3083 was valid and legal.

08. Mr. Awlad Ali, learned Senior Advocate appearing for respondent No. 1 made submissions in support of the impugned judgement and order of the High Court Division.

09. We have considered the submissions of the learned advocates appearing for the parties concerned, perused the impugned judgement and decree as well as other materials on record.

10. The crux of the cases relate to the character of the suit property namely 1.20 acres of plot No. 16 of Khatian No. 21. The High Court Division considered the fact that the district Judge considered the properties as waqf property because 18 persons failed affidavit supporting the property to be waqf property. And since the waqf administrator was not a party in Title suit No. 981 of 1933 that decision was not binding upon him. However, the High Court Division observed that the property was declared as waqf by custom and there was no deed made for the dedication. In such view of the matter, the High Court Division decided that only 0.8 acre of the suit land on which the mosque and mazar was situated was waqf property and the remaining property was secular property.

11. The High Court Division observed that the finding arrived at by the learned Munsif in Title suit No. 981 of 1933 has not been set aside by the competent Court and as such the nature and character of the suit property has been declared as secular property and still stands as such and hence the Waqf Administrator acted illegally in declaring the same as waqf property.

<u>12. We are of the view that unless any property is specifically designated as waqf property by the waqif in the deed of waqf any property cannot be declared as waqf property simply because it is occupied and used by the persons managing any waqf property, Certainly, the property in question was meant for the use and benefit of those persons who were entrusted with the looking after of the mosque. But that does not mean that the whole property takes the character of being waqf property. Unless the whole of the property is specifically declared as waqf property only that portion of it that is used for mosque or mazar can be treated as waqf. The rest of the property used by the mutwalli or those who serve the mazar of mosque, is not ipos facto waqf property.</u>

13. We find from the judgement of the appellate Court that the judgement and decree of Title Suit No. 981 of 1993 was considered but held to be not binding upon the Waqf Administrator since he was not made a party in that suit. The appellate Court went on to observe that the papers on record indicated that a mutwalli was appointed to maintain the mosque and other religious structures and, therefore, the property was accepted as waqf property.

<u>14. However, as noted above, we are of the view that only the property which is specifically used for any religious purpose, namely Mosque and Mazar, may be automatically classified as waqf property. The remaining property, unless otherwise designated by the waqif as part of the waqf property, will not be waqf property only on the ground that the mutwalli and or his family members utilize the same.</u>

15. In view of the above discussion, we do not find any infirmity or illegality in the impugned judgement and order.

16. Accordingly, the civil petition for leave to appeal is dismissed.

End.

caseno:
First Miscellaneous Appeal No. 38 of 2014
with
Civil Rule No.666 (FM) of 2013.
lawyer:
Serajul Hoque, Advocate ------ For the Appellant.
